I-3.text: I prostrate to all buddhas and bodhisattvas.
I-3.en_text: I bow with respect to all enlightened beings and all those working toward enlightenment to help others.

I-0.text: Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva ^0 0. Introduction
I-0.en_text: Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva (One Who Works to Free All Beings)

I-2.text: In Tibetan: Byang chub sems dpa’i spyod pa la ’jug pa
I-2.en_text: In Tibetan: Byang chub sems dpa'i spyod pa la 'jug pa

1-0.en_text: 1. The Benefits of the Wish to Help All Beings

1-1.text: I prostrate with respect to the sugatas, Who have the dharmakaya, and their offspring, And also to all worthy of veneration. I’ll teach in brief, according to the scriptures, The way to enter the bodhisattva’s vows.
1-1.en_text: I bow with respect to the buddhas, who embody perfect truth, and to their spiritual children, and to all who deserve honor. Following the scriptures, I will briefly teach the way to take up the bodhisattva's commitment to help all beings.

1-2.text: I won’t say anything not said before, Nor have I any skill in poetry. Thus I have not intended this for others— I’ve written it to cultivate my mind.
1-2.en_text: I won't say anything that hasn't been said before, and I have no skill as a poet. So I haven't written this for the sake of others - I've written it to train my own mind.

1-3.text: Meanwhile, this will increase the power of My faith so that I cultivate the virtues. If someone else whose fortune equals mine Should see it, then it may be meaningful.
1-3.en_text: Still, writing it will strengthen my faith and help me grow in goodness for now. And if someone else with a similar outlook happens to see it, then it may be worthwhile for them too.

1-4.text: I’ve gained what is most difficult to get— The leisures and resources to benefit beings. If I do not accomplish good while here, How will I ever come to them again?
1-4.en_text: I have gained something extremely hard to find - the freedom and opportunity to truly benefit others. If I don't make good use of this chance now, how will I ever find it again?

1-5.text: Just as between the clouds on pitch-black nights, Lightning reveals the heavens for an instant, Thoughts of the merits of the world arise For a rare moment through the buddhas’ power.
1-5.en_text: Just as lightning briefly lights up a pitch-black, cloudy night sky, so too, through the buddhas' power, good thoughts about helping the world rarely and briefly arise in people's minds.

1-6.text: Thus virtues are perpetually weak; The powers of misdeeds are terribly dreadful. Besides the wish for perfect enlightenment, What other virtue triumphs over them?
1-6.en_text: This is why goodness is always so weak, while the power of wrongdoing is terribly strong. Apart from the wish to reach full enlightenment for the sake of all, what other kind of goodness can overcome it?

1-7.text: The lords of sages, who have contemplated For many aeons, see just this will help. Immeasurable multitudes of beings Through this will gain the sublime bliss with ease.
1-7.en_text: The great sages, who reflected deeply over countless ages, saw that only this wish truly helps. Through it, countless beings can easily reach the highest happiness.

1-8.text: No one should ever forsake bodhichitta Who wants to dispel beings’ unhappiness, Vanquish the hundreds of miseries of existence, And partake in the many hundreds of joys.
1-8.en_text: No one who wants to end the unhappiness of all beings, overcome the many miseries of existence, and share in life's many joys should ever give up this wish to help everyone.

1-9.text: If they rouse bodhichitta, in an instant The wretched, fettered in samsara’s prison, Are named the offspring of the sugatas And revered in the worlds of gods and humans.
1-9.en_text: The moment this wish arises, even someone trapped and suffering in the endless cycle of rebirth is called a child of the buddhas, and is honored by gods and humans alike.

1-10.text: Just like the greatest kind of alchemy, It takes this unclean body and transforms it Into a priceless jewel, a buddha’s body, So firmly grasp ahold of bodhichitta.
1-10.en_text: Like the finest alchemy, it takes this impure body and turns it into something priceless - the body of a buddha. So hold firmly onto this wish to help all beings.

1-11.text: Examined well by the sole leader of beings With his immeasurable mind, it has great value. So you who wish to leave the places of beings, Firmly grasp hold of precious bodhichitta.
1-11.en_text: The one guide of all beings, with his boundless wisdom, examined it closely and found it of immense worth. So all of you who wish to leave behind the realms of suffering, hold firmly onto this precious wish.

1-12.text: All other virtues, like banana trees, Are spent once they have produced a result. The tree of bodhichitta constantly Bears fruit, thus thriving inexhaustibly.
1-12.en_text: Every other kind of goodness is like a banana tree - it bears fruit once and is then used up. But the tree of this wish to help all beings bears fruit endlessly, growing richer without end.

1-13.text: Like those who in great danger, rely on heroes, Why would the careful not rely on that Which liberates them in a single instant, Even if they have done horrendous wrongs?
1-13.en_text: Just as someone in great danger relies on a hero to save them, why wouldn't a careful person rely on this, which frees them instantly, even from terrible wrongs they've done?

1-14.text: Like the inferno at an age’s end, It burns up great misdeeds in a single instant. The wise protector Maitreya explained Its countless benefits to Sudhana.
1-14.en_text: Like the fire at the end of an age, it burns away great wrongdoing in a single instant. The wise guardian Maitreya explained its countless benefits to the young seeker Sudhana.

1-15.text: To summarize, it’s understood There are two types of bodhichitta: The mind aspiring for awakening And engagement in awakening.
1-15.en_text: In short, this wish comes in two forms: the wish that longs for full awakening, and the wish that actively engages in reaching it.

1-16.text: Just as they know the difference Between the wish to go and going, The wise should understand the contrast Between these two, respectively.
1-16.en_text: Just as one can tell the difference between wanting to go somewhere and actually going there, the wise understand the difference between these two respectively.

1-17.text: Even in samsara, great results Come from aspiring bodhichitta, Though unlike engaged bodhichitta, The merit is not continuous.
1-17.en_text: Even while still caught in the cycle of rebirth, the longing wish brings great results. But unlike the engaged wish, its good effects don't continue without a break.

1-18.text: But from the moment, when for the sake Of freeing beings in infinite realms, You truly take up this intent With irreversible resolve,
1-18.en_text: But from the very moment you truly take up this resolve - firmly, without turning back - in order to free beings across countless realms,

1-19.text: From that time on, the many powers Of merit flow forth unremitting In torrents equal to the sky Even when you’re asleep or careless.
1-19.en_text: from that moment on, endless streams of goodness flow forth without pause, vast as the sky itself, even while you sleep or aren't paying attention.

1-20.text: The Tathagata himself explained This and its reasons for the sake Of beings inclined to the Foundation In the Sutra Requested by Subahu.
1-20.en_text: The Buddha himself explained this, and the reasons for it, for the sake of those inclined toward a more basic path, in the discourse requested by Subahu.

1-21.text: If someone who benevolently Intends to merely eliminate Sharp pains in sentient beings’ heads Possesses immeasurable merit,
1-21.en_text: If someone who simply wishes, out of kindness, to relieve another person's headache holds boundless goodness in doing so,

1-22.text: What need to speak of those who wish To rid all sentient beings of Untold distresses and endow Each one with boundless qualities?
1-22.en_text: what need is there to mention someone who wishes to free every single being from countless troubles, and to give each one boundless good qualities?

1-23.text: Who has such altruism as this? Does even a father or a mother? Or do the gods or else the rishis? Do even Brahmas harbor this?
1-23.en_text: Who else has ever had such caring concern as this? Not even a father or mother. Do the gods have it? Do the great sages? Do even the highest divine beings have it?

1-24.text: If sentient beings themselves have never Had such a wish as this before Even for their own sake in dreams, How could they have it for another?
1-24.en_text: If beings have never had such a wish before, even for their own sake, even in their dreams, how could they possibly have it for the sake of someone else?

1-25.text: The wish to benefit beings that others Have never had for their own sake— This special jewel of mind—is born, A wonder without precedent.
1-25.en_text: This wish to help others - a wish that even they themselves have never held for their own sake - this rare and precious state of mind arises as a wonder never seen before.

1-26.text: The cause of every wanderer’s joy, The cure for beings’ suffering; How could one take the measure of The merit of this precious mind?
1-26.en_text: It is the source of joy for every being, and the cure for their suffering. How could anyone ever measure the goodness of this precious mind?

1-27.text: If merely intending to benefit Is greater than revering the Buddha, What need to speak of striving for The sake of all beings’ happiness?
1-27.en_text: If simply intending to benefit others is greater than honoring the Buddha himself, how much more true is this for someone who actually strives for the happiness of all beings?

1-28.text: They wish to cast off suffering But rush toward suffering itself. They wish for happiness, but deluded, Crush their own pleasure like a foe.
1-28.en_text: Beings want to escape suffering, yet they run straight toward it. They long for happiness, but out of confusion, they destroy their own well-being as if it were an enemy.

1-29.text: For those deprived of happiness Who suffer many miseries, This satisfies with every pleasure And severs every suffering.
1-29.en_text: For those who lack happiness and suffer in so many ways, this wish provides every kind of joy and cuts through every kind of suffering.

1-30.text: It also will dispel delusion. How could there be such good as this? How could there be a friend like this? How could there be such merit as this?
1-30.en_text: It also clears away confusion about how things really are. Could there be any goodness greater than this? Could there be any friend better than this? Could there be any merit greater than this?

1-31.text: If to reciprocate a kind deed Is praiseworthy for a short while, What need to speak of bodhisattvas Who do good unsolicited?
1-31.en_text: If it's praiseworthy to repay a kindness done for you, even briefly, how much more so for the bodhisattvas, who do good for others without even being asked?

1-32.text: People extol as doing something good Those who provide a few with regular meals, Donating scornfully for a short time Plain food that satisfies for half a day.
1-32.en_text: People praise as generous those who give a few people an occasional meal - even grudgingly, and only plain food enough to last half a day.

1-33.text: What need to speak of those who always give To beings of untold number for a long time The sublime happiness of the sugatas, Fulfilling every one of their desires?
1-33.en_text: What need is there to mention those who, for a very long time, constantly give countless beings the sublime happiness of the buddhas, fulfilling every one of their wishes?

1-34.text: Someone who rouses a malicious thought Toward such a patron, offspring of the victors, Will dwell in hell as many aeons as The count of their bad thoughts, the Sage has said.
1-34.en_text: Anyone who has an unkind thought toward such a giver - a child of the buddhas - will, the Buddha said, remain in a hellish state for as many ages as they had bad thoughts.

1-35.text: But the results of someone feeling faith Proliferate in far greater abundance. With bodhisattvas, even grave events Don’t bring misdeeds; good naturally increases.
1-35.en_text: But the good results that come from feeling faith toward them grow far more abundantly. Even in difficult times, being around bodhisattvas doesn't lead to wrongdoing - it naturally produces more goodness.

1-36.text: I prostrate to the bodies of those in whom This jewel, the sublime attitude, is born. Even harming them will lead to happiness. I go for refuge to the wellsprings of joy.
1-36.en_text: I bow to the very bodies of those in whom this precious attitude has been born. Even harming them somehow leads toward happiness. I go for protection and guidance to these wellsprings of joy.

2-0.text: The first chapter, “Explaining the Benefits of Bodhichitta,” from Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva. ^1-a 2. Confessing Misdeeds
2-0.en_text: The first chapter, "The Benefits of the Wish to Help All Beings," from Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva. 2. Admitting My Wrongdoings

2-1.text: In order to grasp that precious attitude, I make fine offerings to the tathagatas, To the true dharma, the immaculate jewel, And to the oceans of qualities, bodhisattvas.
2-1.en_text: In order to hold onto that precious wish to help everyone, I make the finest offerings to the buddhas, to the true teachings - that flawless jewel - and to the bodhisattvas, whose good qualities are as vast as oceans.

2-2.text: As many fruits and flowers as there are, Whatever kinds of medicine exist, However many jewels there are in the world, All clean and pleasant waters there may be,
2-2.en_text: Whatever fruits and flowers there are, whatever kinds of medicine exist, however many jewels there are in the world, and all the clean, pleasant waters there may be,

2-3.text: Mountains of jewels and likewise forest groves In solitary and delightful places, Bushes adorned with ornamental flowers, And trees whose branches bow with splendid fruit,
2-3.en_text: mountains of jewels, peaceful forest groves in solitary and delightful places, bushes decorated with beautiful flowers, and trees whose branches bend low with wonderful fruit,

2-4.text: Incense and perfumes as from divine worlds And so forth, wish-fulfilling trees, jewel trees, And crops that grow without need to be plowed, All ornaments that are fit to be offered,
2-4.en_text: incense and perfumes like those from the heavenly realms, and wish-fulfilling trees, jeweled trees, and crops that grow without needing to be planted - all ornaments fit to be offered,

2-5.text: And lakes and pools bedecked with lotuses, Where lovely swans have most delightful calls— Everything that’s unowned extending to The edges of the realms of infinite space—
2-5.en_text: lakes and pools covered with lotus flowers, where lovely swans call out sweetly - everything unclaimed by anyone, all the way to the edges of infinite space -

2-6.text: I imagine taking these and offer them well To the sages, greatest of beings, and their offspring, Sublime and greatly compassionate recipients. Think of me lovingly; accept these from me.
2-6.en_text: I picture taking all of this and offering it fully to the great sages and their spiritual children, these sublime and deeply compassionate beings. Please think of me kindly and accept these offerings from me.

2-7.text: I am bereft of merit, destitute, And have no other wealth that I could offer. May the protectors, who think of others’ weal, Accept these through their power for my sake.
2-7.en_text: I have no store of goodness, I am truly poor, and I have nothing else of worth to offer. May the guardians, who care for the well-being of others, accept these gifts for my sake through their own power.

2-8.text: Forevermore I offer all my bodies To the victorious ones and to their offspring. O sublime beings, accept me entirely, And I will be your dedicated servant.
2-8.en_text: From now on, I offer my whole body and being to the buddhas and their spiritual children. Sublime beings, please accept me completely - I will be your devoted servant.

2-9.text: Because you have accepted me completely, Not fearing existence, I will benefit beings. I will transcend my previous misdeeds And never do another wrong again.
2-9.en_text: Because you have accepted me completely, I will no longer fear this life, and I will work to benefit all beings. I will rise above my past wrongdoings and never do wrong again.

2-10.text: Within this sweetly fragrant house for bathing, Where the bright and lustrous floors are paved with crystal, Alluring pillars are aglow with jewels, And glistening pearls are draped in canopies,
2-10.en_text: In this sweetly scented bathing house, where the bright, gleaming floor is paved with crystal, where lovely pillars shine with jewels, and glistening pearls hang from the canopy above,

2-11.text: I bathe the sugatas and bodhisattvas From precious vases that have been filled full Of water imbued with many fragrances, Accompanied by song and harmonies.
2-11.en_text: I bathe the buddhas and bodhisattvas, pouring water scented with many fragrances from precious vases, while music and song fill the air.

2-12.text: With cloths that are beyond compare and clean, Infused with a fine scent, I dry their bodies. And then I offer them the finest robes, Well dyed and most delightfully perfumed.
2-12.en_text: With cloths beyond compare, clean and delicately scented, I dry their bodies. Then I offer them the finest robes, beautifully dyed and delightfully perfumed.

2-13.text: I drape Samantabhadra, Lokeshvara, Manjushri, and the other noble beings With fabrics that are delicate and soft And hundreds of the finest ornaments.
2-13.en_text: I drape Samantabhadra, Lokeshvara, Manjushri, and the other noble bodhisattvas in soft, delicate fabrics and hundreds of the finest ornaments.

2-14.text: Like polishing the purest refined gold, I apply the finest scents, whose fragrances Waft everywhere throughout the billion worlds, To the radiant bodies of all sugatas.
2-14.en_text: Like polishing the purest gold, I apply the finest fragrances - scents that spread through billions of worlds - onto the radiant bodies of all the buddhas.

2-15.text: I offer the great beings I venerate, The lords of sages, every fragrant flower— Mandarava, lotus, jasmine, and so forth— And pleasing garlands strung attractively.
2-15.en_text: To these great beings I honor, these foremost sages, I offer every fragrant flower - mandarava blossoms, lotuses, jasmine, and more - along with beautifully arranged garlands.

2-16.text: I also offer billowing clouds of incense Filled with the sweetest, most enchanting scents. And royal feasts I offer them as well, Replete with an assortment of food and drink.
2-16.en_text: I also offer billowing clouds of incense filled with the sweetest, most enchanting scents, along with royal feasts of every kind of food and drink.

2-17.text: Further, I make an offering of jeweled lamps Arranged in rows on golden lotuses. I scatter the petals of attractive flowers On a paved floor anointed with perfume.
2-17.en_text: I offer jeweled lamps arranged in rows atop golden lotuses, and I scatter beautiful flower petals over a floor anointed with perfume.

2-18.text: I offer those who are compassionate Numberless palaces adorning the sky, Beautifully glowing with strings of pearls and jewels And echoing with melodious songs of praise.
2-18.en_text: To these compassionate beings, I offer countless palaces that adorn the sky, glowing beautifully with strings of pearls and jewels, filled with the sound of melodious songs of praise.

2-19.text: I always offer to the lords of sages Beauteous, jeweled parasols with golden staves, Fine shaped, upright, and pleasing to the eye, Their rims festooned with winsome ornaments.
2-19.en_text: I continually offer to the great sages beautiful jeweled parasols with golden handles, finely shaped and pleasing to look at, their edges trimmed with lovely ornaments.

2-20.text: And furthermore, may there extend Clouds of attractive offerings, With lovely tunes and harmonies, That soothe all beings’ sufferings.
2-20.en_text: And may there also arise endless clouds of beautiful offerings, filled with lovely music and harmony, that soothe the suffering of every being.

2-21.text: May rains of gems and flowers and more Continuously shower down On all the jewels of the true dharma As well as on stupas and likenesses.
2-21.en_text: May showers of jewels, flowers, and more fall continuously upon every treasure of the true teachings, as well as upon shrines and sacred images.

2-22.text: As Manjughosha and the rest Make offerings to the victorious ones, I offer to the tathagatas— The protectors—and their offspring.
2-22.en_text: Just as Manjughosha and the other great bodhisattvas made offerings to the buddhas, I too offer these things to the buddhas - the protectors - and their spiritual children.

2-23.text: I extol the oceans of qualities With oceans of melodies of praise. May clouds of hymns in praise of them Arise just so continuously.
2-23.en_text: I praise these beings, whose good qualities are as vast as oceans, with oceans of praise and beautiful words. May clouds of songs praising them arise continuously like this.

2-24.text: I prostrate, bowing as many bodies As there are atoms in all realms, To all the buddhas of the three times, The dharma, and the sublime sangha.
2-24.en_text: I bow down, prostrating with as many bodies as there are specks of dust in the universe, to all the buddhas of past, present, and future, to their teachings, and to the sublime spiritual community.

2-25.text: I prostrate to the sacred sites And stupas of the bodhisattva. I also prostrate to the abbots, The masters, and the supreme adepts.
2-25.en_text: I bow to the sacred places and shrines of the bodhisattva. I also bow to the senior teachers, the masters, and the greatest practitioners.

2-26.text: Until I reach enlightenment’s essence, I go for refuge to the buddhas. I go for refuge to the dharma And sangha of bodhisattvas too.
2-26.en_text: Until I reach the very essence of enlightenment, I turn to the buddhas for guidance and protection. I also turn to their teachings, and to the community of bodhisattvas, for guidance and protection.

2-27.text: To the perfect buddhas and bodhisattvas Who dwell in every direction— To those endowed with great compassion— I join my palms and supplicate:
2-27.en_text: To the perfect buddhas and bodhisattvas who dwell in every direction, filled with great compassion, I join my palms together and make this request:

2-28.text: In this and in my other lives Throughout beginningless samsara, Deluded, I have done misdeeds. I’ve instigated them, and also—
2-28.en_text: In this life and in all my other lives throughout this beginningless cycle of rebirth, confused as I've been, I have done wrong. I have caused others to do wrong, and -

2-29.text: Compelled by ignorant confusion— I have rejoiced in them. I see They were mistakes, and I confess To the protectors from my depths.
2-29.en_text: driven by ignorance and confusion - I have even taken pleasure in wrongdoing. Now I see these were mistakes, and I confess them from the depths of my heart to the guardians.

2-30.text: I have, because of the afflictions, Caused harm with body, speech, and mind To the three jewels and to my parents And to the gurus, among others.
2-30.en_text: Because of my inner afflictions - my anger, greed, and confusion - I have caused harm through my body, speech, and mind to the Three Jewels, to my parents, to my teachers, and to others.

2-31.text: I, who am wicked and am stained By numerous failings, have committed Misdeeds that are most terrible. Before the guides, I confess them all.
2-31.en_text: I, who am flawed and stained by so many failings, have committed terrible wrongs. Before these guides, I confess all of them.

2-32.text: I am going to perish quickly, Before I’m cleansed of my misdeeds. How can I be rescued from them? I beg you, please deliver me.
2-32.en_text: I may die quickly, before I've cleansed myself of these wrongs. How can I be freed from them? I beg you, please save me.

2-33.text: The Lord of Death, untrustworthy, Won’t tarry for what’s done or undone. So no one, whether or not they’re ill, Should place their trust in fleeting life.
2-33.en_text: Death is untrustworthy - it won't wait for things to be finished or unfinished. So no one, whether healthy or sick, should place their trust in this fleeting life.

2-34.text: I must leave all behind and go, But I have not yet recognized that. For the sake of those I like or dislike, I have done various misdeeds.
2-34.en_text: I must leave everything behind and go, yet I still haven't truly understood this. For the sake of those I like or dislike, I have done all kinds of wrong.

2-35.text: Those I don’t like will cease to be, And those I like will cease to be. I myself will cease to be, And everyone will cease to be.
2-35.en_text: Those I dislike will cease to exist. Those I love will cease to exist. I myself will cease to exist. Everyone, in the end, will cease to exist.

2-36.text: All of the things that I have used Will become objects of memory, As if experienced in a dream. I’ll never see what’s past again.
2-36.en_text: Everything I have ever experienced will become nothing but a memory, like something recalled from a dream. I will never again see what has already passed.

2-37.text: Even during this life, many of those I like and dislike have passed away. And yet the terrible misdeeds I’ve done for their sake remain before me.
2-37.en_text: Even in this one lifetime, many people I've loved or disliked have already passed away. Yet the terrible wrongs I did for their sake still remain with me.

2-38.text: Because I have not recognized That I, as well, am ephemeral, I have committed many wrongs Out of delusion, greed, and hatred.
2-38.en_text: Because I failed to recognize that I too am impermanent, I have done many wrongs out of confusion, greed, and hatred.

2-39.text: Not pausing even a day or night, This life’s continuously depleted, And there is no extending it. So why would one like me not die?
2-39.en_text: Without pausing even a single day or night, this life is constantly running out, with no way to add more time to it. So why wouldn't someone like me eventually die?

2-40.text: While I am lying in my bed Surrounded by all my relatives, I will experience alone The feeling of my life being cut.
2-40.en_text: While I lie in my bed, surrounded by all my family, I alone will feel the sensation of my life being cut off.

2-41.text: When seized by Yama’s messengers, What good are friends? What good are kin? Merit alone will guard me then, But I, alas, haven’t practiced that.
2-41.en_text: When death's messengers come to seize me, what good will friends do? What good will family do? Only goodness I have built up can protect me then - and sadly, I haven't built up much.

2-42.text: Protectors, I have carelessly Committed numerous misdeeds For the sake of this ephemeral life, Oblivious there is such a danger.
2-42.en_text: Guardians, I have carelessly committed countless wrongs for the sake of this brief, passing life, never realizing such danger existed.

2-43.text: If people who are being led To have their limbs chopped off today Look different than they did before With their parched mouths and bloodshot eyes,
2-43.en_text: If people being led away today to have their limbs cut off already look different - mouths parched, eyes bloodshot with fear -

2-44.text: What need to say how wretched I’ll be When Yama’s henchmen have me seized, Their physiognomies dire and dread, And I am gripped by terrible pain?
2-44.en_text: how much more wretched will I be when death's agents seize me, their faces terrifying, and I am gripped by unbearable pain?

2-45.text: “Who will protect me truly from This horrifying danger,” I’ll cry, Eyes bulging with terror, as I search In the four directions for a refuge.
2-45.en_text: "Who will truly protect me from this terrifying danger?" I will cry out, eyes wide with fear, searching in every direction for somewhere safe.

2-46.text: But seeing no protection in The four directions, I’ll then despair. If there’s no refuge in that place, What will I do at such a time?
2-46.en_text: But finding no protection anywhere, I will fall into despair. If there is no safety to be found there, what will I do at such a moment?

2-47.text: Thus from today, I’ll go for refuge To the victors, guardians of beings, Who strive to protect all wanderers, Those with great power who dispel all fear.
2-47.en_text: So from today onward, I turn for refuge to the buddhas, the guardians of all beings, who work to protect every wandering being, who have great power to dispel all fear.

2-48.text: Likewise I truly go for refuge To the dharma they have realized, which Dispels the terrors of samsara, And to the sangha of bodhisattvas.
2-48.en_text: In the same way, I truly turn for refuge to the truth they have realized, which dispels the terrors of endless rebirth, and to the community of bodhisattvas.

2-49.text: Petrified with dread, I give Myself over to Samantabhadra. I also make an offering To Manjughosha of my body.
2-49.en_text: Terrified, I give myself completely into the care of Samantabhadra. I also offer my own body to Manjughosha.

2-50.text: I cry a miserable wail To guardian Avalokiteshvara, Whose acts of mercy are unmistaken. I beg, protect me who have done wrong.
2-50.en_text: I cry out in distress to the guardian Avalokiteshvara, whose acts of compassion never fail. I beg: please protect me, who have done such wrong.

2-51.text: To noble Akashagarbha and To Kshitigarbha, to every one Of the protectors with great compassion, I cry from my heart in search of refuge.
2-51.en_text: To noble Akashagarbha, to Kshitigarbha, and to every one of these deeply compassionate guardians, I cry out from my heart in search of protection.

2-52.text: I go for refuge to Vajrapani, Upon the sight of whom, from fear, Malevolent beings like the henchmen Of Yama flee in the four directions.
2-52.en_text: I turn for refuge to Vajrapani, at the very sight of whom harmful beings - like death's own agents - flee in every direction out of fear.

2-53.text: I have in the past transgressed your word, But now that I’ve seen the great peril, I go to you for refuge and plead: Swiftly eliminate this fear.
2-53.en_text: In the past I have gone against your guidance, but now that I see the great danger clearly, I turn to you for refuge and plead: quickly remove this fear from me.

2-54.text: If one must do as doctors say From fear of ordinary illness, What need to speak of being infected Continually by the sickness of The hundred wrongs of lust and such?
2-54.en_text: If people must follow a doctor's advice out of fear of an ordinary illness, how much more so when constantly infected by the hundred illnesses of craving and the like?

2-55.text: If even one of these can ruin All people who live in Jambudvipa And no other medicine to cure it Can be obtained in any direction,
2-55.en_text: If even one of these afflictions could destroy everyone in the world, and no other medicine to cure it could be found anywhere,

2-56.text: To think that I might not do as Directed by the omniscient healer Who removes every pain would be Blameworthy and completely deluded.
2-56.en_text: then it would be foolish and deeply confused to ignore the guidance of the all-knowing healer who can remove every one of these afflictions.

2-57.text: If I must be quite careful of A minor, ordinary chasm, What need to mention the abyss Where I’d fall a thousand leagues for long?
2-57.en_text: If I must be careful even around a small, ordinary cliff edge, how much more careful should I be around the endless fall of a thousand miles that awaits me?

2-58.text: It is not right to sit content And say “I will not die today.” It is inevitable the time Will come when I will cease to be.
2-58.en_text: It isn't right to sit back comfortably and say, "I won't die today." The time when I cease to exist is unavoidable - it will surely come.

2-59.text: Who will grant me freedom from fear? And how will I escape from this? I certainly will no longer be. How can my mind remain at ease?
2-59.en_text: Who will free me from this fear? How will I ever escape it? I will certainly cease to exist one day. How can my mind possibly stay at ease?

2-60.text: My past experiences are gone, And what do I have left of them? But out of my fixation on them, I’ve gone against the gurus’ words.
2-60.en_text: My past experiences are gone, and what do I have left from them now? Yet out of my attachment to them, I have gone against the guidance of my teachers.

2-61.text: If I must leave this life behind Along with family and friends And go off somewhere else alone, What good all those I like or dislike?
2-61.en_text: If I must leave this life behind, along with my family and friends, and go on alone to somewhere else, what good will all those I liked or disliked have done me?

2-62.text: It would be right to only think In just this way all day and night: “Nonvirtue leads to suffering. How can I be freed from it?”
2-62.en_text: It would be right to think, day and night, only this: "Wrongdoing leads to suffering. How can I free myself from it?"

2-63.text: Whatever misdeeds I have done From being ignorant and deluded, Whether they’re naturally unwholesome Or disobedient misdeeds,
2-63.en_text: Whatever wrongs I have done out of ignorance and confusion - whether they were naturally harmful or against my own better judgment -

2-64.text: Within the presence of the protectors, From fear of suffering, I join My palms and prostrate repeatedly, Confessing every one of them.
2-64.en_text: in the presence of the guardians, out of fear of the suffering that follows, I join my palms and bow again and again, confessing every one of them.

2-65.text: I supplicate you, guides! Accept That my misdeeds have been mistaken. They were not good, and for that reason, I’ll never do such acts again.
2-65.en_text: I ask you, guides, to accept that my wrongdoings were mistakes. They were not good, and for that reason, I will never do such things again.

3-0.text: The second chapter, “Confessing Misdeeds,” from Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva. ^2-a 3. Embracing Bodhichitta
3-0.en_text: The second chapter, "Admitting My Wrongdoings," from Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva. 3. Taking Up the Wish to Help All Beings

3-1.text: Delighted, I rejoice in virtue— Respite from the pains Of lower realms—and in those who suffer Dwelling in happiness.
3-1.en_text: With joy, I celebrate the goodness that brings relief from the pain of the lower realms, and the happiness of those who suffer but now dwell in well-being.

3-2.text: I celebrate the virtues gathered That cause enlightenment.
3-2.bo_text:
བྱང་ཆུབ་རྒྱུར་གྱུར་དགེ་བསགས་པ། །
དེ་ལ་རྗེས་སུ་ཡི་རང་ངོ་། །
ལུས་ཅན་འཁོར་བའི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ལས། །
ངེས་པར་ཐར་ལ་ཡི་རང་ངོ་། །
སྐྱོབ་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་བྱང་ཆུབ་དང་། །
རྒྱལ་སྲས་ས་ལའང་ཡི་རང་ངོ་། །
3-2.en_text: I celebrate all the goodness that leads toward enlightenment.

3-3.text: I rejoice in beings’ emancipation From the suffering of samsara, In the protectors’ buddhahood, And the bodhisattvas’ levels.
3-3.en_text: I celebrate beings' freedom from the suffering of endless rebirth, the buddhahood of the guardians, and the bodhisattvas' stages of realization.

3-4.text: I rejoice gladly in the ocean Of bodhichitta that brings All sentient beings to happiness And gives them benefit.
3-4.en_text: I joyfully celebrate the vast, ocean-like wish to help everyone, which brings all beings to happiness and benefits them.

3-5.text: With my palms joined, I implore the buddhas In all directions: Light The lamp of dharma in the gloom Of ignorant beings’ woes!
3-5.en_text: With my palms joined, I ask the buddhas in every direction: please light the lamp of your teachings in the darkness of confused beings' suffering!

3-6.text: Joining my palms, I beseech the victors Who wish to pass to nirvana, Don’t leave these wanderers in blindness— Stay for countless aeons!
3-6.en_text: With my palms joined, I ask the buddhas who wish to pass into final peace: please don't leave these wandering beings in the dark - stay with us for countless ages!

3-7.text: May the virtue I have amassed By doing all of this Eliminate all the suffering Of every sentient being.
3-7.en_text: May the goodness I have gathered by doing all of this remove all the suffering of every single being.

3-8.text: As long as sentient beings are ill, Until their ailments are cured, May I be their medicine, their doctor, And their nurse as well.
3-8.en_text: For as long as beings are sick, until their illnesses are cured, may I be their medicine, their doctor, and their caregiver.

3-9.text: May showers of food and drink relieve The torments of hunger and thirst. In intermediate aeons of famine, May I become food and drink.
3-9.en_text: May showers of food and drink relieve the pain of hunger and thirst. In times of terrible famine, may I myself become food and drink for those in need.

3-10.text: May I be an inexhaustible treasure For poor and deprived beings And stay nearby them as the various Things they need and want.
3-10.en_text: May I be an endless treasure for those who are poor and lacking, and may I remain close by them as whatever they need and want.

3-11.text: To benefit all sentient beings, I give without hesitation My body, my belongings, and All virtues of the three times.
3-11.en_text: To benefit all beings, I give without hesitation my body, my possessions, and all the goodness I have built up, past, present, and future.

3-12.text: Nirvana’s relinquishing everything. My wish is to gain nirvana. At some point, all must be relinquished— It’s best to give it to beings.
3-12.en_text: Final peace means letting go of everything, and that is what I wish to attain. Since everything must be given up eventually, it is best to give it all to benefit others now.

3-13.text: As I have given living beings This body for their pleasure, May they always do with it as they like— Let them kill, revile, or beat it.
3-13.en_text: Just as I have given this body to living beings for their use, may they always do with it as they wish - even if they choose to harm it, insult it, or strike it.

3-14.text: They may make my body a cause for sport, Or jest or snickering, But I have given them my body. Why bother holding it dear?
3-14.en_text: Even if they treat my body as a joke, mock it, or laugh at it, I have already given it to them - why would I cling to it now?

3-15.text: So let them do whatever acts Will not bring them any harm. May thinking of me never be Meaningless for any.
3-15.en_text: So let them do whatever they wish with it, so long as it brings them no harm. May thinking of me never be pointless for anyone.

3-16.text: When someone thinks of me and has A thought of anger or faith, May that be the cause of what fulfills Their every benefit.
3-16.en_text: Whether someone who thinks of me feels anger or trust, may that response become the very cause that fulfills everything good for them.

3-17.text: May anyone who slanders me, Any others who cause harm, And all who criticize me have The fortune to awaken.
3-17.en_text: May anyone who speaks badly of me, anyone who harms me, and anyone who criticizes me all have the good fortune to reach enlightenment.

3-18.text: May I be a guardian of the defenseless, A leader of travelers, A boat or ship or even a bridge For those who wish to cross,
3-18.en_text: May I be a protector for those with no one to defend them, a guide for travelers, and a boat, a ship, or a bridge for those who need to cross over.

3-19.text: The land for those who seek the land, A bed for those without. For all those beings who want a servant, May I become their slave.
3-19.en_text: May I be solid ground for those seeking ground, a bed for those without one, and for all beings who need help, may I become their willing servant.

3-20.text: May I be a wish-fulfilling jewel, Fine vase, accomplished mantra, Great medicine, a heaven tree, And bountiful cow for beings.
3-20.en_text: May I be a wish-fulfilling jewel, a vase that grants every need, a powerful remedy, the finest medicine, a tree that grants heavenly wishes, and a bountiful cow that provides for all beings.

3-21.text: Like earth and the other elements, Like space, may I always be The ground, supporting in many ways The lives of sentient beings.
3-21.en_text: Like the earth and the other basic elements, and like open space itself, may I always be the ground that supports the lives of beings in every way.

3-22.text: Likewise in all ways for all beings Out to the edges of space, May I be, till all pass to nirvana, What gives them sustenance.
3-22.en_text: In this same way, for all beings without exception, to the very edges of space, may I be their source of support and sustenance until every one of them reaches final peace.

3-23.text: Just as the sugatas of the past Aroused the mind of bodhichitta, Just as they followed step-by-step The training of the bodhisattvas,
3-23.en_text: Just as the buddhas of the past first gave rise to the wish to help all beings, and just as they trained step by step in the bodhisattva path,

3-24.text: So, too, shall I, to benefit wanderers, Arouse the mind of bodhichitta. So, too, shall I follow step-by-step The bodhisattvas’ training.
3-24.en_text: so too will I, for the benefit of all wandering beings, give rise to this same wish to help everyone, and I too will train step by step in the bodhisattva path.

3-25.text: Once the intelligent have thus Embraced sincerely bodhichitta, They take delight in their resolve So that it may continue to grow.
3-25.en_text: Once a wise person has sincerely taken up this wish to help all beings in this way, they take joy in their resolve so that it continues to grow ever stronger.

3-26.text: My life has become fruitful now. I’ve gained this human existence well. Now I’ve been born in the buddhas’ family And have become the buddhas’ child.
3-26.en_text: My life has now become truly worthwhile. I have made good use of this precious human existence. Today I have been born into the family of the buddhas, and I have become their child.

3-27.text: From now on I shall always act In ways that befit my family So as to bring no blemish on This stainless, venerable family.
3-27.en_text: From now on, I will always act in ways that honor this family, so that I never bring shame upon this pure and venerable lineage.

3-28.text: Like a blind man who has discovered A jewel amidst a heap of garbage, Somehow, by a coincidence, Bodhichitta has been born in me.
3-28.en_text: Like a blind man who happens to find a precious jewel buried in a heap of garbage, this wish to help all beings has, by some rare chance, arisen within me.

3-29.text: This is the great elixir that Vanquishes the Lord of Death. It is the inexhaustible treasure Dispelling the poverty of beings.
3-29.en_text: This is the great elixir that overcomes death itself. It is the endless treasure that ends the poverty of every being.

3-30.text: This is the supreme medicine That cures the maladies of the world, A resting tree for beings exhausted From wandering the paths of existence.
3-30.en_text: This is the finest medicine, curing the sicknesses of the world - a resting tree for beings who are worn out from wandering the many paths of existence.

3-31.text: This is the universal bridge That frees all beings from lower realms, The rising moon of mind that soothes The torments of sentient beings’ afflictions.
3-31.en_text: This is the universal bridge that frees all beings from the lower realms, the rising moon of the mind that eases the torment of every being's inner afflictions.

3-32.text: It’s the great sun that brings an end To the darkness of beings’ ignorance. It is the butter that emerges From churning the milk of the true dharma.
3-32.en_text: It is the great sun that dispels the darkness of beings' confusion. It is the purest essence, drawn out like butter churned from the milk of the true teachings.

3-33.text: For travelers roaming on the paths of existence, Desiring to partake of happiness, This sublime blissfulness is close at hand To satisfy the supreme guests, sentient beings.
3-33.en_text: For all travelers wandering the paths of existence, longing to taste happiness, this sublime joy stands close at hand, ready to satisfy every one of these honored guests - all sentient beings.

4-0.text: The third chapter, “Embracing Bodhichitta,” from Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva. ^3-a 4. Teachings on Carefulness
4-0.en_text: The third chapter, "Taking Up the Wish to Help All Beings," from Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva. 4. Teachings on Carefulness

4-1.text: The victors’ offspring who have thus Grasped bodhichitta steadfastly Must strive without any lassitude To never violate the precepts.
4-1.en_text: The buddhas' children who have firmly taken up this wish to help all beings must strive without any laziness never to break their commitments.

4-2.text: When something has been started rashly Or is not properly thought out, Even if promised, it is best To examine whether to act or not.
4-2.en_text: When something has been started hastily, or wasn't properly thought through, it's best to consider carefully whether to go ahead with it - even if a promise was already made.

4-3.text: But why should I put off that which The buddhas and their offspring have Investigated with great prajna And I myself have also examined?
4-3.en_text: But why would I delay something that the buddhas and their spiritual children have examined with great wisdom, and that I myself have also carefully considered?

4-4.text: If now that I have made a promise, I don’t fulfill it with my actions, I will have hoodwinked all those beings, And what will be my destiny?
4-4.en_text: If, having made this promise, I now fail to carry it out through my actions, I will have let down every being who was counting on me - so what will become of me?

4-5.text: A person who thinks in their mind To give some trifling, little thing But does not give it will become A hungry ghost, it has been said.
4-5.en_text: It is said that someone who thinks of giving even a small, trivial thing, but then doesn't follow through, will be reborn as a hungry, suffering spirit.

4-6.text: Having invited them from my heart As guests to sublime happiness, If I deceive all wanderers, Will I go to the higher realms?
4-6.en_text: Having invited all beings from my heart to share in the highest happiness, if I then let them all down, will I really reach the higher realms?

4-7.text: People who give up bodhichitta Still being liberated is An inconceivable way of karma That only the omniscient know.
4-7.en_text: How it is that people who abandon their wish to help all beings can still eventually be freed is a workings of cause and effect so subtle that only a fully enlightened being can understand it.

4-8.text: This downfall, for a bodhisattva, Is the most serious of all. If it occurs, their benefit To all sentient beings is diminished.
4-8.en_text: For a bodhisattva, breaking this commitment is the most serious failure of all. When it happens, their ability to benefit all beings is badly weakened.

4-9.text: Anyone else who thwarts their merit Even a moment will be born Endlessly in the lower realms Since they’ve decreased all beings’ welfare.
4-9.en_text: Anyone else who blocks even a moment of this goodness will be reborn endlessly in the lower realms, since they have diminished the well-being of all beings.

4-10.text: If one who spoils the happiness Of even a single being is ruined, Why mention ruining the well-being Of infinite beings throughout space?
4-10.en_text: If someone who ruins the happiness of even a single being brings ruin on themselves, how much more true is this for someone who ruins the well-being of countless beings throughout all of space?

4-11.text: If swinging back and forth between Strong downfalls and strong bodhichitta, You mix them in samsaric cycles, It will take long to reach the levels.
4-11.en_text: If I keep swinging back and forth between serious failures and a strong wish to help everyone, mixing the two together through repeated rebirths, it will take a very long time to reach the higher stages of the path.

4-12.text: Therefore I will, with dedication, Accomplish what I promised to do. If from now on, I make no effort, I’ll go from lower to lower realm.
4-12.en_text: So I will dedicate myself fully to carrying out what I have promised. If I make no effort from now on, I will keep falling from one lower state to another.

4-13.text: Though countless buddhas have appeared And benefited all sentient beings, Due to my wrongs, I have not been A beneficiary of their succor.
4-13.en_text: Even though countless buddhas have appeared and benefited every being, because of my own past wrongs, I was never among those who received their help.

4-14.text: If I still act in such a way, Over and over again I will Experience in the lower realms Being sick, bound, hacked, and stabbed, and such.
4-14.en_text: If I keep acting this way, I will continue, again and again, to experience sickness, imprisonment, mutilation, and worse in the lower realms.

4-15.text: It’s rare a tathagata appears, Rare to gain faith, a human body, And the ability to cultivate virtue. When will I ever have these again?
4-15.en_text: It is rare for a buddha to appear, rare to gain genuine faith, a human life, and the ability to cultivate goodness. When will I ever have all of this again?

4-16.text: Although on days such as today, I may be healthy, fed, and safe, Life will deceive me in an instant— This body’s a momentary loan.
4-16.en_text: Although today I may be healthy, well fed, and safe, life can betray me in an instant - this body is only borrowed for a short while.

4-17.text: Behaving like this, I will not get A human body ever again. If I don’t gain a human body, There’s only wrong and never good.
4-17.en_text: If I keep behaving this way, I will never gain a human life again. And without a human life, there is only wrongdoing ahead, never goodness.

4-18.text: If I do not act virtuously Despite my fortune to do good, What will I do when stupefied By the suffering of the lower realms?
4-18.en_text: If I fail to act with goodness despite having this good fortune now, what will I do once I'm overwhelmed by the suffering of the lower realms?

4-19.text: If I do not perform any virtues And accumulate misdeeds, I’ll never, for billions of aeons, Even hear the words “the higher realms.”
4-19.en_text: If I do no good and instead pile up wrongdoing, I won't even hear the words "the higher realms" for billions of ages to come.

4-20.text: Therefore the Bhagavan taught gaining A human body is as hard As for a turtle to stick its neck Through a yoke tossed on the vast seas.
4-20.en_text: This is why the Buddha taught that gaining a human life is as rare as a sea turtle happening to poke its neck through a wooden yoke floating on a vast ocean.

4-21.text: If due to a wrong done in an instant, One will stay aeons in the Incessant, What need to say that due to misdeeds I’ve done in beginningless samsara, I will not go to the higher realms?
4-21.en_text: If a single moment of wrongdoing can lead to ages spent in the deepest hell of endless suffering, how could the wrongs I've done throughout this beginningless cycle of rebirth possibly lead me to the higher realms?

4-22.text: After I have experienced That much, I won’t be freed from there, For while I am experiencing it, I will produce still more misdeeds.
4-22.en_text: And after I've endured all of that, I still won't be free of it, because while I'm experiencing that suffering, I'll likely create even more wrongdoing.

4-23.text: Now that I’ve gained such leisure as this, If I don’t cultivate the virtues, There’s no deception other than this, Nor any greater idiocy.
4-23.en_text: Now that I have gained such a rare opportunity as this, if I still don't cultivate goodness, there is no greater self-deception, and no greater foolishness, than this.

4-24.text: And if, once I have realized this, I am, deluded, still despondent, When the time comes for me to die, I’ll feel tremendous grief well up.
4-24.en_text: And if, even after realizing this, I remain confused and discouraged, then when the time comes for me to die, I will feel overwhelming grief.

4-25.text: When the intolerable flames Of hell have burned my body long, There is no doubt that blazing fires Of dreadful rue will wrack my mind.
4-25.en_text: When the unbearable flames of hell have burned my body for a very long time, there is no doubt that a fire of terrible regret will also burn through my mind.

4-26.text: Somehow, by luck, I’ve gained a place Of benefit so hard to get. If I, while I am cognizant, Am led back to those hells again,
4-26.en_text: By sheer good fortune, I have gained this rare opportunity to do good. If, even while fully aware, I let myself be led back into those hells again,

4-27.text: It is as if I’ve been bewitched By spells and have no will in this. I don’t know what’s deluded me— What do I have inside of me?
4-27.en_text: it would be as if I've been placed under some spell, with no will of my own. I don't even know what has confused me so - what is really going on inside me?

4-28.text: Aversion, craving, and so forth— My enemies—have no limbs and such. They are not brave or wise, and yet They’ve somehow made me like a slave.
4-28.en_text: Aversion, craving, and all the rest - these enemies of mine - have no limbs, no weapons, no courage, and no wisdom, and yet they've somehow made me their slave.

4-29.text: As long as they dwell in my mind, They’ll cause me harm at their own pleasure. It’s wrong to bear that without anger— Being patient would be blameworthy.
4-29.en_text: As long as they live in my mind, they will keep harming me however they please. It's wrong to simply accept this without resistance - staying passive here would be a mistake.

4-30.text: If all the gods and demigods Arose against me as my foes, They could not take or force me to The fires of the Incessant Hell.
4-30.en_text: Even if every god and demigod rose up against me as enemies, they could not force me into the fires of the deepest hell.

4-31.text: This powerful enemy, afflictions, Will cast me in an instant there Where even Mount Meru would be turned To ash on contact, nothing left.
4-31.en_text: But this powerful enemy - my own negative emotions - can throw me there in an instant, into a fire so intense it could reduce even the greatest mountain to ash without a trace.

4-32.text: The adversaries, my afflictions, Last long, without beginning or end. No other enemy is able To endure so long a time as them.
4-32.en_text: These adversaries, my negative emotions, have lasted without any real beginning or end. No other enemy could ever endure as long as they have.

4-33.text: Everyone, when attended kindly, Is helpful and will try to please, But when afflictions are appeased, They inflict more suffering in return.
4-33.en_text: Everyone else, when treated kindly, tends to become helpful and pleasant in return. But my negative emotions, no matter how well I treat them, only cause me more suffering.

4-34.text: If thus my long and constant enemies— The only cause of the proliferation Of manifold harms—remain within my heart, Can I be safe and happy in samsara?
4-34.en_text: If these long-standing, constant enemies - the sole source of every kind of harm - continue to live within my heart, how can I possibly be safe or happy anywhere in this cycle of rebirth?

4-35.text: If the keepers of the prison of samsara, Such as the murderous butchers in the hells, Live in the webs of greed within my mind, How can there be any happiness for me?
4-35.en_text: If the very jailers of this endless cycle - like the cruel executioners of the hells - live on within the grip of greed in my own mind, how can there be any happiness for me at all?

4-36.text: Therefore, until I see that I have truly slain This enemy, I will not slacken in my efforts. Those who are filled with pride, once angered, cannot sleep Until those who have caused a slight offense are killed.
4-36.en_text: So until I see clearly that I have truly defeated this enemy, I will not ease up in my efforts. Just as someone consumed by pride, once angered, cannot rest until they've dealt with even a minor insult,

4-37.text: Once the afflicted, who suffer from a mortal nature, Enter the fray of battle with a strong wish to triumph, They scorn the pain of being struck by spears and arrows And won’t retreat until they have attained their goal.
4-37.en_text: just as those driven by aggression, facing death, charge fearlessly into battle wanting only to win - ignoring the pain of being struck by spears and arrows, refusing to retreat until they succeed -

4-38.text: For me, who strives to vanquish my true, natural foes That always are the cause of every suffering, What need is there to say—I won’t now be dismayed Or daunted by the hundred causes of misery.
4-38.en_text: how much more should I, striving to conquer my true, natural enemies, which are the actual cause of every suffering, refuse to be discouraged or intimidated by the countless small causes of misery I meet along the way.

4-39.text: If someone wounded pointlessly by enemies Will flaunt their scars as decorations on their body, How then is suffering a cause of injury For me who truly strives to accomplish a great purpose?
4-39.en_text: If someone wounded pointlessly by an enemy proudly shows off their scars as if they were decorations, then how could hardship possibly harm me when I'm striving toward something truly worthwhile?

4-40.text: If fishermen, outcasts, farmers, and so forth With only thought of their own livelihood, Forbear the harms of heat and cold and such, Why don’t I bear with those for beings’ weal?
4-40.en_text: If fishermen, outcasts, farmers, and others endure the pain of heat, cold, and hardship just to make a living, why shouldn't I endure the same for the sake of helping all beings?

4-41.text: When I swore I would free all beings To the ends of space in all directions From the afflictions, I myself Was not yet free of the afflictions.
4-41.en_text: When I vowed to free every being throughout all of space from their negative emotions, I myself was, at that time, still not free of them.

4-42.text: How is it speaking without knowing My limitations was not insane? Therefore I’ll never be turned back In subjugating the afflictions.
4-42.en_text: Wasn't it senseless to make such a promise without even knowing my own limits? So I will never turn back from the task of overcoming these negative emotions.

4-43.text: I’ll cling to this tenaciously And enter battle bearing a grudge Against afflictions other than The type that conquers the afflictions.
4-43.en_text: I will hold onto this resolve firmly and go into battle bearing a real grudge - but only against the kind of negative emotion that stands in the way of finally overcoming negative emotions altogether.

4-44.text: It would be better to be slain By being burnt or decapitated. In no way shall I ever bow Before my enemy, the afflictions.
4-44.en_text: It would be better to be burned alive or beheaded than to ever bow down before my true enemy - my own negative emotions.

4-45.text: Though ordinary enemies, when banished, Will stay in other lands, which they adopt To build their power until their return, The enemy affliction is not so.
4-45.en_text: Ordinary enemies, when driven out, simply settle elsewhere and rebuild their strength before returning. But the enemy of negative emotion is not like that at all.

4-46.text: Wretched afflictions, cast out by the eye of prajna! When they are driven from my mind, where can they go? Where can they stay so that they can return to harm me? It’s just that I, weak-minded, have not persevered.
4-46.en_text: Once these troublesome negative emotions are driven out of my mind by the sharp eye of wisdom, where could they possibly go? Where could they hide, waiting to return and harm me again? The only real problem is that I, weak-minded as I am, haven't made the effort to keep them out.

4-47.text: Afflictions do not dwell in objects, in the senses, or between. Nor are they somewhere else. Where do they dwell that harm all beings? They’re like illusions. Rid your heart of fear, and apply diligence For the sake of prajna. Why let them torment you pointlessly in hell?
4-47.en_text: These negative emotions don't live in outer objects, in the senses, or anywhere in between, nor do they live somewhere else entirely. So where exactly do they live, that they can harm all beings this way? They are like illusions - nothing more. So let go of your fear, and put in the effort needed to gain wisdom. Why suffer needlessly in hell for no good reason?

4-48.text: I’ve contemplated thus and now will strive To undertake the precepts as described. How can a patient who needs medicine Be cured if they ignore the doctor’s advice?
4-48.en_text: Having thought this through, I will now strive to take up these practices as described. After all, how can a sick person be cured if they ignore what the doctor tells them?

5-0.text: The fourth chapter, “Teachings on Carefulness,” from Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva. ^4-a 5. Guarding Awareness
5-0.en_text: The fourth chapter, "Teachings on Carefulness," from Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva. 5. Guarding Awareness

5-1.text: All those who wish to keep the precepts Should concentrate and guard their minds. If you do not protect your mind, You won’t be able to keep the precepts.
5-1.en_text: All those who wish to keep their commitments should focus and guard their minds closely. If you don't protect your mind, you won't be able to keep any commitment at all.

5-2.text: An untamed elephant amok Does not create as much harm here As letting the elephant of mind Run loose will cause in the Incessant.
5-2.en_text: A wild elephant running loose doesn't cause nearly as much harm in this world as letting the "elephant" of an untamed mind run wild - which can lead all the way to the hell of endless suffering.

5-3.text: The elephant of mind tied tight With ropes of mindfulness all round, All dangers will amount to naught; All virtues will come into your hands.
5-3.en_text: But when the elephant of the mind is tied securely with the rope of mindfulness, every danger comes to nothing, and every kind of goodness falls naturally into your hands.

5-4.text: All tigers, lions, elephants, Bears, snakes, and enemies, The keepers of the beings in hell, The dakinis and rakshasas—
5-4.en_text: Tigers, lions, elephants, bears, snakes, and every kind of enemy, the guardians of hell, evil spirits, and demons -

5-5.text: By binding just this mind alone, All of these will be bound. By taming just the mind alone, All of these will be tamed.
5-5.en_text: all of these are bound simply by binding this mind alone. All of these are tamed simply by taming this mind alone.

5-6.text: For he who spoke the truth has taught That everything we fear And sufferings beyond all measure Originate from mind.
5-6.en_text: The one who spoke the truth has taught that everything we fear, and every kind of suffering beyond measure, comes from the mind.

5-7.text: Who is it that specifically made The weapons of the hells? Who made the ground of burning iron? Whence come the lovers in hell?
5-7.en_text: Who specifically crafted the weapons used in the hells? Who created the ground of burning iron? Where did the tormenting lovers found in hell come from?

5-8.text: The Sage has said that all of these Arise from wicked thoughts. Therefore there is in the three worlds No danger other than mind.
5-8.en_text: The wise teacher has said that all of these arise from harmful thoughts. So in all of existence, there is truly no danger other than the mind itself.

5-9.text: If ridding the world of poverty Made generosity transcendent, There are still paupers, so how could The past protectors have transcended?
5-9.en_text: If simply ending poverty in the world were what made generosity perfect, then since there are still poor people today, how could the guardians of the past ever have perfected it?

5-10.text: The wish to give all your belongings And the results to everyone Is taught to be transcendent giving, And therefore that is mind itself.
5-10.en_text: Perfect generosity is taught to be the wish to give away all your possessions - along with the good results of doing so - for the benefit of everyone. And that wish is a matter of the mind itself.

5-11.text: And where could fish, et cetera, Be sent where they would not be killed? Discipline’s taught to be transcendent From gaining the intent to abstain.
5-11.en_text: Where, after all, could fish and other creatures be sent so that they would never be killed? Perfect discipline is taught to come from gaining the sincere intention to abstain from harm.

5-12.text: How could one kill belligerent beings Who are as infinite as space? Vanquishing this one angry mind Is like defeating all those foes.
5-12.en_text: How could anyone ever defeat hostile beings, who are as endless as space itself? But overcoming this one angry mind is the same as defeating every one of those enemies.

5-13.text: How could there be sufficient leather To cover the earth entirely? With just the leather for my soles, It is as if the whole earth’s covered.
5-13.en_text: Where could enough leather ever be found to cover the whole surface of the earth? Yet with just the leather covering the soles of my feet, it is as if the entire earth were covered.

5-14.text: Likewise, although I am unable To keep external things at bay, I’ll keep this mind of mine in check— What need to ward off anything else?
5-14.en_text: In the same way, although I can't hold back every external threat, I can hold this mind of mine in check - so why bother trying to control everything else?

5-15.text: Even with body and speech, results Of feeble conduct are not like The fruit of rousing one clear thought— Rebirth in such as Brahma’s Realm.
5-15.en_text: Even careful conduct with body and speech, if done half-heartedly, cannot match the result of rousing just one clear, wholehearted good thought - which can lead to rebirth in the very highest heavenly realms.

5-16.text: No matter how long they are practiced, All liturgies and austerities Are futile, said the knower of suchness, If something else distracts the mind.
5-16.en_text: No matter how long they're practiced, the Buddha - who understands reality as it truly is - taught that all rituals and hardships are pointless if the mind is distracted elsewhere.

5-17.text: Those who don’t know this secret of mind— The sublime, paramount of dharmas— Want to gain joy and end suffering But wander to no avail or end.
5-17.en_text: Those who don't understand this secret of the mind - the most sublime of all teachings - want to find joy and end suffering, yet they simply wander on and on, achieving nothing.

5-18.text: Thus I will grasp and protect well This mind of mine. This discipline Of guarding mind aside, why bother With multifarious disciplines?
5-18.en_text: So I will take hold of this mind of mine and protect it well. Setting aside this discipline of guarding the mind, what use would any other discipline be?

5-19.text: Like those who in a boisterous crowd Concentrate and take care of their wounds, Those in the crowds of evil people Should always guard the wound of mind.
5-19.en_text: Just as someone in a rough, jostling crowd carefully protects an open wound, so too, when surrounded by people acting harmfully, one should always guard the tender wound that is the mind.

5-20.text: If you are careful of a wound From fear of its slight, minor pain, Why not protect the wound of mind From fear of crushing mountains in hell?
5-20.en_text: If you're careful with a physical wound out of fear of even slight pain, why not protect the wound of the mind out of fear of being crushed under the weight of hell?

5-21.text: Living by conduct such as this, A steadfast monk who keeps his vows, Whether in crowds of evil people Or among women, will not fall.
5-21.en_text: Living with this kind of conduct, a steadfast person who keeps their commitments will not fall, whether surrounded by harmful people or in any tempting situation.

5-22.text: It would be better to lose my things, Life, limbs, respect, or livelihood; Better that other virtues lapse Than ever my intent diminish.
5-22.en_text: It would be better to lose my possessions, my life, my limbs, my reputation, or my livelihood, and even let other good qualities slip, than to ever let this resolve weaken.

5-23.text: I join my palms in prayer and urge All those who wish to guard their minds: With all your efforts, please protect Your mindfulness and your awareness.
5-23.en_text: With my palms joined, I urge everyone who wishes to protect their mind: with all your effort, please protect your mindfulness and your awareness.

5-24.text: People who are beset by illness Have no strength to do anything, And minds beset by ignorance Have no strength to do anything.
5-24.en_text: People weakened by illness have no strength to do anything at all, and minds weakened by confusion have no strength to do anything at all either.

5-25.text: Even if those who lack awareness Should listen, ponder, or meditate, It won’t stay in their memory, Like water in a leaky jar.
5-25.en_text: Even if someone lacking awareness listens to teachings, reflects on them, or meditates, none of it will stick in their memory - like water poured into a leaky jar.

5-26.text: Due to the fault of nonawareness, Many of those with learning, faith, And dedicated perseverance Will be polluted by the downfalls.
5-26.en_text: Because of this lack of awareness, even many people with real learning, faith, and dedicated effort end up tainted by their own failures.

5-27.text: The robbers that are a lack of awareness, Following weakened mindfulness, Will seize the merits you have gathered While you go to the lower realms.
5-27.en_text: This band of robbers - carelessness and lack of awareness - follows behind a weakened mindfulness, ready to steal away all the goodness you've built up, even as you head toward the lower realms.

5-28.text: This gang of bandits, the afflictions, Are seeking opportunities. Given a chance, they’ll plunder virtue And slaughter life in higher realms.
5-28.en_text: This gang of thieves, our own negative emotions, are always watching for an opportunity. Given the chance, they will plunder your goodness and destroy your chances of a higher rebirth.

5-29.text: Thus never let your mindfulness Stray from the gateway to your mind, And if it goes, recall the pains Of the lower realms to bring it back.
5-29.en_text: So never let your mindfulness wander from the door of your mind. And if it does wander off, bring it back at once by remembering the suffering of the lower realms.

5-30.text: From keeping company with a master, Instruction from the abbot, and fear, Those who have fortune and respect Develop mindfulness easily.
5-30.en_text: Through the company of a good teacher, through instruction from a mentor, and through a healthy sense of caution, those who are fortunate and respected develop mindfulness with ease.

5-31.text: “The buddhas and the bodhisattvas See everywhere without obstruction. Therefore I always am indeed Within the presence of them all.”
5-31.en_text: "The buddhas and bodhisattvas see everything, everywhere, without any obstruction. So I am always, in truth, standing in their very presence."

5-32.text: Thinking thus conscientiously, Respectfully, and fearfully, The recollection of the buddha Will then arise repeatedly.
5-32.en_text: Thinking this way, with conscientious care, respect, and a healthy sense of caution, the memory of the Buddha will then arise again and again.

5-33.text: When mindfulness is stationed there To guard the gateway to the mind, Awareness will then also come And return if it has departed.
5-33.en_text: When mindfulness is set in place like this to guard the door of the mind, awareness too will come, and will return even if it has wandered off.

5-34.text: In every moment, first of all, I must know if my mind is tainted, And at that time, I must be able To hold still like a block of wood.
5-34.en_text: First of all, in every moment, I must notice whether my mind has become clouded by negative emotion, and at that point I must be able to stay perfectly still, like a block of wood.

5-35.text: I’ll never allow myself to look Around in purposeless distraction. With my mind focused, I’ll instead Look always with my gaze cast down.
5-35.en_text: I will never let myself glance around aimlessly out of distraction. Instead, with my mind focused, I will keep my gaze lowered.

5-36.text: But sometimes I might glance about To rest my eyes when they’re fatigued. If someone should come into sight, I’ll look at them and say, “Hello!”
5-36.en_text: But now and then I might look around briefly to rest my tired eyes. And if someone happens to come into view, I'll look at them and greet them warmly.

5-37.text: To know the perils on the road, I’ll look in the four directions often. Pausing, I first will turn around Before I look behind myself.
5-37.en_text: To notice any dangers along the road, I'll look often in all four directions, and before turning around, I'll pause first to check behind me.

5-38.text: Having thus looked ahead and behind, I’ll then proceed or else return. In every situation, I will Act knowing the necessity.
5-38.en_text: Having looked both ahead and behind in this way, I will then either move forward or turn back. In every situation, I will act only once I understand what is actually needed.

5-39.text: Beginning endeavors with the thought “With body, I will stay like this,” I’ll then occasionally examine “How is my body situated?”
5-39.en_text: When beginning any task, I'll set the intention, "I will hold my body just so," and then check in from time to time: "How is my body positioned right now?"

5-40.text: With all my efforts, I must check That the crazed elephant of mind Has not slipped loose from being tied To the great post of thoughts of dharma.
5-40.en_text: With all my effort, I must keep checking that the wild elephant of my mind hasn't slipped free from the sturdy post of good, wholesome thoughts.

5-41.text: Exerting myself in samadhi, I shall examine my own mind By thinking “What is my mind doing?” To not lose it for even a moment.
5-41.en_text: Striving to stay focused and calm, I will examine my own mind by asking, "What is my mind doing right now?" - so as not to lose track of it even for a moment.

5-42.text: If due to danger, feasts, and such, You cannot, do what’s easiest. It’s taught that in a time of giving, You may ignore some discipline.
5-42.en_text: If, because of danger, a feast, or some similar situation, you truly can't manage this, then do whatever is easiest. It is taught that in moments such as generous giving, some rules may be set aside.

5-43.text: Once you’ve considered and begun A task, don’t think of anything else. Focusing your attention there, You should accomplish that one first.
5-43.en_text: Once you've thought something through and begun a task, don't let your attention wander to something else. Keep your focus there and finish that one task first.

5-44.text: If you do this, all is done well. Otherwise neither will get done. In this way, you will not increase The near affliction nonawareness.
5-44.en_text: If you do this, everything gets done properly. Otherwise, neither task will be completed well. In this way, you won't feed the nearby danger of carelessness.

5-45.text: If you engage in idle chat Or in amazing spectacles Of various and different kinds, Give up your eagerness for them.
5-45.en_text: If you find yourself drawn into idle gossip or various kinds of entertaining spectacles, let go of your eagerness for them.

5-46.text: If you should dig the ground, cut plants, Or draw in dirt without a purpose, Recall the words of the Sugata And at that moment, stop from fear.
5-46.en_text: If you're about to dig the ground, cut plants, or draw idly in the dirt without any real purpose, remember the Buddha's guidance and stop yourself out of a healthy sense of caution.

5-47.text: Whenever you have a wish to move Or else you feel a wish to speak, Examine your mind first, and then Be firm in acting properly.
5-47.en_text: Whenever you feel the urge to move or the urge to speak, check your own mind first, and then act firmly in a proper way.

5-48.text: At times when my mind feels the lust Of greed or else the urge of anger, I must not act and must not speak— I’ll hold still like a block of wood.
5-48.en_text: Whenever my mind feels the pull of craving or the urge of anger, I must not act and must not speak - I will hold still, like a block of wood.

5-49.text: When I’m excited or else gleeful, When I feel pride or arrogance, When I’ve the thought to dig up faults, Revive disputes, or be deceitful,
5-49.en_text: When I'm overexcited or overjoyed, when pride or arrogance arises, when I feel the urge to point out others' faults, stir up old conflicts, or act deceitfully,

5-50.text: At times when I’m intent on boasting Or being disparaging of others, When I’m abusive or contentious, I’ll hold still like a block of wood.
5-50.en_text: when I'm inclined to boast or to put others down, when I become abusive or argumentative, I will hold still, like a block of wood.

5-51.text: When I want gains, respect, and fame Or long for a cortege of servants, When my mind wants that I be served, I’ll hold still like a block of wood.
5-51.en_text: When I crave profit, recognition, or fame, or long to be surrounded by attendants, or want to be waited on by others, I will hold still, like a block of wood.

5-52.text: A wish to give up on others’ weal And seek out my own benefit, A yen for talk—if these arise, I’ll hold still like a block of wood.
5-52.en_text: When the wish arises to give up on others' well-being and focus only on my own benefit, or when I simply feel like chattering, I will hold still, like a block of wood.

5-53.text: And when impatience, laziness, Fear, impudence, or garrulousness Or bias toward my own arises, I will hold still like a block of wood.
5-53.en_text: And when impatience, laziness, fear, rudeness, or excessive talking arises, or a bias in favor of myself, I will hold still, like a block of wood.

5-54.text: Thus noticing when their mind becomes Afflicted or occupied pointlessly, The heroes use the antidotes To keep it firmly in control.
5-54.en_text: Noticing this way whenever their mind becomes clouded by negative emotion or occupied with something pointless, true practitioners use the right remedies to keep it firmly under control.

5-55.text: I will be resolute, full of faith, Steady, respectful, courteous, Conscientious, fearful, calm, And dedicated to pleasing others.
5-55.en_text: I will be resolute, full of trust, steady, respectful, courteous, conscientious, appropriately cautious, calm, and dedicated to putting others at ease.

5-56.text: I won’t despair at the wishes of The childish who don’t get along. I will be loving, thinking that Such thoughts are due to the afflictions.
