5-56.en_text: I won't lose heart over the conflicting wishes of immature people who can't get along. I will meet them with kindness, understanding that such behavior comes from their own negative emotions.

5-57.text: Directed by myself and beings Toward things that are irreproachable, I’ll always keep my mind held fast, Without a me, like an emanation.
5-57.en_text: Guided by what is truly blameless, for my own sake and for the sake of others, I will always keep my mind steady - without clinging to a fixed sense of self - as if I were simply a helpful presence in the world.

5-58.text: Over and over again, I’ll think How after so long I have found The greatest leisure, and keep my mind Unshakable as Mount Sumeru.
5-58.en_text: Again and again, I will remind myself how, after such a long time, I have finally found this greatest of opportunities, and I will keep my mind as unshakable as the greatest mountain in existence.

5-59.text: If, mind, you will not be distressed When vultures lusting for its meat Together tear the body apart, Why do you cherish it so now?
5-59.en_text: If, mind, you won't be troubled when vultures hungry for flesh tear this body apart together, why do you cherish it so dearly right now?

5-60.text: O mind, why is it that you grasp This body as yours and guard it so? If you and it are separate, Then what good does it do for you?
5-60.en_text: Mind, why is it that you cling to this body as "yours" and guard it so carefully? If you and it are truly separate things, what good does it actually do you?

5-61.text: Deluded mind, why don’t you cling To a clean wooden figurine? How is it sensible to protect This festering machine of filth?
5-61.en_text: Confused mind, why don't you instead cling to a clean wooden figure? What sense is there in protecting this festering machine full of impurity?

5-62.text: First with your intellect, dissect And separate the layers of skin. Dissever with the blade of prajna The flesh apart from the cage of bones.
5-62.en_text: First, with careful thought, peel back and separate the layers of skin. Then, with the blade of wisdom, cut the flesh away from the cage of bones.

5-63.text: Then chop apart the bones as well. Look in as far as to the marrow And analyze it for yourself. What essence does it have?
5-63.en_text: Then break open the bones themselves. Look all the way in to the marrow, and examine it closely for yourself. What real essence does it actually contain?

5-64.text: If even searching with such effort, You don’t see in it any essence, Why is it that you still protect This body in such an attached manner?
5-64.en_text: If, even after searching this carefully, you find no essence there at all, why do you still protect this body with such attachment?

5-65.text: Its filth is not fit for you to eat, Nor is its blood fit to drink either. Its entrails are unfit to suck. What does the body do for you?
5-65.en_text: Its filth isn't fit for you to eat, nor its blood fit to drink, nor its insides fit to consume. So what exactly does this body do for you?

5-66.text: Instead, it’s logical it be kept As food for jackals and for vultures. The bodies of all human beings Are merely something to be used.
5-66.en_text: It would actually make more sense to leave it as food for jackals and vultures. The bodies of all human beings are, in the end, simply something to be used.

5-67.text: Even though you protect it so, When the merciless Lord of Death Takes it to give to birds and dogs, Will there be anything you can do?
5-67.en_text: Even with all your protecting, when merciless death eventually takes this body to be given to birds and dogs, will there be anything at all you can do about it?

5-68.text: If you do not give clothes and such To servants who can’t be employed, Why tire yourself to keep this body That will, though fed, go somewhere else?
5-68.en_text: If you wouldn't even bother clothing a servant who refuses to work for you, why exhaust yourself keeping up this body, which - however well you feed it - will eventually move on regardless?

5-69.text: Now that you’ve given it a wage, Put it to work for your own sake. Do not give everything to it If there’s not any benefit.
5-69.en_text: Now that you've paid its wages, so to speak, put this body to work for your own true benefit. Don't give it everything unconditionally if there's no real benefit in doing so.

5-70.text: Think of this body as a boat, A mere support for coming and going. Make it so it fulfills your wish To benefit all sentient beings.
5-70.en_text: Instead, think of this body as a boat - simply a vehicle for getting from one place to another. Make it serve your true purpose: benefiting all beings.

5-71.text: In such a way, be self-controlled, And always have a smiling face. Abandon glowering brows and scowls. Be friendly to beings and straightforward.
5-71.en_text: In this way, stay self-controlled and always keep a warm, smiling face. Let go of frowning and scowling. Be friendly toward others and straightforward.

5-72.text: Do not shove chairs and such about Impetuously and noisily. Don’t violently open doors. Always delight in being quiet.
5-72.en_text: Don't shove chairs and furniture around carelessly or noisily. Don't slam doors open forcefully. Always take pleasure in being quiet and gentle.

5-73.text: Cranes, cats, and burglars move around In silence, unobtrusively, To achieve the ends that they desire. The sages always behave likewise.
5-73.en_text: Cranes, cats, and burglars all move quietly and unobtrusively to accomplish what they set out to do. Wise practitioners should behave in just the same way.

5-74.text: Ever a student of everyone, Respectfully accept advice That’s helpful or unsolicited From those skilled in advising others.
5-74.en_text: Always ready to learn from anyone, respectfully accept advice - whether it's asked for or not - from those who are skilled at helping others improve.

5-75.text: To all those who have spoken well, Say, “You have spoken virtuously.” When you see someone perform merit, Make them feel glad by praising them.
5-75.en_text: To anyone who has spoken well, say, "That was well said." When you see someone doing something good, make them feel encouraged by praising them.

5-76.text: Speak of good qualities discreetly; Repeat them when they’re spoken of. When someone speaks of your good traits, Understand they know qualities.
5-76.en_text: Speak of others' good qualities quietly and sincerely, and repeat them when others mention them too. When someone speaks of your own good qualities, understand that they simply recognize goodness when they see it.

5-77.text: All efforts are for happiness’s sake, But even bought with wealth, it’s rare. So I’ll enjoy the pleasure of Delight in the good that others do.
5-77.en_text: All effort is ultimately aimed at happiness, yet even happiness bought with wealth is hard to find. So instead, I will find my own joy simply by delighting in the goodness that others do.

5-78.text: For me, there will be no loss here, And in the next, great happiness. Wrongdoing brings gloom and suffering, And in the next, great miseries.
5-78.en_text: In doing this, I lose nothing in this life, and I gain great happiness in lives to come. Wrongdoing, by contrast, brings unease and suffering now, and great misery later.

5-79.text: When talking, you should speak sincerely, Coherently, clearly, pleasantly, Without attachment or aversion, Gently, and in moderation.
5-79.en_text: When speaking, be sincere, clear, easy to follow, pleasant to hear, free from both craving and irritation, gentle, and appropriately brief.

5-80.text: When you look at a sentient being, Think that it’s only due to them That you’ll awaken to buddhahood, And look sincerely, lovingly.
5-80.en_text: When you look at another being, think, "It is only because of this being that I will one day reach full enlightenment," and look at them with sincere warmth and love.

5-81.text: Inspired continuously by yearning Or by the antidotes, great virtues Are found in the fields of qualities, Of benefit, and of suffering.
5-81.en_text: Whether inspired by genuine longing or by consciously applying the right remedies, great goodness is found in three fields: the field of good qualities, the field of those who help us, and the field of those who suffer.

5-82.text: Both skillfully and cheerfully, I’ll always do my tasks myself. I won’t, in any of my actions, Be dependent on anyone.
5-82.en_text: Both skillfully and with a cheerful spirit, I will always carry out my own tasks myself. In none of my actions will I simply depend on others to do the work for me.

5-83.text: Transcendent giving and so forth Progress, each greater than the last. Don’t drop the greater for the lesser. Think mainly of others’ benefit.
5-83.en_text: The perfections - generosity, discipline, and so on - each build on the one before, each more important than the last. Don't set aside the greater one for the sake of the lesser. Keep the benefit of others foremost in mind.

5-84.text: Realizing this, continually Make efforts for the sake of others. The merciful, far-seeing one Allows for them what was forbidden.
5-84.en_text: Understanding this, make continual effort for the sake of others. The compassionate, far-seeing Buddha permits, for their sake, things that would otherwise not be allowed.

5-85.text: Sharing with those who’ve fallen low, The unprotected, and ascetics, Eat moderately. Give away All except the three dharma robes.
5-85.en_text: Share what you have with those who have fallen on hard times, with the unprotected, and with those practicing austerity. Eat only what you need, and give away everything except the three robes needed for practice.

5-86.text: For minor ends, don’t harm this body That is for practicing true dharma. By doing so, you’ll soon fulfill The wishes of all sentient beings.
5-86.en_text: Don't harm this body - which exists for practicing the true teachings - over minor matters. Taking care of it this way, you will soon be able to fulfill the wishes of all beings.

5-87.text: Unless your compassionate intent Is pure, don’t sacrifice your body, But give it as a cause to achieve Great aims in this and in the next.
5-87.en_text: Unless your compassionate intention is genuinely pure, don't give away your own body. Instead, use it as a means to accomplish great goals both now and in the future.

5-88.text: Dharma should not be taught to those Who lack respect, who though not sick, Wear turbans, or hold parasols Or staves or weapons, or veil their heads.
5-88.en_text: Don't teach the deeper truths to those who show no respect - those who, though not actually sick, cover their heads with turbans or parasols, or who carry staffs or weapons.

5-89.text: Don’t teach the lesser the vast and deep, Or women unless a man is present. Approach with equal reverence Foundational and higher dharmas.
5-89.en_text: Don't teach vast and profound truths to those not yet ready for them, and don't teach women unless a man is present as well. Treat the more basic and the more advanced teachings with equal respect.

5-90.text: Don’t introduce a lesser dharma To those who are vessels for the vast. Also, do not disregard conduct Or lead astray with sutras and mantras.
5-90.en_text: Don't offer only a basic teaching to someone genuinely ready for the deeper truths. Also, don't ignore proper conduct, and don't mislead people by misusing scriptures or sacred formulas.

5-91.text: Cover it up when you discard A tooth stick or else when you spit. It is disgraceful to urinate And such on usable land and water.
5-91.en_text: Cover it up when you discard a used tooth-cleaning stick or when you spit. It's disrespectful to urinate or do similar things on land or in water that others rely on.

5-92.text: When eating, do not cram your food, Eat noisily, or open mouthed. Do not sit with your legs stretched out; Don’t rub both arms at the same time.
5-92.en_text: When eating, don't stuff your mouth, eat noisily, or chew with your mouth open. Don't sit with your legs stretched out carelessly, and don't rub both arms at the same time.

5-93.text: Don’t be alone with another’s spouse On rides, beds, seats, or other places. Observe, inquire, and then give up All that makes people lose their faith.
5-93.en_text: Don't be alone with someone else's spouse while traveling, resting, or sitting together. Watch carefully, ask when unsure, and avoid anything that would cause people to lose their trust in you.

5-94.text: Don’t point at anything with one finger. Instead, use your entire right hand To gesture in a respectful way, Showing the path in such a manner.
5-94.en_text: Don't point at things with a single finger. Instead, gesture respectfully using your whole right hand, such as when showing someone the way.

5-95.text: To give a signal, do not wave Your entire arm; just move it slightly And make a noise such as by snapping. Otherwise it is unrestrained.
5-95.en_text: To get someone's attention, don't wave your whole arm wildly - just move it slightly and make a small sound, such as by snapping your fingers. Anything more looks undisciplined.

5-96.text: Like the Protector at nirvana, Lie down in your preferred direction, And from the outset, with awareness, Resolve that you will get up promptly.
5-96.en_text: Lie down to sleep in whatever direction you prefer, just as the Buddha did at the time of his final passing, and from the very start, resolve with clear awareness that you will get up promptly.

5-97.text: The bodhisattva’s practices Are taught to be innumerable. Among them, surely first embrace The ways of purifying the mind.
5-97.en_text: The bodhisattva's practices are said to be countless in number. Among all of them, be sure to first take up the practice of purifying your own mind.

5-98.text: Three times each day, three times each night, Recite the Sutra in Three Sections. Because of the buddhas and bodhichitta, This pacifies remaining downfalls.
5-98.en_text: Three times during the day and three times during the night, recite the verses that call to mind the buddhas and the wish to help all beings - this eases the weight of any remaining failures.

5-99.text: Whatever you do at any time Whether for your or others’ sakes, Make efforts to train in the precepts That have been taught for that situation.
5-99.en_text: Whatever you're doing, at any time, whether for your own sake or for others', make the effort to train according to the guidance given for that particular situation.

5-100.text: There is not anything at all The victors’ offspring should not learn, And for the wise who live like this, There’s nothing that will not be merit.
5-100.en_text: There is nothing at all that a buddha's spiritual child should refuse to learn, and for someone wise who lives this way, there is nothing that cannot become a source of goodness.

5-101.text: Do nothing but what benefits Beings directly or indirectly. Dedicate solely for beings’ sakes Everything to enlightenment.
5-101.en_text: Do nothing except what benefits beings, whether directly or indirectly. Dedicate everything, purely for the sake of all beings, toward full enlightenment.

5-102.text: Even at cost of your own life, Never forsake the spiritual friend Who’s learned in the Mahayana And great in the bodhisattva vow.
5-102.en_text: Even at the cost of your own life, never abandon a spiritual guide who is well versed in the path of universal compassion and firmly committed to helping all beings.

5-103.text: Train in the ways to serve the guru From the life story of Shri Sambhava. This and the Buddha’s other teachings Are to be learned by reading sutras.
5-103.en_text: Learn how to properly serve a teacher from the story of Shri Sambhava. This, along with the Buddha's other teachings, should be studied by reading the scriptures.

5-104.text: The precepts are described in them, So therefore you should read the sutras. As a beginning, you should read The Sutra of Akashagarbha.
5-104.en_text: The guidelines for practice are laid out in the scriptures, so you should read them. As a good starting point, read the Sutra of Akashagarbha.

5-105.text: Because it teaches in detail What must be practiced constantly, Over and over again, you should Read the Compendium of Trainings.
5-105.en_text: Because it explains in detail what must be practiced continually, you should also read the Compendium of Trainings.

5-106.text: Or else, for the time being, read The shorter Compendium of Sutras, And also you should try to study The two by noble Nagarjuna.
5-106.en_text: Or, for now, you can read the shorter Compendium of Sutras, and you should also try to study the two texts written by the great teacher Nagarjuna.

5-107.text: What those do not prohibit is The merit you should act upon. To guard the minds of worldly people, Noting the precepts, act correctly.
5-107.en_text: Whatever these texts don't specifically prohibit is good to act upon. And to guard the minds of ordinary people, act correctly, mindful of these guidelines.

5-108.text: In brief, the characteristic of Maintaining awareness is just this: Examine over and over again The status of your mind and body.
5-108.en_text: In short, the essence of maintaining awareness is simply this: check again and again on the state of your own mind and body.

5-109.text: With body, I will practice these— What does just mouthing words achieve? Does merely reading medical books Bring benefit to patients?
5-109.en_text: I will put all of this into practice with my very body - what good is merely reciting the words? Does simply reading a medical textbook actually help a sick patient get well?

6-0.text: The fifth chapter, “Guarding Awareness,” from Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva. ^5-a 6. Transcendent Patience
6-0.en_text: The fifth chapter, "Guarding Awareness," from Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva. 6. The Perfection of Patience

6-1.text: One moment’s anger shatters all Good acts accumulated In a thousand aeons, such as giving Or offering to the buddhas.
6-1.en_text: A single moment of anger can shatter all the goodness built up over a thousand ages - goodness such as generosity or honoring the buddhas.

6-2.text: There is no misdeed like hatred; No austerity like patience. So cultivate assiduously Patience in various ways.
6-2.en_text: There is no wrongdoing like hatred, and no discipline like patience. So work diligently, in every way you can, to cultivate patience.

6-3.text: When pangs of hatred clutch the mind, It does not feel any peace. No joy, no comfort, and no sleep, No constancy can be had.
6-3.en_text: When the grip of hatred takes hold of the mind, it finds no peace at all - no joy, no comfort, no restful sleep, no steadiness of any kind.

6-4.text: Even though he has shown them favor With riches and respect, Dependents will confront and kill A master filled with hate.
6-4.en_text: Even someone who has been treated with wealth and respect will be turned on and even killed by those who depend on them, if that person is filled with hatred.

6-5.text: He will distress his friends and kin. Those gathered with gifts won’t serve. In brief, there is not anything That makes the angry happy.
6-5.en_text: Hatred drives away friends and family. Even those drawn in by gifts won't stay loyal. In short, there is nothing at all that makes an angry person happy.

6-6.text: The enemy anger will create Sufferings such as these. Those bent on overcoming anger Are happy here and elsewhere.
6-6.en_text: This enemy, anger, creates exactly this kind of suffering. Those who work to overcome it find happiness both now and in the future.

6-7.text: When what I do not want is done, Or my desires are blocked, Displeasure will then fuel my hatred, Which will grow to destroy me.
6-7.en_text: When something happens that I don't want, or when my wishes are blocked, frustration arises and fuels my hatred, which then grows enough to destroy me.

6-8.text: Thus I’ll destroy the sustenance Of this, my nemesis. Other than causing harm to me, This enemy has no function.
6-8.en_text: So I will cut off the very fuel of this, my true enemy. Apart from causing me harm, this enemy serves no purpose at all.

6-9.text: Whatever happens, I will not Upset my cheerfulness. Displeasure won’t fulfill my wishes But strip away my virtues.
6-9.en_text: Whatever happens, I won't let it disturb my sense of well-being. Being upset never gets me what I want - it only strips away my own goodness.

6-10.text: If something can be fixed, what need Is there to be displeased? If something can’t be fixed, what good Is it to be displeased?
6-10.en_text: If a problem can still be fixed, what is the use of being upset about it? And if it can't be fixed, what good does being upset do either way?

6-11.text: We don’t want pain, humiliation, Insults, or disrepute Either for us or for our friends. It’s the opposite for our foes.
6-11.en_text: None of us wants pain, humiliation, insults, or a bad reputation - for ourselves or for those we care about. Yet we wish exactly that on those we consider our enemies.

6-12.text: The causes of happiness are rare; The causes of pain are frequent. Without pain, there’s no wish for freedom, So, mind, you must be steadfast.
6-12.en_text: The causes of happiness are rare, while the causes of suffering are everywhere. Without suffering, there would be no wish to be free of it - so, mind, stay steady and resolved.

6-13.text: The Durga cults and Karnatans Pointlessly bear the sensations Of burns and wounds, so why am I A coward for freedom’s sake?
6-13.en_text: Certain ascetics pointlessly endure burns and wounds for the sake of their own rituals - so why would I be too cowardly to endure hardship for the sake of true freedom?

6-14.text: There’s nothing at all that is not easy If you are used to it. By getting used to minor pains, You’ll bear great harms as well.
6-14.en_text: There is nothing at all that doesn't become manageable once you're used to it. By growing accustomed to small discomforts, you'll come to bear even great hardships.

6-15.text: Don’t I see this with pointless pains Of serpents and mosquitoes, Of feelings of hunger, thirst, and such, And rashes and so forth?
6-15.en_text: Don't I already put up with pointless discomforts like snake and mosquito bites, hunger, thirst, and skin rashes?

6-16.text: Thus I won’t be thin-skinned about Heat, cold, and wind and rain, Or illness, bondage, beatings, and such— Being so makes them worse.
6-16.en_text: So I won't be overly sensitive about heat, cold, wind, rain, illness, confinement, or being struck - reacting too strongly only makes these things worse.

6-17.text: Some, seeing their own blood, become Exceptionally courageous, And some, on seeing another’s blood, Will faint and fall unconscious.
6-17.en_text: Some people, seeing their own blood, become unusually brave, while others, seeing someone else's blood, faint and lose consciousness entirely.

6-18.text: This is from steadfastness of mind Or else from cowardice. Thus disregard the injuries— Do not let pains affect you.
6-18.en_text: This difference comes either from steadiness of mind or from a kind of timidity. So disregard your injuries - don't let pain get the better of you.

6-19.text: Though pain occurs, the wise do not Disturb their joy of mind. When waging war against afflictions, Harm’s plentiful in battle.
6-19.en_text: Even when pain arises, those who are wise don't let it disturb their inner peace. When waging war against negative emotions, plenty of hardship is only to be expected in the fight.

6-20.text: Triumphant heroes are they who Ignore all pain and quash Hatred and such—the enemy. Everyone else kills corpses.
6-20.en_text: True heroes are those who ignore all pain and overcome enemies like hatred. Everyone else, by comparison, is merely striking down lifeless bodies.

6-21.text: Plus, suffering has benefits: Weariness dispels arrogance; Compassion arises for the samsaric; Shunning misdeeds, you delight in virtue.
6-21.en_text: What's more, suffering has real benefits: it humbles arrogance, awakens compassion for those trapped in this cycle of rebirth, turns you away from wrongdoing, and draws you toward goodness.

6-22.text: We don’t get angry at bile and such, Great sources of suffering, So why be angry at the sentient? Conditions provoke them too.
6-22.en_text: We don't get angry at bile or other bodily imbalances, even though they're major sources of suffering - so why get angry at other people? They too are driven by conditions beyond their control.

6-23.text: Just as such illnesses occur Involuntarily, Afflictions are compelled to arise Involuntarily.
6-23.en_text: Just as such illnesses arise involuntarily, negative emotions also arise involuntarily, without anyone choosing them.

6-24.text: Though people don’t think, “I’ll get angry,” The commonplace angers them. Though they don’t think, “I shall arouse it,” Their fury still arises.
6-24.en_text: People don't decide in advance, "I will get angry now," yet everyday annoyances provoke them anyway. They don't decide, "I will feel this rage," yet it arises regardless.

6-25.text: All the offenses that there are, All manifold misdeeds, Occur because of their conditions— They have no self-control.
6-25.en_text: Every kind of wrongdoing, every variety of misdeed, arises because of its underlying conditions - none of it happens through some independent free choice.

6-26.text: And the assembly of conditions Has no thought “I’ll produce,” Nor does what it produces have The thought “I’ll be produced.”
6-26.en_text: The collection of conditions that produces something has no intention of "I will produce this," and what it produces has no intention of "I will be produced" either.

6-27.text: The primal substance that they claim And self that they imagine Do not think, “I will come to be,” And arise intentionally.
6-27.en_text: Even the "primal substance" some claim exists, or the fixed "self" people imagine, doesn't think, "I will now come into being," and arise on purpose.

6-28.text: Without arising, they don’t exist— What then would want to arise? Always distracted by an object, It also would never cease.
6-28.en_text: Before it comes into being, it doesn't exist yet - so what exactly would there be to want to arise? And if it's always fixed on some object, it could never stop existing either.

6-29.text: If permanent, the self, like space, Would clearly have no action. When it encounters other conditions, What acts on the unchanging?
6-29.en_text: If the self were permanent, like space itself, it clearly couldn't do anything at all. So when it meets other conditions, what part of something unchanging could possibly act?

6-30.text: If during the action, it’s like before, What does the action do to it? If you say, “This is what acts on it,” What is it that’s related?
6-30.en_text: If, during the action, it stays exactly the same as before, what did the action actually do to it? And if you say something else is what acts on it, then how is that connected to the self at all?

6-31.text: In this way, everything’s dependent And thus has no control. When you know that, you won’t get angry At any illusory thing.
6-31.en_text: In this way, everything arises dependent on conditions and has no independent control of its own. Once you understand this, you won't get angry at anything - it's all like an illusion.

6-32.text: “Who averts what? Even averting Would be illogical.” It’s logical to say suffering Will cease, dependent on that.
6-32.en_text: "But who is stopping what? Even the idea of stopping something would then make no sense." It does make sense, though, to say that suffering can end when its causes are removed.

6-33.text: Thus when you see a friend or foe Acting improperly, Think happily that this occurred Because of such conditions.
6-33.en_text: So when you see a friend or an enemy acting badly, remind yourself calmly that this is simply happening because of certain conditions.

6-34.text: If things were accomplished by free will, No living being at all Would ever have any suffering, For no one wants to suffer.
6-34.en_text: If everything happened purely through free choice, as people imagine, then no living being would ever suffer at all, since nobody actually wants to suffer.

6-35.text: They injure themselves by being careless Of thorns, et cetera. From lust, they starve themselves and such For sake of sex and the like.
6-35.en_text: Yet out of carelessness, people injure themselves on thorns and the like. Driven by craving, they starve themselves and do all sorts of things for the sake of romance and pleasure.

6-36.text: Some hang themselves or jump from cliffs, Take poison or eat poorly, Or behave unmeritoriously, Causing themselves harm.
6-36.en_text: Some hang themselves, jump from cliffs, take poison, eat harmful food, or otherwise act in destructive ways, causing harm to themselves.

6-37.text: When overcome by the afflictions, They’ll kill their own dear selves. At such a time, how would they not Cause harm to others’ bodies?
6-37.en_text: When overwhelmed by negative emotions, people will even kill the very self they cherish most. Given that, how could they possibly refrain from harming others as well?

6-38.text: Though rarely do we feel compassion For those who kill themselves And so forth when afflictions arise, What good is getting angry?
6-38.en_text: Even though we rarely feel compassion for those whose negative emotions drive them to kill themselves or do similar things, what good does it do to get angry at them instead?

6-39.text: If causing harm to others is The nature of the childish, Anger at them is as senseless as Resenting fire for heat.
6-39.en_text: If harming others were simply the fixed nature of foolish, untrained people, then being angry at them would make as little sense as resenting fire for being hot.

6-40.text: But if the fault is adventitious And beings’ natures are gentle, Anger at them would not be right, Like begrudging the sky for wafting smoke.
6-40.en_text: But if this fault is just a passing condition, and people's underlying nature is actually gentle, then anger at them makes no more sense than resenting the sky for carrying smoke.

6-41.text: If I, ignoring the main thing— The stick—get angry at its wielder, Who is impelled by ire, it’s right To get incensed at hatred.
6-41.en_text: If I overlook the real cause - the stick itself - and instead get angry only at the person who swings it, driven as they are by their own anger, then it would make far more sense to direct my anger at the anger itself.

6-42.text: I, in the past, have caused such harms To other sentient beings, So it is right these ills occur To me who have hurt beings.
6-42.en_text: I myself, in the past, have caused this same kind of harm to other beings, so it's only fitting that harm of this kind should now come back to me, who once hurt others.

6-43.text: Their weapons and my body both Are causes of suffering. They wield the weapons, I the body. With whom should I get angry?
6-43.en_text: Both their weapon and my own body are, in truth, the causes of this suffering. They wield the weapon; I supply the body. So which of us should I really be angry at?

6-44.text: Blinded by craving, I have grasped This human body-like blister That, prone to pain, can’t bear being touched. Whom to get mad at when it’s hurt?
6-44.en_text: Blinded by craving, I have grasped onto this human body - fragile as a blister, unable to bear even a light touch. When it gets hurt, who exactly is there to be angry at?

6-45.text: The childish don’t want suffering, But thirst for suffering’s causes. Can I resent another being When harmed by my own wrongs?
6-45.en_text: Foolish, untrained people don't want suffering, and yet they can't stop craving its very causes. So when I'm harmed because of my own past wrongs, how can I really resent the other person?

6-46.text: If like the guardians of hell And like the sword-leaf forests, This is produced by my own actions, At whom should I get angry?
6-46.en_text: If this harm, like the punishments dealt out in hell or the forests of sword-like leaves there, is ultimately produced by my own past actions, then who exactly should I be angry at?

6-47.text: If those who, goaded by my karma, Appear and do me harm Should go to hell because of that, Have I not brought them ruin?
6-47.en_text: If those who, prompted by the results of my own past actions, appear and harm me will themselves end up in a hellish state because of it, then haven't I, in effect, brought about their downfall?

6-48.text: Because of them, I’ll purify My many misdeeds through patience. Because of me, they’ll go to hell’s Long-lasting agonies.
6-48.en_text: Because of them, I get to purify many of my own past wrongs through practicing patience. Because of me, they will face long and terrible suffering in return.

6-49.text: If I am causing harm to them While they are helping me, Why, O cruel mind, do you get angry Mistakenly at them?
6-49.en_text: If, in truth, I am the one harming them, even while they seem to be helping me purify my wrongs, then why, cruel mind, are you getting angry at them by mistake?

6-50.text: If I’ve the quality of intention, I will not go to hell, And what can happen to them now If I protect myself?
6-50.en_text: If I can maintain a good intention throughout, I won't end up in a hellish state myself - so what would even happen to them now, if I simply protect my own state of mind?

6-51.text: But if I harm them in return, They will not be protected While my own conduct is debased; Austerity destroyed.
6-51.en_text: But if I strike back at them in return, then they won't be protected from harm either, and meanwhile my own conduct will be corrupted, and my discipline undone.

6-52.text: Because the mind’s not physical, No one can wound it at all. Because of fixation on the body, The body is harmed by pain.
6-52.en_text: Because the mind has no physical form, nothing can actually wound it directly. It's only because of our attachment to the body that pain is able to harm us at all.

6-53.text: Contemptuousness, abusive speech, And words that are unpleasant Inflict no harm upon the body. Mind, why do they incense you?
6-53.en_text: Contempt, harsh words, and unpleasant speech cause no real injury to the body. So mind, why do you let them provoke you so strongly?

6-54.text: Displeasure others show for me Will not devour me In this or in another life. So why do I dislike it?
6-54.en_text: Other people's displeasure with me won't devour me in this life or in any future one - so why do I dislike it so much?

6-55.text: Though I do not want that because It blocks material gain, I’ll leave my things behind me here, While wrongs will long remain.
6-55.en_text: Even though I dislike it because it blocks material gain, I will leave all my possessions behind when I die, while any wrongdoing I've done will follow me for a long time.

6-56.text: It’s better I die now than live Long with wrong livelihood. Even were I to live for long, The pain of death’s the same.
6-56.en_text: It would be better to die right now than to live a long life through wrong ways of making a living. Even if I lived a very long time, the pain of death would be just the same in the end.

6-57.text: Someone feels bliss a hundred years In a dream and then wakes up. Another experiences bliss A moment and then wakes.
6-57.en_text: One person feels pleasure for a hundred years in a dream, then wakes up. Another experiences pleasure for just a single moment, then wakes up.

6-58.text: For either of the two who wake, That bliss will never return. A long life and a short life both Are finished when we die.
6-58.en_text: For both of them, once awake, that pleasure never returns. In the same way, a long life and a short life both come to the very same end when death arrives.

6-59.text: Though we acquire many things And enjoy them a long time, We will go as if robbed by bandits— Naked and empty-handed.
6-59.en_text: Even if I gain many possessions and enjoy them for a long time, I will still leave this life as if robbed by bandits - empty-handed, with nothing at all.

6-60.text: If I live off my gains to abate My wrongs and practice virtue, Won’t anger for the sake of goods Waste virtue and be a wrong?
6-60.en_text: If I'm living off my gains in order to reduce my wrongdoing and practice goodness, then wouldn't getting angry over material things itself waste that goodness and become a wrongdoing in its own right?

6-61.text: And if the purpose of my living Itself should be debased, What good’s this life when all I do Is to commit misdeeds?
6-61.en_text: And if the very purpose of my life becomes corrupted this way, what good is this life at all, if all I end up doing is committing more wrongs?

6-62.text: Those who disparage you harm beings So you get angry, you say. Why don’t you also get upset When others are disparaged?
6-62.en_text: You say you get angry at someone who insults you because it harms others too. But then why don't you also get upset when someone else is insulted?

6-63.text: If losing faith depends on others So you forgive the faithless, Afflictions depend on conditions, So why not forgive your critics?
6-63.en_text: If you can forgive people who lose faith in something simply because it depends on outside causes, then since negative emotions also depend on conditions, why not forgive your critics in just the same way?

6-64.text: It’s not right to get angry at those Who insult or destroy Statues, stupas, and the true dharma— The buddhas and such aren’t harmed.
6-64.en_text: It isn't right to get angry at those who insult or destroy sacred images, shrines, or the true teachings - the buddhas themselves are not actually harmed by any of this.

6-65.text: As taught above, see those who harm Your master, kin, and friends As doing so from circumstances And thus stave off your anger.
6-65.en_text: As explained earlier, see anyone who harms your teacher, family, or friends as acting out of the very same web of conditions, and let that understanding hold back your anger.

6-66.text: If both the sentient and nonsentient Cause harm to living beings, Why single out and resent the sentient? Forbear their harms instead.
6-66.en_text: If harm to living beings comes from both living and non-living causes alike, why single out and resent only the living cause? Better to simply bear the harm patiently either way.

6-67.text: Some, being ignorant, do wrong. Some, being ignorant, get angry. What would make either innocent? Which of the two is guilty?
6-67.en_text: Some people, out of ignorance, do wrong. Others, out of ignorance, get angry in response. Which of the two, if either, is truly innocent, and which is truly guilty?

6-68.text: Why in the past did they do acts That would make others harm them? Since everything depends on karma, Why hold a grudge for the other?
6-68.en_text: Why did they, in the past, do the kinds of things that would lead others to harm them now? Since everything unfolds according to cause and effect, why hold a grudge against the other person at all?

6-69.text: Realizing this, no matter what, I will endeavor at merits So everyone will come to have Mutually loving thoughts.
6-69.en_text: Understanding this, whatever happens, I will make every effort to build goodness, so that all beings might come to hold loving thoughts toward one another.

6-70.text: When fire that has burned one house Spreads to another home, You gather up and throw away The straw and such that fuel it.
6-70.en_text: When a fire that has burned down one house threatens to spread to another, you quickly gather up and throw away the straw and kindling that would feed it.

6-71.text: Likewise throw away instantly Whatever you’re attached to That fuels the fires of hatred, fearing It will consume your merit.
6-71.en_text: In the very same way, immediately let go of anything you're attached to that feeds the fire of hatred - out of fear that it will burn away all the goodness you've built.

6-72.text: What’s wrong if someone condemned to death, Their hand cut off, is freed? What’s wrong with human suffering Removing you from the hells?
6-72.en_text: What's wrong with someone condemned to death having their sentence reduced to just losing a hand instead? What's wrong with ordinary human suffering being the thing that spares you from the hells?

6-73.text: If I cannot bear this amount Of suffering in the present, Why then do I not stop my anger, Cause of hell’s agonies?
6-73.en_text: If I can't even bear this small amount of suffering here and now, then why don't I let go of my anger, which is the very cause of the far greater suffering of the hells?

6-74.text: For sake of desire, a thousand times I have experienced Being burned and such in hell but done No good for myself or others.
6-74.en_text: For the sake of fleeting desires, I have already endured being burned and tormented in hell a thousand times over, and it accomplished nothing good for myself or for anyone else.

6-75.text: But this is not that great a harm, And a great aim will be accomplished. It’s right to only be delighted At pains that dispel harm to beings.
6-75.en_text: But this present hardship is nothing compared to that, and it serves a truly great purpose. I should actually be glad to endure suffering that removes far greater harm to beings.

6-76.text: If others are pleased when they praise someone As having qualities, Why then, O mind, do you not as well Praise them and take delight?
6-76.en_text: If people feel happy when someone is praised for their good qualities, then why, mind, don't you also praise them and share in that same joy?

6-77.text: Your pleasure from rejoicing is A blameless source of delight Allowed by those with qualities— The best way to gather others.
6-77.en_text: The joy you feel from celebrating others' goodness is a completely blameless source of happiness - one that good people themselves encourage, and the very best way to draw others closer.

6-78.text: “But others will be happy too.” If you don’t want this joy, You’ve stopped paying wages and will thus Destroy the seen and unseen.
6-78.en_text: "But if I do that, others will end up happy too." If you don't want that kind of shared joy for yourself, then you should stop paying anyone kindness at all, and you'll end up losing benefit both now and later.

6-79.text: When yours are the qualities described, You want that others be pleased. When others’ qualities are described, You don’t want to be pleased yourself.
6-79.en_text: When your own good qualities are praised, you want others to feel pleased about it. But when someone else's good qualities are praised, you don't want to feel pleased yourself.

6-80.text: If you roused bodhichitta because You want all beings to be happy, When beings find themselves happiness, Why does that make you angry?
6-80.en_text: If you gave rise to the wish to help all beings because you want everyone to be happy, then why does it upset you when beings actually find happiness on their own?

6-81.text: If you want for beings the buddhahood Adored in the three worlds, Why does it gall you so to see Them have some paltry honor?
6-81.en_text: If you wish for beings to reach the full enlightenment honored throughout the universe, why does it bother you so much to see them receive some small measure of recognition now?

6-82.text: If a relative whom you support— Someone to whom you give— Should gain a livelihood, would you Be angry instead of pleased?
6-82.en_text: If a family member you support were to find their own means of living, would that make you angry, or would it make you glad?

6-83.text: If you don’t want even that for beings, How can you wish them enlightenment? If you are irked by others’ wealth, How can you have bodhichitta?
6-83.en_text: If you don't even want that much for other beings, how can you claim to wish them full enlightenment? And if you're bothered by others having wealth, how can you really have the wish to help all beings?

6-84.text: If they get something or it remains Inside the patron’s house, In either case, it is not yours. Given or not, why care?
6-84.en_text: Whether what someone gains stays with them or ends up somewhere else entirely, either way, it was never yours to begin with. So whether it's given away or not, why does it concern you at all?

6-85.text: Why do you throw away your merits, Your faith, and qualities? Tell why you’re not angry at the one Who doesn’t hold on to their gains.
6-85.en_text: Why would you throw away your own goodness, your faith, and your good qualities like this? Tell me - why aren't you instead angry at yourself, for not being able to let go of your own attachment to gain?

6-86.text: Do you not only feel no sorrow For the wrongs you’ve done yourself But also want to vie against Those who have performed merit?
6-86.en_text: Not only do you feel no regret over the wrongs you've done yourself, but you even want to compete with those who have actually done good?

6-87.text: Even when enemies are displeased, What’s there for you to enjoy? The wishes in your mind alone Won’t cause them any harm.
6-87.en_text: Even when your enemies are made unhappy, what benefit is that really to you? The wishes in your own mind alone cannot actually cause them any harm.

6-88.text: How would it please you to accomplish The pain you wish for them? You say you would be satisfied— What greater ruin than that?
6-88.en_text: And even if your wish for their suffering somehow came true, what real satisfaction would that bring you? You might say you'd feel satisfied - but what could be more ruinous than that?

6-89.text: Unbearably sharp, the hook cast by The fishermen, afflictions. Caught on it, surely I’ll be cooked In cauldrons by hell’s keepers.
6-89.en_text: The hook cast by these fishermen - our own negative emotions - is unbearably sharp. Once caught on it, I will surely be dragged off to be tormented by the guardians of hell.

6-90.text: Praise, fame, and honor will not beget Merit or a long life. They will not bring me strength, good health, Or physical well-being.
6-90.en_text: Praise, fame, and honor will not bring you goodness or a longer life. They won't give you strength, good health, or physical well-being either.

6-91.text: If I know what is good for me, What’s good for me in those? If all you want is mental pleasure, Use drink and dice and such.
6-91.en_text: If I truly understood what's good for me, what benefit would I find in these things? If all you're really after is a pleasant feeling in the mind, you might as well seek it through drink or games of chance.

6-92.text: For sake of fame, some squander wealth Or even get themselves killed. What use are words? When you are dead, Who will they make happy?
6-92.en_text: For the sake of fame, some people waste their wealth, or even get themselves killed. What use are mere words of praise, when you're dead - who exactly do they make happy then?

6-93.text: When their sand castles are destroyed, Children wail in distress. Likewise when I lose praise and fame, My mind is like a child’s.
6-93.en_text: When their sandcastles are destroyed, children cry out in distress. In just the same way, when I lose praise and fame, my own reaction is really no different from a child's.

6-94.text: Words have no mind; for them to wish To praise me is impossible. Though hearing that another likes me May be a cause of pleasure,
6-94.en_text: Words themselves have no mind, so it's impossible for them to actually intend to praise me. Still, hearing that someone approves of me might genuinely bring me pleasure -

6-95.text: What good does someone else’s fondness For me or another do me? That like and pleasure is their own; I won’t get even a bit.
6-95.en_text: but what real good does someone else's approval - of me or of anyone - actually do for me? That liking and pleasure belongs entirely to them; I don't gain even the smallest share of it myself.

6-96.text: If their being happy makes me pleased, I should be so for all. Why aren’t I pleased when they’re made happy By their love for another?
6-96.en_text: If their happiness makes me happy, then I should feel that way about everyone's happiness. So why don't I feel pleased when people are made happy by their fondness for someone else instead of me?

6-97.text: Therefore my pleasure that arises When I am being praised Is irrational and nothing more Than just a child’s behavior.
6-97.en_text: So the pleasure that arises in me from being praised is simply unreasonable - nothing more than childish behavior.

6-98.text: Praise and so forth bring distraction, Destroy world weariness, Cause envy of those with qualities, And ruin prosperity.
6-98.en_text: Praise and the like distract the mind, undermine a healthy sense of the world's shortcomings, stir up envy of those who are genuinely good, and can ruin one's own progress.

6-99.text: So haven’t those who lurk nearby To wreck my acclaim and such Come to protect me against falling Into the lower realms?
6-99.en_text: So haven't those nearby who try to wreck my reputation actually done me a service, by helping protect me from falling into the lower realms?

6-100.text: What need have I, who seek liberation, Of the fetters, gain and respect? And why should I get angry at those Who release me when I’m bound?
6-100.en_text: What use do I, who am seeking freedom, have for the shackles of gain and reputation? And why would I get angry at those who release me when I'm bound by them?

6-101.text: When I want to rush into suffering, How is it I get angry At those who, as if blessed by the Buddha, Don’t let me, blocking the way?
6-101.en_text: When I'm about to rush headlong into suffering, why would I get angry at those who, as if guided by the Buddha himself, block my way and stop me?

6-102.text: It makes no sense to get angry at those Who I think thwart my merit. If there’s no austerity like patience, Should I not dwell in that?
6-102.en_text: It makes no sense to be angry at those I think are blocking my chance to build goodness. After all, if there's no discipline equal to patience, shouldn't I be glad to practice exactly that?

6-103.text: If I cannot be patient with them Because of my own faults, Then all I’ve done is block the cause Of merit that was at hand.
6-103.en_text: If I fail to be patient with them simply because of my own shortcomings, then I am the one blocking the very cause of goodness that was right there in front of me.

6-104.text: If the cause of something is that which If absent, it won’t be, And with which, it will come to be, How is that called an obstruction?
6-104.en_text: If the cause of something is simply that which, when absent, prevents the result, and which, when present, brings the result about, then how could this possibly be called an obstruction?

6-105.text: A beggar appearing at the right time Does not prevent your giving. It is not right to say your abbot Stopped you from going forth.
6-105.en_text: A beggar showing up at the right moment doesn't prevent you from giving - it's the occasion for it. In the same way, it's not right to say that your teacher "stopped" you from progressing by presenting a difficulty.

6-106.text: Though there are beggars in this world, Those who cause harm are rare, For if you do no harm to others, No one will harm you back.
6-106.en_text: Although there are plenty of beggars in this world, those who actually cause real harm are rare - because if you cause no harm to others, few will ever harm you in return.

6-107.text: Therefore just like a trove appearing Painlessly in a home, I will delight in enemies, My friends in enlightened conduct.
6-107.en_text: So, just as an unexpected treasure appearing in one's own home brings no hardship, I will welcome enemies with the same delight, since they help me build the goodness that comes from patient conduct.

6-108.text: Since they and I created it, It’s right to give the fruits Of patience to my enemies first, For they’re the cause of patience.
6-108.en_text: Since both my enemy and I together create the occasion for it, it's only right that the benefit of my patience should go to my enemies first, since they are the very cause of that patience.

6-109.text: If enemies deserve no honor Since they’ve no thought to make you patient, Why would you honor the true dharma, The cause of accomplishment?
6-109.en_text: If you say enemies deserve no honor because they have no actual intention to help you build patience, then why would you honor the true teachings themselves, which are simply the cause of your progress?

6-110.text: Though you won’t honor your enemies Because they want to harm you, If they, like doctors, wished to help, How could they make you patient?
6-110.en_text: You might say you won't honor your enemies because they intend to harm you. But if they intended instead to help you, like a doctor would, how would that even give you the opportunity to practice patience?

6-111.text: Thus since malevolent intent Is what produces patience, Just they are the cause of patience and worthy Of veneration, like true dharma.
6-111.en_text: So, since it is precisely their harmful intent that gives rise to patience, it's the enemy themselves who are the true cause of patience, and worthy of honor for that reason, just as the true teachings are.

6-112.text: These are the fields of sentient beings And victors, said the Sage. Many who have respected them Have gone beyond to perfection.
6-112.en_text: The wise teacher has said that both ordinary beings and the buddhas are, in this sense, sources of great benefit. Many who have honored them in this way have gone on to reach perfection.

6-113.text: A buddha’s qualities are gained From beings and buddhas alike. How is it right to have respect For victors but not beings?
6-113.en_text: A buddha's good qualities are cultivated through both ordinary beings and the buddhas alike. So how is it right to honor the buddhas but not ordinary beings?

6-114.text: It’s not from qualities of intention But due to the results That beings have qualities like theirs And therefore are their equals.
6-114.en_text: It's not that beings share the buddhas' inner qualities of realization, but rather that, through the results they help bring about, beings become similar to the buddhas in that respect, and so deserve to be honored just the same.

6-115.text: Offering to those with loving-kindness Is sentient beings’ greatness. The merit of having faith in the buddhas Is the buddhas’ greatness.
6-115.en_text: Making offerings to those with loving-kindness reveals the true greatness of sentient beings. And the goodness that comes from having faith in the buddhas reveals the greatness of the buddhas themselves.

6-116.text: For gaining a buddha’s traits, they have A part and are thus equal. Infinite oceans of qualities, The buddhas are equaled by none.
6-116.en_text: Since beings play a part in bringing about a buddha's supreme qualities, they share, to that extent, in that greatness - though nothing can truly equal the buddhas, whose good qualities are as vast as endless oceans.

6-117.text: Offering even the three realms To those who appear to have A tiny share of the qualities Of those who are the unique Collection of sublime qualities Would be inadequate.
6-117.en_text: Even offering the three entire worlds would not be enough repayment to those who hold even a small share in giving rise to the unique and perfect qualities found only in the buddhas.

6-118.text: Since beings have a part in the birth Of a buddha’s supreme traits, They’re similar to that extent And thus deserve veneration.
6-118.en_text: Since beings have a real part in bringing about a buddha's supreme qualities, they deserve honor to that same extent.

6-119.text: Other than pleasing sentient beings, What way is there to repay Those stalwart friends who act to bring Immeasurable benefit?
6-119.en_text: Other than working to make beings happy, what other way is there to repay these steadfast friends who bring about immeasurable benefit for us?

6-120.text: Since helping them repays those who forsake Their bodies and go to the Incessant Hell, Even when they inflict on you great harm, Make all your actions solely excellent.
6-120.en_text: Since it is a fitting way to repay those who gave up even their own bodies and entered the deepest suffering for the sake of beings, make every one of your actions excellent, even when beings cause you great harm in return.

6-121.text: Meanwhile, how is it I—an ignoramus— Am prideful and don’t act like a true servant To those for whose sake they who are my lords Have disregarded even their own bodies?
6-121.en_text: How is it, then, that I - so foolish - remain full of pride and fail to act like a true servant toward those for whose sake my spiritual guides disregarded even their own bodies?

6-122.text: Making them happy, whose happiness delights And injuries distress the lords of sages, Brings all the lords of sages gratification, While harming them brings injury to the sages.
6-122.en_text: Making beings happy brings joy to the compassionate ones, whose happiness depends on beings' well-being and who are pained by beings' suffering. Harming beings, in turn, brings pain to those same compassionate ones.

6-123.text: Just as no object of desire will bring Happiness when your body is on fire, If you harm sentient beings, there is no way That those with great compassion could be pleased.
6-123.en_text: Just as nothing brings pleasure while your own body is on fire, there is no way for those of great compassion to feel pleased if you cause harm to other beings.

6-124.text: Therefore I now confess all my misdeeds, Which, as they have caused harm to sentient beings, Distress all those endowed with great compassion. May all those whom I have displeased forgive me.
6-124.en_text: So I now confess all the wrongs I have done that have caused harm to other beings and, in doing so, brought distress to all those filled with great compassion. May everyone I have displeased forgive me.

6-125.text: To please the tathagatas, from today onward I shall be the world’s slave. I won’t strike back, No matter how many people stomp my crown Or kill me. Guardians of the world, be happy!
6-125.en_text: From today on, in order to please the buddhas, I will be the willing servant of the world. I will not strike back, no matter how many people might attack or even try to kill me. Guardians of the world, be at peace!

6-126.text: There’s no doubt they whose nature is compassion Regard all of these beings as themselves. Those who are seen as sentient beings in nature Are guardians in essence—why disrespect them?
6-126.en_text: There is no doubt that those whose very nature is compassion regard all these beings as no different from themselves. Since beings, in essence, are exactly what these compassionate guardians cherish most, how could they ever deserve disrespect?

6-127.text: Just this is what will please the tathagatas. Just this is what fulfills my very own aims. Just this dispels the sufferings of the world, And therefore I will always do just this.
6-127.en_text: This alone is what truly pleases the buddhas. This alone is what truly fulfills my own deepest purpose. This alone removes the suffering of the world. So this is what I will always strive to do.

6-128.text: Just as, when one of the king’s men Wreaks havoc on many people, Even if able, the farsighted Do not retaliate
6-128.en_text: Just as a farsighted person, even if capable of retaliation, would not strike back against one of the king's soldiers who was causing widespread harm,

6-129.text: For he is not alone—his forces Are the forces of the king— Likewise do not look down upon Weak people who cause harm,
6-129.en_text: because that soldier is not acting alone, but backed by the full power of the king - in just the same way, don't look down on seemingly weak people who cause you harm,

6-130.text: For theirs are the forces of hell’s keepers And of the compassionate. Just as his subjects propitiate A tyrant, respect beings.
6-130.en_text: for behind them stand the forces of the lower realms and the power of the compassionate ones. Just as subjects appease even a harsh ruler, treat all beings with the same kind of respect.

6-131.text: Even if angered, could a king Inflict what is experienced Because of making beings despair— The agonies of hell?
6-131.en_text: Even an angry king could never inflict on you the kind of suffering that comes from causing beings despair - the agonies of the deepest hell.

6-132.text: Even if pleased, a king could not Provide what is achieved By making sentient beings happy— Buddhahood itself.
6-132.en_text: And even a delighted king could never grant you what comes from making beings genuinely happy - nothing less than full enlightenment itself.

6-133.text: Leave future buddhahood aside, Do you not see in this life That pleasing sentient beings brings Much glory, fame, and joy?
6-133.en_text: Setting aside future enlightenment altogether, don't you already see in this very life that making beings happy brings you great renown, good standing, and joy?

6-134.text: While in samsara, patience brings Beauty and so forth, Good health, prestige, a very long life, And a chakravarti’s pleasures.
6-134.en_text: While still within this cycle of rebirth, patience brings beauty, good health, a respected standing, a very long life, and even the greatest pleasures a ruler of the world could know.

7-0.text: The sixth chapter, “Transcendent Patience,” from Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva. ^6-a 7. Teachings on Diligence
7-0.en_text: The sixth chapter, "The Perfection of Patience," from Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva. 7. Teachings on Diligence

7-1.text: Thus with patience, be diligent. Enlightenment dwells in striving so. There is no motion without wind; No merit without diligence.
7-1.en_text: So, with patience established, be diligent. Enlightenment depends on this kind of sustained effort. Just as there's no movement without wind, there's no real goodness without diligence.

7-2.text: Diligence is a zest for virtue. What’s contrary to that? To explain, It’s laziness—clinging to the bad And sloth and self-disparagement.
7-2.en_text: Diligence means having real enthusiasm for doing good. What's its opposite? To put it simply, it's laziness - clinging to unhelpful habits, sluggishness, and putting yourself down.

7-3.text: Laziness arises from Not wearying of samsaric pain, From craving sleep and savoring The pleasures of being indolent.
7-3.en_text: Laziness comes from not being tired enough of the pain of this endless cycle of rebirth, from craving sleep, and from savoring the comfort of doing nothing.

7-4.text: Stalked by the hunters, the afflictions, You’ve walked into the trap of birth. Yet do you still not understand You’ve entered the maw of the Lord of Death?
7-4.en_text: Stalked by the hunters that are your own negative emotions, you have already walked straight into the trap of rebirth. Yet do you still not realize you have already entered the very jaws of death?

7-5.text: Have you not seen that your compeers Are being killed, one after another? Still, even so you fall asleep, Just like a buffalo with a butcher.
7-5.en_text: Haven't you seen your peers being taken away, one after another? And still, even now, you drift off to sleep, just like cattle led calmly toward the slaughterhouse.

7-6.text: When all around the ways are blocked And the Lord of Death is watching you, How is it you enjoy your food? How can you like so much to sleep?
7-6.en_text: When every escape route is blocked, and death itself is watching your every move, how can you still enjoy your food? How can you still want so badly to sleep?

7-7.text: You will die soon, so until then Gather the accumulations. For then, when there is no more time To give up sloth, what will you do?
7-7.en_text: You will die soon enough, so until then, gather all the goodness you can. Because when the time comes and there's no more time left to give up laziness, what will you do then?

7-8.text: This is undone, this just begun, And this remains but halfway done. The Lord of Death will suddenly come, And you will think, “Alas, I’m finished!”
7-8.en_text: This task is left unfinished, this one barely begun, and this other one only halfway done. Death will arrive without warning, and you'll think, "I'm not ready - it's too late!"

7-9.text: You’ll watch your relatives lose all hope As tears from shock of grief roll down Their faces, their eyes red and swollen. You’ll see the faces of Yama’s henchmen.
7-9.en_text: You'll watch your loved ones lose all hope, tears streaming down their faces from shock and grief, their eyes red and swollen. And you'll see the terrifying faces of death's own agents.

7-10.text: Recalling your misdeeds with anguish And hearing the din of hell, the dread Will make you foul yourself with filth. You’ll be in torment—what will you do?
7-10.en_text: Recalling your past wrongs with anguish, and hearing the terrible sounds of hell, dread will overtake you completely. Caught in torment, what will you do then?

7-11.text: If like a living, writhing fish, You have such terror in this life, What of the intense suffering Of hell from the misdeeds you’ve done?
7-11.en_text: If even now, like a fish thrashing out of water, you feel this much fear in ordinary life, imagine the intense suffering that awaits in the hells because of the wrongs you've done.

7-12.text: Your flesh is tender when it’s touched By scalding water, yet you have done The karma of the hottest hells. Why do you stay so comfortably?
7-12.en_text: Your skin is so sensitive that even scalding water hurts it, yet you have done the kind of things that lead to the hottest hells. Why, then, do you still feel so at ease?

7-13.text: You want results without any effort— Such pain for one so delicate! When grasped by death, you’re like a god. Alas! Suffering will destroy you!
7-13.en_text: You want good results without any effort - what a delicate soul, wanting so much yet fearing so little pain! When death finally seizes you, you act as though you were untouchable. But it will only bring suffering that destroys you.

7-14.text: Free yourself with the human boat From the great river of suffering. Such a boat is hard to get again. Now is no time for sleep, you fool.
7-14.en_text: Use this rare human life, like a sturdy boat, to cross the great river of suffering. A boat like this is extremely hard to come by again. Now is no time to sleep, foolish mind.

7-15.text: Forsaking the sublime joy of dharma, The cause of infinite delight, Why do you relish such distractions And games that will cause suffering?
7-15.en_text: Turning away from the sublime joy of genuine practice - the true source of boundless happiness - why do you instead chase after distractions and pastimes that will only lead to suffering?

7-16.text: Don’t be discouraged; practice with The forces, purpose, and self-control: The equality of self and others And exchanging yourself for others.
7-16.en_text: Don't lose heart. Instead, practice using four supports: real inner strength, a clear sense of purpose, genuine joy in the work, and the ability to set it aside and rest when needed - along with seeing yourself and others as fundamentally equal, and learning to place others' well-being where you once placed only your own.

7-17.text: Don’t get demoralized and think, “How is it I could be awakened?” For the Tathagata who speaks The truth has spoken truly thus:
7-17.en_text: Don't become discouraged and think, "How could someone like me ever become enlightened?" Because the Buddha, who always speaks the truth, has said this, and it is entirely true:

7-18.text: If they should rouse the strength of effort, Even gnats, mosquitoes, bees, and worms Will gain what is so hard to achieve— Unexcelled enlightenment.
7-18.en_text: Even gnats, mosquitoes, bees, and worms, if they were to summon the strength of real effort, could attain what is otherwise so hard to reach - unsurpassed enlightenment itself.

7-19.text: If I, born in the human race, Can recognize what helps and harms And don’t give up enlightened conduct, Why wouldn’t I reach enlightenment?
7-19.en_text: So if I, born into human life, am able to tell what helps from what harms, and don't abandon the way of living that leads to enlightenment, why wouldn't I reach it myself?

7-20.text: “But I’m afraid of sacrificing My limbs and such,” I say, not thinking What is severe and what is light— Delusion has left me in fear.
7-20.en_text: "But I'm afraid of having to give up my limbs and so on," I say - without really thinking through what's actually serious and what's minor. This is simply confusion leaving me needlessly afraid.

7-21.text: For countless millions of aeons, I will be hacked and stabbed and burnt And rent asunder many times, But not achieve enlightenment.
7-21.en_text: For countless millions of ages, I have already been cut, stabbed, burned, and torn apart again and again, all without ever achieving enlightenment.

7-22.text: The suffering for me to achieve Enlightenment, though, has a limit, Like pain from an incision made To excise a painful foreign object.
7-22.en_text: But the suffering needed to actually reach enlightenment has a clear limit - like the brief pain of a surgical cut made to remove something harmful lodged inside the body.

7-23.text: All physicians cure disease Through the discomfort of a treatment. Therefore put up with small distress To overcome myriad sufferings.
7-23.en_text: Every doctor cures illness through some amount of uncomfortable treatment. In the same way, put up with a little discomfort now in order to overcome far greater suffering later.

7-24.text: The Supreme Physician does not use Commonplace treatments such as those. He cures unfathomably great diseases With the most gentle of remedies.
7-24.en_text: Yet the Buddha, the supreme healer, doesn't rely only on such ordinary treatments. He cures immeasurably serious conditions using the gentlest of remedies.

7-25.text: Initially, the Guide prescribes Giving away vegetables and the like. Eventually, when used to that, You will be able to give your flesh.
7-25.en_text: At first, the Buddha, our guide, suggests simply giving away things like vegetables and food. Only later, once you're accustomed to that, will you be ready to give away even your own body.

7-26.text: For once you understand your body To be like vegetables and such, What difficulty would there be In relinquishing your flesh and such?
7-26.en_text: Because once you truly understand your body to be just like those vegetables and other simple things, what real difficulty would there be in giving up your own flesh as well?

7-27.text: There is no pain from giving up wrong, No melancholy from being wise, For harm to the body is from misdeeds And harm to the mind from misconceptions.
7-27.en_text: There is no real pain in giving up wrongdoing, and no real sorrow that comes from wisdom, because physical suffering comes from past wrongdoing, and mental suffering comes from mistaken ways of thinking.

7-28.text: If physical pleasure is from merit And mental pleasure from being wise, Would the compassionate despair To stay in samsara for others’ sake?
7-28.en_text: If physical well-being comes from goodness, and mental well-being comes from wisdom, then why would someone truly compassionate ever feel discouraged about remaining in this cycle of rebirth for the sake of others?

7-29.text: Because the power of bodhichitta Exhausts one’s misdeeds from the past And gathers oceans of merit, it’s taught That they surpass the shravakas.
7-29.en_text: Because the power of the wish to help all beings both clears away one's past wrongs and gathers vast, ocean-like goodness, it's taught that this path surpasses even that of those who seek liberation for themselves alone.

7-30.text: So ride the horse of bodhichitta That banishes all weariness. Who in their senses would be lazy To go from one joy to the next?
7-30.en_text: So mount the horse that is this wish to help all beings - a horse that carries away all exhaustion. What sensible person would be lazy about moving from one joy straight into the next?

7-31.text: To benefit beings, the forces are Longing, steadfastness, joy, and deferring. Longing is born of fearing suffering And contemplating its benefits.
7-31.en_text: To truly benefit beings, four supports are needed: genuine longing, steady resolve, real joy in the effort, and the ability to set the work aside when needed. Longing arises from being afraid of suffering and reflecting on the benefits of overcoming it.

7-32.text: Thus give up what is contrary. By force of effort and mastery Of longing, pride, joy, putting aside, Strive to increase your diligence.
7-32.en_text: So let go of whatever works against this. Through sustained effort and by mastering longing, healthy confidence, joy in the work, and the ability to pause and rest, strive to build up your diligence.

7-33.text: My own and others’ infinite wrongs Are mine indeed to eliminate, But every single fault will take An ocean of aeons to extinguish,
7-33.en_text: There are countless wrongs, both my own and others', that I need to overcome, yet even a single one of these faults could take an entire ocean of ages to fully clear away.

7-34.text: And I don’t see that I’ve begun To exhaust them even the slightest bit. Infinite suffering is my lot; Why does my heart not burst apart?
7-34.en_text: And I don't see that I've even begun to make the slightest dent in them. With this much suffering ahead of me, why doesn't my heart break with urgency?

7-35.text: My own and others’ numerous Qualities are for me to accomplish, And though each quality will take An ocean of aeons to cultivate,
7-35.en_text: There are also countless good qualities, both my own and others', that I need to cultivate, and even a single one of these could take an entire ocean of ages to develop.

7-36.text: I’ve never cultivated even A fraction of a quality. It is astounding how I’ve squandered This birth that somehow I’ve achieved.
7-36.en_text: Yet I have never cultivated even a fraction of a single one of them. It's astonishing how completely I've squandered this rare human life I somehow managed to gain.

7-37.text: I haven’t worshipped the Bhagavan Or given the pleasures of great feasts. I have not acted for the teachings, Fulfilled the wishes of the poor,
7-37.en_text: I have not honored the Buddha, nor offered the joys of great feasts in his name. I have done nothing for the sake of the teachings, nor fulfilled the needs of the poor,

7-38.text: Provided safety to those in fear, Or given comfort to the wretched. All I’ve created is suffering And pain inside my mother’s womb.
7-38.en_text: nor given safety to those who were afraid, nor offered comfort to those in misery. All I have really produced is suffering - even the suffering I caused my own mother while still in her womb.

7-39.text: Because I have not longed for dharma, Such tribulations have occurred To me before and even now. Who would forsake the wish for dharma?
7-39.en_text: Because I have never truly longed for genuine practice, hardships like these have happened to me before, and continue to happen even now. Who, understanding this, would ever give up the wish for genuine practice?

7-40.text: The Sage has said the basis of Everything virtuous is longing. The root of that is meditating On the full ripening of results.
7-40.en_text: The wise teacher has said that longing is the very foundation of all goodness. And the root of that longing is reflecting carefully on how our actions truly ripen into results.

7-41.text: Sufferings, unhappiness, Dangers of assorted types, And deprivation of desires Occur because of committing misdeeds.
7-41.en_text: Suffering, unhappiness, dangers of every kind, and being deprived of what we want - all of this happens because of the wrongs we commit.

7-42.text: Wherever they go, those who perform The virtue that their heart desires Will be welcomed with offerings Resulting from their acts of merit.
7-42.en_text: Wherever they go, those who do the good their heart truly desires are welcomed everywhere with honor and support, as a natural result of their good actions.

7-43.text: Wherever they go, those who commit Misdeeds, though they want happiness, Will be destroyed because of their wrongs By the weapons of suffering.
7-43.en_text: Wherever they go, those who commit wrongs, even while wanting happiness, will instead be struck down by the very weapons of suffering that come from their wrongdoing.

7-44.text: From virtues, you will dwell within the heart Of a vast, cool, and fragrant lotus flower, Where nourished by the pleasing voices of The victors, you will grow in majesty. And when, because of light rays from the sages, The lotus blossoms, you will then emerge Before the victors with a supreme body— You will become a child of the sugatas.
7-44.en_text: Because of your goodness, you will come to rest within the heart of a vast, cool, and fragrant lotus flower, nourished by the pleasing voices of the buddhas, growing there in splendor. And when, touched by rays of light from these great beings, the lotus finally opens, you will emerge before them with a wonderful new form - you will have become a child of the buddhas.

7-45.text: But from your many nonvirtues, the henchmen Of Yama will entirely flay your skin, And you will be most miserable and wretched. Then molten copper melted over the most Intense of fires will pour all over your body, And blows rained down by blazing swords and spears Will hack your flesh into a hundred pieces, And you will fall onto the burning iron ground.
7-45.en_text: But because of your many wrongs, death's agents will strip away your very skin, leaving you in complete misery and wretchedness. Then molten metal, melted over the most intense of fires, will be poured over your entire body, and blows from blazing swords and spears will hack your flesh into pieces, as you fall onto burning iron ground.

7-46.text: Therefore you should long for virtue And cultivate it with dedication. Once started, meditate on pride With the methods from the Vajradhvaja.
7-46.en_text: So you should genuinely long for goodness and cultivate it wholeheartedly. Once you begin, build up a healthy confidence in your own ability, following methods such as those taught in the Vajra Banner scripture.

7-47.text: Examine first your resources And then begin or don’t begin. Not starting may well be the best; Do not turn back once you’ve begun.
7-47.en_text: Examine your own resources and abilities first, and only then decide whether to begin or not. It may well be best not to start at all if you're not ready - but once you have begun, never turn back.

7-48.text: For with that habit, in other lives Misdeeds and suffering will increase, Or else the time of the result Will be diminished, unaccomplished.
7-48.en_text: Because if you make a habit of giving up midway, wrongdoing and suffering will only increase in future lives, or else the results you're working toward will be delayed or never accomplished at all.

7-49.text: Be prideful of these three: your acts, Afflictions, and ability. To say, “I shall do this alone,” Is in itself the pride of action.
7-49.en_text: Have healthy confidence in three things: your actions, your ability to overcome negative emotions, and your own capability. Saying, "I will do this myself," is itself the confidence needed for action.
