7-50.text: The worldly, overcome by afflictions, Cannot accomplish their own good. Beings are not as able as I, And therefore I’ll do this myself.
7-50.en_text: Ordinary people, overwhelmed by their own negative emotions, are unable to accomplish even their own good, let alone anyone else's. Since other beings aren't as capable as I am in this respect, I will take on this task myself.

7-51.text: How can I just sit there when Another does the menial work? If out of pride, I won’t do that, It’s best for me to have no pride.
7-51.en_text: How could I simply sit back while someone else does the hard, humble work? If pride keeps me from doing that kind of work myself, then it would be far better to have no such pride at all.

7-52.text: When it encounters a dead snake, Even a crow acts like a garuda. When I myself am weak, a downfall— Even if small—will cause me harm.
7-52.en_text: Even a crow, coming across a dead snake, will act boldly, as if it were a mighty bird of prey. In the same way, if I am weak-minded, even a small setback can end up causing me real harm.

7-53.text: Can there be freedom from privation For the disheartened who have stopped trying? It’s hard for even the great to best Those who have roused their pride and effort.
7-53.en_text: Can someone who has become discouraged and given up trying ever truly find freedom from lack? It's genuinely difficult, even for the strong, to overcome those who have built up real confidence and sustained effort.

7-54.text: Therefore with a steadfast mind, I’ll vanquish downfalls. If instead They conquer me, my wish to triumph Over the three realms is laughable.
7-54.en_text: So, with a steady and resolved mind, I will overcome every setback. But if setbacks overcome me instead, then my wish to triumph over all the difficulties of existence becomes laughable.

7-55.text: I’ll be victorious over all. I will let nothing vanquish me. A child of the lion, the Victor, I shall abide within such pride.
7-55.en_text: I will be the one who prevails over everything. I will let nothing defeat me. As a child of the fearless Buddha, I will hold fast to this kind of healthy confidence.

7-56.text: Those beings whom pride has subjugated Do not have pride; they are afflicted. They have succumbed to the foe pride— The proud are not controlled by foes.
7-56.en_text: Those who are ruled by arrogance don't actually have real confidence at all - they are simply overcome by a negative emotion. They have fallen under the power of the enemy that is arrogance. Someone with genuine confidence is never controlled by their enemies in this way.

7-57.text: Inflated by afflicted pride, That pride will lead you to lower realms, Destroying the feast of being human. A slave who feeds on others’ scraps, You will be stupid, ugly, and weak.
7-57.en_text: Puffed up with arrogance, that same arrogance will drag you down to the lower realms, destroying even the great fortune of your human life - you'll become like a servant surviving on others' leftovers, dull, unattractive, and weak.

7-58.text: You’ll be reviled everywhere. If wretched folk inflated with pride Are also counted among the proud, Do say, then, what the lowly are like.
7-58.en_text: You will be looked down upon everywhere. And if pitiful people puffed up with arrogance are still counted among the truly confident, then tell me - what would the truly lowly even look like?

7-59.text: Those who grasp pride in order to defeat the enemy pride, They are the proud, the victorious who are themselves the heroes. The ones who thus destroy the growing enemy of pride Will perfect the result of victory that beings desire.
7-59.en_text: But those who build genuine confidence specifically in order to overcome the enemy that is arrogance - they are the ones with real confidence, true heroes and victors. Those who defeat this ever-growing enemy of arrogance bring about the very victory that all beings truly long for.

7-60.text: Amidst the crowd of the afflictions, Persevere in a thousand ways. Like lions with jackals, do not let The hosts of the afflictions strike.
7-60.en_text: Surrounded by a crowd of negative emotions, persevere in every way you can - a thousand different ways if needed. Like a lion among jackals, don't let this pack of negative emotions strike you down.

7-61.text: No matter how great the danger is, People always guard their eyes. Likewise when you are in grave peril, Do not fall under afflictions’ control.
7-61.en_text: No matter how great the danger, people instinctively protect their eyes. In the same way, when you're in serious spiritual danger, never let yourself fall under the control of negative emotions.

7-62.text: It’s better to be burnt to death Or have my head decapitated— Never in any way shall I Bow to the enemy, affliction.
7-62.en_text: It would be better to be burned to death or have my head cut off than to ever bow down before the enemy that is negative emotion, in any way at all.

7-63.text: Likewise in every situation, I’ll never act any way but right.
7-63.en_text: In just the same way, in every situation, I will never act in any way except what is genuinely right.

7-64.text: Like wanting the pleasure that results From play, they are enchanted with The acts that are for them to do— Delighted, never satisfied.
7-64.en_text: Just as children are enchanted by the pleasure of play, always wanting more and never satisfied, so too people become absorbed in whatever activities please them, endlessly seeking more.

7-65.text: We act for sake of happiness, Not knowing whether pleasure will come. How can all those whose deeds are pleasure Be happy if they do not act?
7-65.en_text: We act for the sake of happiness, though we never really know for certain whether that happiness will actually come. So how can people whose actions themselves are the source of pleasure be truly happy if they stop acting altogether?

7-66.text: If you aren’t sated by desires, Which are like honey on a razor, How can you then be sated by merit, Whose ripening is peace and pleasure?
7-66.en_text: If you're never satisfied chasing after desires - which are like honey smeared on a razor's edge - how could you possibly be satisfied pursuing goodness instead, whose result is genuine peace and lasting happiness?

7-67.text: So therefore to complete your task, Immerse yourself in action, like An elephant scorched in midday sun Who sees a lake and plunges in.
7-67.en_text: So, in order to complete your task, throw yourself fully into the effort, like an elephant scorched by the midday sun who spots a cool lake and plunges straight in.

7-68.text: But when your strength diminishes, Put work aside to act again later. Once it’s well done, leave it behind— Look forward to the next and later.
7-68.en_text: But when your strength runs low, set the work aside for a while so you can return to it later with fresh energy. Once something is finished well, let it go, and look ahead to what comes next.

7-69.text: Like parrying the enemy’s blade When you are in the thick of battle, Evade the weapons of afflictions, And strike the foe afflictions hard.
7-69.en_text: Just as a skilled fighter deflects an opponent's blade in the thick of battle, learn to dodge the attacks of your negative emotions, and strike back firmly against this true enemy.

7-70.text: If you should drop your sword in battle, You’d swiftly pick it up from fear. If you lose mindfulness—your weapon— Take it up quickly, fearing hell.
7-70.en_text: If you dropped your sword in the middle of a battle, you'd snatch it back up right away out of fear. In the same way, if you lose your mindfulness - your true weapon - pick it back up quickly, out of a healthy fear of suffering.

7-71.text: Just as a poison spreads throughout The body through the flow of blood, Likewise if they can get a chance, Your wrongs will spread throughout your mind.
7-71.en_text: Just as poison spreads quickly through the whole body once it enters the bloodstream, in the same way, if given any opening at all, wrongdoing will spread quickly through your entire mind.

7-72.text: Practitioners should concentrate, As fearful as someone holding a bowl That brims with oil before a swordsman Who threatens death if any spills.
7-72.en_text: Anyone practicing this path should stay as focused and careful as someone carrying a bowl brimming with oil while a swordsman stands behind them, threatening death at the first drop spilled.

7-73.text: So just as you would spring up quick If a snake should get into your lap, If sleep and slothfulness should come, Then counteract them with great haste.
7-73.en_text: So just as you'd leap up instantly if a snake landed in your lap, the moment sleepiness or sluggishness arises, counter it right away without delay.

7-74.text: For every single wrong that occurs, Chastise yourself and ponder long, “However I can, I’ll make it so This never happens to me again.”
7-74.en_text: Whenever any wrongdoing occurs, take yourself to task over it and reflect carefully: "By whatever means I can, I will make sure this never happens to me again."

7-75.text: “In circumstances such as this, How shall I practice mindfulness?” With that as cause, you should seek out A meeting and appropriate action.
7-75.en_text: "In situations like this one, how should I actually practice mindfulness?" With that question in mind, you should seek out the guidance of others and figure out the right course of action.

8-0.text: The seventh chapter, “Teachings on Diligence,” from Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva. ^7-a 8. Teachings on Meditation
8-0.en_text: The seventh chapter, "Teachings on Diligence," from Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva. 8. Teachings on Meditation

8-1.text: After thus rousing diligence, Settle your mind into samadhi. A person whose mind wanders perches Between the fangs of the afflictions.
8-1.en_text: Having built up diligence in this way, settle your mind into deep meditative focus. Someone whose mind wanders about sits exposed between the fangs of their own negative emotions.

8-2.text: With solitude of body and mind, Distraction won’t occur. So you should thus forsake the world And also give up discursive thoughts.
8-2.en_text: With solitude of body and mind, distraction simply won't arise. So you should let go of worldly busyness and also set aside restless, scattered thinking.

8-3.text: You won’t renounce the world if attached Or else if you crave goods and such. In order to abandon those, The wise should contemplate like this:
8-3.en_text: You won't be able to let go of worldly busyness if you're still attached to it, or if you crave possessions and similar things. In order to release that attachment, someone wise should reflect in the following way:

8-4.text: Realizing that afflictions are destroyed By shamatha and insight in conjunction, First seek out shamatha, which comes from joy For having no attachment to the world.
8-4.en_text: Understanding that negative emotions are only truly overcome by calm focus and clear insight working together, first cultivate that calm focus, which arises from the joy of no longer being attached to worldly life.

8-5.text: Who is someone ephemeral To cling to the impermanent? In a thousand lives, you’ll never see The ones who were so dear to you.
8-5.en_text: Given that we ourselves are impermanent, why cling so tightly to others, who are equally impermanent? Across a thousand lifetimes, you will never again see those who were once so dear to you.

8-6.text: Not seeing them, you’ll feel no joy. Your mind won’t rest in equipoise. Even seeing them won’t be enough— Craving will plague you as before.
8-6.en_text: Not seeing them brings no real joy, and your mind won't settle into peace either way. Even when you do see them, it's not enough - the same old craving will trouble you exactly as before.

8-7.text: Being attached to sentient beings Obscures completely the true nature And wrecks world weariness as well. Grief will torment you in the end.
8-7.en_text: Being attached to other people completely obscures the true nature of things, and it also destroys any healthy sense of the world's shortcomings. In the end, this attachment will only bring grief.

8-8.text: Because you only think of them, Your life will pass by pointlessly. Inconstant friends and relatives Will ruin even constant dharma.
8-8.en_text: Because your thoughts stay fixed on them, your life ends up passing by pointlessly. Fickle friends and family can end up undoing even long-practiced spiritual habits.

8-9.text: Acting the same as childish folk, You’ll surely go to the lower realms. They lead you to unsuitable states— What good’s the company of fools?
8-9.en_text: Behaving just like untrained, ordinary people will surely lead you to the lower realms. They lead you toward things that don't actually suit you - what good, really, comes from keeping company with the foolish?

8-10.text: One moment, friends, but in the next They’re enemies. They are incensed By what should please them. It is hard To gratify ordinary beings.
8-10.en_text: One moment they're friends, the next they're enemies. They get angry even at things that should please them. It is genuinely difficult to keep ordinary people satisfied.

8-11.text: Angered by talk of what is helpful, They turn me away from my own welfare. If I don’t listen to their words, They’ll go to lower realms, enraged.
8-11.en_text: Angered by well-meaning advice, they turn away from their own best interests. And if I don't go along with what they say, they become furious and head toward the lower realms.

8-12.text: They’re jealous of superiors; Competitive with their own equals. They’re proud toward their inferiors And arrogant when they are praised. When you reproach them, they get angry. When is there benefit from the childish?
8-12.en_text: They're envious of those above them, competitive with their equals, arrogant toward those beneath them, and conceited when praised. Point out a fault, and they get angry. When is there ever real benefit in dealing with the untrained?

8-13.text: When you keep company with the childish, You praise yourself, belittle others, Talk of samsara and such with them— Nonvirtue inevitably occurs.
8-13.en_text: When you keep company with untrained, ordinary people, it tends to lead to boasting about yourself, putting others down, and idle talk about worldly life - wrongdoing follows almost inevitably.

8-14.text: In this way, my associating With them will only bring me ruin. They will not bring me benefit, And I won’t benefit them either.
8-14.en_text: In this way, associating with them will only bring me ruin. They won't actually benefit me, and I won't be able to truly benefit them either.

8-15.text: Flee far away from childish folk. Be friendly when you do meet them, And without getting too familiar, Dispassionately behave well.
8-15.en_text: So stay well away from untrained, ordinary company. When you do happen to meet them, be friendly, but without becoming too familiar - keep a healthy, balanced distance and behave well.

8-16.text: Just like a bee with flower nectar, I’ll only take for dharma’s sake And live unacquainted with anyone, As though I’d never seen them before.
8-16.en_text: Like a bee gathering nectar from a flower, I will take only what serves genuine practice, and otherwise remain unattached to people, as if I'd never really known them.

8-17.text: “I get a lot and am respected; Many people are fond of me.” If you cling to conceits like these, You will face terrors after death.
8-17.en_text: "I receive a lot, I'm well respected, many people are fond of me" - if you cling to conceited thoughts like these, you will face real terror after death.

8-18.text: The passions of a deluded mind, Whatever it may be they are for, Are multiplied a thousand times To then rise up as suffering.
8-18.en_text: Whatever a confused mind becomes passionately attached to, no matter the object, that attachment multiplies a thousandfold and eventually rises up again as suffering.

8-19.text: Therefore the wise do not desire. It’s from desires that fear arises. They’ll be discarded naturally, So understand this and be steadfast.
8-19.en_text: So the wise do not indulge their desires, because fear itself arises out of desire. Once you truly understand this, such desires will fall away naturally on their own - so understand this clearly and stay steady.

8-20.text: Even if you gain many things And become popular and renowned, It is uncertain where you’ll go Along with all those goods and fame.
8-20.en_text: Even if you gain a great many possessions and become popular and well known, it is entirely uncertain where you'll end up afterward, along with all that wealth and fame.

8-21.text: When someone else disparages me, What joy is there for me in praise? When someone else is lauding me, Why be displeased when I am slandered?
8-21.en_text: When someone else criticizes me, what real joy is there in being praised by another? And when someone else praises me, why be upset when I'm criticized by someone else?

8-22.text: If even buddhas cannot please Beings with various inclinations, What need to speak of a wretch like me? Thus I will give up worldly thoughts.
8-22.en_text: If even fully enlightened buddhas cannot satisfy every being's different preferences, what hope does someone as ordinary as me have of doing so? So I will let go of these worldly concerns entirely.

8-23.text: They revile people who get nothing And speak ill of those who get much. What pleasure comes from those whose nature Is to be hard to get along with?
8-23.en_text: People speak badly of those who have nothing, and they also speak badly of those who have a great deal. What real pleasure can come from people whose very nature makes them so hard to please?

8-24.text: As the tathagatas have said, No childish being is a friend Because unless it suits their purpose, The childish are not gratified.
8-24.en_text: As the buddhas themselves have said, an untrained, ordinary person is never truly a reliable friend, because unless something suits their own purposes, they simply won't be satisfied.

8-25.text: In forests, animals and birds And trees don’t speak disparagingly. When is it I will live together With them, whose company is pleasant?
8-25.en_text: In the forest, animals and birds and even the trees never speak unkindly. When will I get to live among such pleasant company instead?

8-26.text: When will it be that I can stay In caves or in abandoned temples Or under trees, not looking back, And not attached to anything?
8-26.en_text: When will I be able to stay in caves, in abandoned shrines, or beneath trees, never looking back, free of attachment to anything at all?

8-27.text: When will it be that I can dwell In places naturally vast That no one owns where I can act In freedom and without attachment?
8-27.en_text: When will I be able to dwell in wide open, natural places that belong to no one, where I can act freely, without attachment to anything?

8-28.text: When will I keep a plain alms bowl And such, and clothes that no one wants? When will I live free from all fear Even if I don’t protect this body?
8-28.en_text: When will I live with just a simple begging bowl and clothing no one else wants, free from all fear, without even needing to protect this body of mine?

8-29.text: When will I go to charnel grounds To see that other people’s bones And my own body are the same In being perishable things?
8-29.en_text: When will I go to a burial ground and see clearly that other people's bones and my own body are exactly the same in being things that will decay and pass away?

8-30.text: This body of my very own Will also become just like those Whose stench is such that even jackals Will not come anywhere close to them.
8-30.en_text: This body of mine will one day become just like those decaying remains - so foul-smelling that even jackals won't come anywhere near it.

8-31.text: This body is born all alone, And if the flesh and bones born with it Will fall apart, be strewn about, What need to speak of other friends?
8-31.en_text: This body is born entirely alone, and its flesh and bones, born together with it, will eventually fall apart and scatter. So what real hope is there in relying on other companions?

8-32.text: At birth, it’s born alone; at death, It dies alone. If no one else Can take a share of the pain, what good Are loved ones who make hindrances?
8-32.en_text: At birth, it's born alone; at death, it dies alone. Since no one else can share even a portion of that pain, what real good are loved ones who only end up getting in the way?

8-33.text: In the same way as travelers Take lodging when they’re on the road, Those on the pathways of existence Take lodging in a place of birth.
8-33.en_text: Just as travelers on the road find lodging for the night and then move on, those journeying through the many forms of existence simply find temporary lodging in each new birth.

8-34.text: Up to the time when four pallbearers Would carry it away from there While people mournfully lament, Till then I shall go to the forest.
8-34.en_text: Until the day when four pallbearers carry this body away while people mourn and grieve, I will make my way, before then, into the solitude of the forest.

8-35.text: With no friends and no grudges either, This body’ll stay in solitude. Considered as if dead already, There’ll be no mourners when it dies.
8-35.en_text: With no friends nearby and no enemies either, this body will remain in solitude. Considered as if already dead, there will be no mourners gathered around when it finally does die.

8-36.text: With no one seated at my side To cause disturbances and grief, There’s no one to distract me from Recalling the buddha and so forth.
8-36.en_text: With no one sitting beside me to cause distraction or grief, there will be nothing to pull my attention away from calling to mind the Buddha and similar wholesome thoughts.

8-37.text: Thus I’ll remain in solitude, In the delightful atmosphere Of joyful forests with few hardships, Where all distractions are quieted.
8-37.en_text: So I will remain in solitude, in the pleasant atmosphere of a peaceful forest, free of hardship, where every distraction settles quietly away.

8-38.text: Relinquishing all other thoughts And with one-pointed mental focus, I’ll strive to settle my mind down In equipoise and to subdue it.
8-38.en_text: Setting aside every other concern, and with my attention gathered into one single point, I will strive to bring my mind to rest in balance and to fully master it.

8-39.text: In this world and the next one too, Desires will lead you to your ruin. Here they bring killing, bonds, and wounds, And in the next, the hells and such.
8-39.en_text: In this life and in future ones as well, desires lead only to ruin. Here they bring killing, imprisonment, and injury; in future lives, they lead to the hells and similar suffering.

8-40.text: The one for whom you earlier Made many requests through go-betweens, For whose sake you did not refrain From misdeeds or even from disgrace,
8-40.en_text: The person you once pursued so eagerly through messengers, for whose sake you avoided neither wrongdoing nor disgrace,

8-41.text: For whom you put yourself in peril And also used up all your wealth, The one whose tight embrace would bring The highest pleasure is nothing but
8-41.en_text: for whom you put yourself in danger and spent all your wealth, whose warm embrace you thought would bring you the greatest pleasure - that person is nothing but

8-42.text: A skeleton—not anything else. What you have lusted for and clung to Has no control, is not a self. Why don’t you go to nirvana instead?
8-42.en_text: a skeleton in the end, and nothing more. What you longed for and clung to has no control of its own and is not a fixed, independent self. So why not turn instead toward lasting peace?

8-43.text: You first took pains to lift her face, But she then bashfully looked down. Whether you’d seen it before or not, It had been shrouded by a veil.
8-43.en_text: At first, you took great pains just to lift her face toward you, and she looked down bashfully. Whether you had seen it before or not, it was always concealed behind a kind of veil.

8-44.text: The thought of it afflicted you, But now her face is visible— You see what vultures have revealed, And why does it now make you flee?
8-44.en_text: The mere thought of that face once stirred you deeply, but now, when you see the same face laid bare by vultures, why do you suddenly want to flee from it?

8-45.text: You guarded it so closely from The glance of anyone else’s eyes. Why don’t you, who are so possessive, Protect it when it’s being eaten?
8-45.en_text: You once guarded that face so carefully from anyone else's gaze. So why, being so possessive, don't you protect it now, while it's being devoured?

8-46.text: You see the pile of flesh that vultures And other animals devour. Would you give someone else’s food Garlands, perfumes, and jewelry?
8-46.en_text: You see the same pile of flesh being eaten by vultures and other animals that you once decorated with jewelry and perfume - would you offer garlands and perfume to someone else's meal?

8-47.text: Seeing it as a skeleton, You’re frightened, though it does not move. Why aren’t you scared when, like a zombie, It’s animated by something else?
8-47.en_text: Seeing it now as a mere skeleton, motionless, you feel afraid. So why aren't you equally afraid of it while it moves around, animated by nothing more than temporary breath and thought?

8-48.text: You lusted for it when it was covered, So why not when it is uncovered? If it will serve no purpose, why Would you embrace it when it’s covered?
8-48.en_text: You desired it when it was covered by skin - so why not desire it now, uncovered? And if it serves no real purpose either way, why did you ever embrace it in the first place, covered or not?

8-49.text: Since both saliva and excrement Are made out of the very same food, Why of the two do you dislike Excrement and yet like saliva?
8-49.en_text: Since both saliva and waste come from exactly the same food, why is it that, of the two, you dislike one and yet enjoy the other?

8-50.text: Not even taking pleasure in A cotton pillow soft to the touch, The lustful say it exudes no stench. They are deluded about filth.
8-50.en_text: Someone driven by lust doesn't even enjoy a soft cotton pillow, claiming instead that the body gives off no unpleasant smell - they are simply confused about what the body really is.

8-51.text: Though cotton may be soft to touch, Deluded, lowly, lustful people Get angry over it and say That it’s unable to make love.
8-51.en_text: Even though cotton is genuinely soft to the touch, someone confused, small-minded, and driven by lust will get angry at it, complaining that it cannot love them back.

8-52.text: If you have no desire for filth, Why then embrace another person, A cage of bones that’s bound by sinews And plastered with the mud of flesh?
8-52.en_text: If you have no real desire for impurity, then why do you embrace another person - a cage of bones held together by sinews, plastered over with flesh like mud?

8-53.text: You have a lot of filth yourself— You should be satisfied with that. Thirsting for the unclean, you lust For yet another sack of filth.
8-53.en_text: You already have plenty of this impurity within your own body - you should be satisfied with just that. Yet, craving what's unclean, you long for yet another sack of the same impurity.

8-54.text: Saying “This flesh is what I like,” You want to touch and gaze on it. Then why don’t you desire the flesh That is devoid of conscious nature?
8-54.en_text: Saying "I like this flesh," you want to touch it and gaze upon it. So then why don't you desire flesh that has no living awareness in it at all, like a corpse?

8-55.text: The consciousness that you desire Cannot be touched or looked upon. What can be is not consciousness. Why bother with a pointless embrace?
8-55.en_text: The awareness you actually desire can't be touched or seen. What can be touched or seen isn't awareness at all. So why bother with such a pointless embrace?

8-56.text: Not realizing another’s body Is filth by nature is no surprise. Not realizing that you yourself Are filth itself is most amazing.
8-56.en_text: It's not surprising that you fail to realize another person's body is, by its nature, simply impure matter. What's truly astonishing is that you fail to realize the very same thing about your own body.

8-57.text: Why does your mind, addicted to filth, Neglect the fresh, young lotus flower Blooming beneath the cloudless sunlight And love instead a cage of filth?
8-57.en_text: Why does your mind, so drawn to impurity, ignore the fresh, young lotus blooming beneath a clear sky, and instead fall in love with a cage full of impurity?

8-58.text: If you have no desire to touch A place befouled by excrement, Why would you want to touch the body Out of which it originates?
8-58.en_text: If you have no desire to touch a spot soiled with waste, why would you want to touch the very body that produces it?

8-59.text: If filth is not what you desire, Then why do you embrace another? The field from which they were born was filth, As were the seeds, as was what grew them.
8-59.en_text: If impurity is truly not what you desire, then why do you embrace another person at all? The very ground they grew from was impure, as were the seed and everything that nourished them.

8-60.text: You do not want the unclean worms Born from manure, even though they’re tiny, And yet you want what’s born from filth, A body of plentiful filth by nature.
8-60.en_text: You don't want the tiny, unclean worms that are born from manure, and yet you desire a body that is, by its very nature, full of the same kind of impurity.

8-61.text: Not only do you not revile Yourself whose nature is unclean, You want another bag of feces, Voraciously desiring filth.
8-61.en_text: Not only do you fail to feel disgust at your own impure nature, you actually crave yet another bag of waste, desiring impurity with real eagerness.

8-62.text: When you put some nice camphor and such Or even rice and vegetables Inside your mouth and spit it out, The ground is dirtied and polluted.
8-62.en_text: When you place something pleasant, like camphor, rice, or vegetables, in your mouth and then spit it back out, the ground where it lands becomes soiled and unpleasant.

8-63.text: If even though it’s evident, You doubt that this is so unclean, Then look at other, fetid bodies Discarded in the charnel grounds.
8-63.en_text: If, even with this evidence in front of you, you still doubt that the body is truly impure in this way, then go look at other decaying bodies left in a burial ground.

8-64.text: And when the skin is flayed from it, You know you will be terrified, And yet how is it you are still Attracted to the very same thing?
8-64.en_text: And once its skin has been stripped away, you know full well you would be horrified - so how is it that you're still drawn to that very same thing while it's intact?

8-65.text: The fragrance applied to the body Is nothing else but sandalwood. Why does the scent of something else Allure you, then, to someone else?
8-65.en_text: The pleasant scent applied to a body is nothing but sandalwood or perfume - nothing that actually belongs to the body itself. So why does a scent that comes from somewhere else make you desire the person wearing it?

8-66.text: Is it not best to not be attracted To this, which naturally smells foul? Why do the worldly, pointlessly craving, Perfume it with nice fragrances?
8-66.en_text: Wouldn't it be better not to be drawn at all to something that naturally has no pleasant smell of its own? Why do people in the world, chasing this pointlessly, cover it over with pleasant fragrances instead?

8-67.text: If that sweet scent is sandalwood, What is it here the body emits? Why would you be attracted to someone Because of something else’s scent?
8-67.en_text: If that sweet scent actually belongs to the sandalwood, then what exactly does the body itself contribute? Why would you be drawn to someone simply because of a scent that comes from something else entirely?

8-68.text: The body naturally has Long hair and nails, stained whitish teeth. It reeks, besmeared with grimy muck. If naked, it is terrifying.
8-68.en_text: By its own nature, the body grows long hair and nails, and its teeth turn a dull, yellowish white. It gives off unpleasant smells and is streaked with grime. Left uncovered, it would be quite unsettling to look at.

8-69.text: Why do you toil to polish up What’s like a sword that injures you? Those crazed by efforts of self-delusion Have set the entire earth in turmoil.
8-69.en_text: Why do you work so hard to polish up something that's really like a blade capable of wounding you? Those caught up in this kind of self-deception have thrown the whole world into turmoil because of it.

8-70.text: If seeing only skeletons In charnel grounds repulses you, Can you like charnel towns that teem With animated skeletons?
8-70.en_text: If seeing nothing but bare skeletons in a burial ground fills you with unease, how could you possibly be drawn to towns full of the same skeletons, just still animated and moving around?

8-71.text: That which is in this way unclean Cannot be got without a cost— Exhaustion from earning for its sake And wounds in hells and other realms.
8-71.en_text: Something this impure cannot be obtained without a real cost - exhaustion from working hard to earn it, and even suffering in the hells or other difficult states because of how it was pursued.

8-72.text: Children aren’t able to earn money. In youth, how is this happiness? You use your life up gathering wealth. When old, what good are your desires?
8-72.en_text: As children, people can't yet earn a living. In youth, how is chasing after this really happiness? You spend your whole life gathering wealth, and by the time you're old, what good do your unfulfilled desires actually do you?

8-73.text: Some passionate but humble folk, Exhausted by a full day’s work, Return home only to lay down Their worn-out bodies like a corpse.
8-73.en_text: Some people, driven by passion yet humble in circumstance, exhausted after a full day's labor, return home only to collapse, their worn-out bodies lying still like a corpse.

8-74.text: Others might go abroad and suffer From weariness and long hard travel. They wish to see their wives and children But won’t see them for a whole year.
8-74.en_text: Others travel far from home and suffer through weariness and long, difficult journeys. Longing to see their spouse and children, they may go a whole year without seeing them at all.

8-75.text: Deluded by want for their own ends, They sell themselves to help themselves. Not gaining that, they’re driven by The winds of others’ futile work.
8-75.en_text: Confused by their own self-interest, some sell themselves into work meant to help themselves get ahead. And even then, having failed to gain what they wanted, they're simply driven along by the pointless demands of serving others instead.

8-76.text: Some sell their bodies and are put To work for others, with no freedom. The women give birth under trees Or in the wild, wherever they can.
8-76.en_text: Some sell their very bodies and are put to work for others, with no freedom of their own. Women give birth wherever they can - under a tree, or out in the wild.

8-77.text: Saying they want a livelihood, Fools who are duped by their desires Fear for their lives but go to battle Or enter servitude for profit.
8-77.en_text: Claiming they just want to make a living, foolish people, deceived by their own desires, risk their lives going into battle or entering servitude, all for the sake of profit.

8-78.text: Some greedy beings get themselves wounded, While others are impaled on stakes. There are those who are gored by spears, And some are even burnt alive.
8-78.en_text: Driven by greed, some end up wounded, others impaled, some pierced through by spears, and some are even burned alive.

8-79.text: Know the travails of getting, keeping, and losing it Make wealth a never-ending source of ill. For those whom greed for wealth distracts, there is no chance For freedom from the suffering of existence.
8-79.en_text: Understand that the effort of getting wealth, keeping it, and eventually losing it makes it an endless source of trouble. For those distracted by greed for wealth, there is no real chance of ever being free from the suffering of this existence.

8-80.text: For the desirous, faults like these Are plentiful, but gains are few, Just as the oxen pulling a cart Get only a few bites of grass.
8-80.en_text: For those driven by desire, problems like these are plentiful, while the actual rewards are small - just as an ox pulling a heavy cart gets only a few mouthfuls of grass along the way.

8-81.text: For sake of paltry gains so common That even oxen manage them, These perfect leisures and resources, Which are so difficult to get, Are crushed by the ordeals of karma.
8-81.en_text: For the sake of such small, common rewards - the kind even oxen manage to get - this rare and precious human opportunity, so hard to come by, ends up crushed under the weight of the effort spent chasing it.

8-82.text: For just a millionth fraction of The arduous efforts that they make Continually for minor ends— Pleasures that definitely perish
8-82.en_text: With just a tiny fraction of the tremendous, ongoing effort that people pour into these minor pursuits - pleasures that are certain to fade away

8-83.text: And cast them to the hells and such— They could be buddhas, but the greedy, Instead of awakened conduct, have Great miseries and no awakening.
8-83.en_text: and that can even lead to the hells - they could instead become fully enlightened. Yet those driven by greed end up with great suffering and no enlightenment at all, instead of a life of true, awakened conduct.

8-84.text: Considering the sufferings Of hell and so forth, there’s no weapon, No poison, fire, abyss, or foe That can compare to the desires.
8-84.en_text: Considering the sufferings of hell and similar states, there is truly no weapon, no poison, no fire, no chasm, and no enemy that compares to the harm caused by desire itself.

8-85.text: Thus weary yourself of desires And rouse delight for solitude. Deep in a peaceful forest free Of quarrels and disturbances,
8-85.en_text: So grow weary of these desires, and cultivate real delight in solitude instead. Deep within a peaceful forest, free of conflict and disturbance,

8-86.text: On broad flat stones—delightful palaces Cooled by the sandalwood of the moon’s rays— The fortunate pace, fanned by a woodland breeze, Serene and silent, pondering other’s weal.
8-86.en_text: on broad, flat stones - like a delightful palace cooled by moonlight as if by sandalwood - those fortunate enough to be there walk calmly, fanned by a gentle woodland breeze, quiet and at ease, reflecting on the well-being of others.

8-87.text: In empty huts, by trees, or else in caves, You may remain as long as you desire. The pains of getting and keeping left behind, You live without a care, dependent on none.
8-87.en_text: In an empty hut, beneath a tree, or inside a cave, you may stay as long as you wish. Leaving behind the burden of acquiring and guarding possessions, you live free of worry, depending on no one.

8-88.text: To freely act with no desires And without ties to anyone— Enjoyable comfort of contentment Is hard for even a prince to find.
8-88.en_text: To act freely, without desires and without being tied down to anyone, is a comfort and contentment so satisfying that even a prince would find it hard to come by.

8-89.text: Once you’ve reflected on these and other Advantages of solitude, Then fully pacify your thoughts And meditate on bodhichitta.
8-89.en_text: Having reflected on these and other benefits of solitude, fully calm your scattered thoughts, and meditate on the wish to help all beings.

8-90.text: First meditate ardently upon The equality of self and other. They’re equal in both pain and pleasure, So protect everyone like yourself.
8-90.en_text: First, meditate wholeheartedly on the basic equality of yourself and others. Since everyone is equal in wanting comfort and avoiding pain, protect all beings just as you would protect yourself.

8-91.text: Although of many different kinds, the hands and so forth Are one as a body to protect. Likewise though beings Are different and separate in their joys and pains, They all are equal, the same as me in wanting comfort.
8-91.en_text: Even though the hands and other parts of the body are many and different, together they form a single body to be cared for. In the same way, even though beings are distinct and separate in their individual joys and pains, they are all equal in this: every one of them, just like me, wants comfort and well-being.

8-92.text: Even though my own suffering Does not cause harm to others’ bodies, My suffering is unbearable Because of ego-clinging.
8-92.en_text: Even though my own suffering doesn't cause any harm to other people's bodies, it still feels unbearable to me - simply because of my attachment to a sense of self.

8-93.text: Likewise the sufferings of others Have no effect on me, but still Their suffering is unbearable Because of ego-clinging.
8-93.en_text: In the same way, even though others' suffering has no direct effect on me, if I truly cared as much about them as myself, their suffering would feel just as unbearable, again because of this same attachment to self.

8-94.text: I will dispel others’ suffering Since it is suffering, like my own. I shall bring benefit to others Since they are beings, like my body.
8-94.en_text: So I will work to remove others' suffering, simply because it is suffering, exactly like my own. And I will work to benefit others, simply because they are living beings, exactly like myself.

8-95.text: For when both I and others are The same in wanting to be happy And they’re no different from me, Why only work for my own pleasure?
8-95.en_text: Since both I and others are equally beings who want happiness, and others are really no different from me in this regard, why would I work only for my own pleasure?

8-96.text: And when both I and others are The same in wanting not to suffer And they’re no different from me, Then why protect myself, not others?
8-96.en_text: And since both I and others are equally beings who want to avoid suffering, and others are really no different from me in this regard, why would I protect only myself and not others?

8-97.text: If I will not protect them since Their suffering does not cause me harm, Then future suffering as well Does not harm me—why guard against it?
8-97.en_text: If I say I won't protect others because their suffering doesn't harm me directly, then by that same logic, my own future suffering doesn't harm me right now either - so why guard against that?

8-98.text: It is erroneous to think, “It’s me who will experience it,” Because it is one being who dies And yet another who is born.
8-98.en_text: It's actually a mistake to think, "It is I who will experience that future suffering," because, strictly speaking, it is one being who dies in that moment and, in effect, another being entirely who is born afterward.

8-99.text: If they whose suffering it is Themselves must guard themselves from it, Since the foot’s pain is not the hand’s, Why should the one protect the other?
8-99.en_text: If you say that whoever experiences a suffering should be the one responsible for guarding against it, well, the foot's pain isn't the hand's pain either - so why would one part protect the other at all?

8-100.text: “Even though it’s illogical, We act from ego-clinging,” you say. We must, as much as possible, Give up fallacious selves and others.
8-100.en_text: "Even though it may not be entirely logical, we act this way out of attachment to self," you might say. Yet we should still work as much as possible to release these mistaken notions of a fixed self and other.

8-101.text: Continua and aggregates, Like series, armies, and such, are false. The suffering one does not exist, So who is it that this belongs to?
8-101.en_text: A stream of moments, or a collection of parts - like a string of beads, an army made of soldiers, and so on - has no independent existence of its own beyond its parts. In the same way, there is no truly independent "self" that suffers - so exactly who does that suffering really belong to?

8-102.text: That suffering has no owner is No different for anyone. I will dispel it since it’s painful— In this, why should I set a limit?
8-102.en_text: Since suffering has no true, independent owner, there's no real difference between anyone's suffering. I will simply work to remove it, precisely because it is suffering - so why would I place any arbitrary limit on that?

8-103.text: There’s no dispute the suffering Of everyone must be prevented. If mine’s prevented, prevent all. Or else, like beings’, not mine either.
8-103.en_text: There's no reasonable argument that suffering, wherever it occurs, shouldn't be prevented. If my own suffering should be prevented, then everyone's suffering should be prevented in just the same way - or else, by that same logic, mine shouldn't be prevented either.

8-104.text: “Compassion is too painful,” you say, “So why arouse it with such effort?” But when you think of beings’ torments, How is the pain of compassion greater?
8-104.en_text: "But compassion causes so much pain," you might say, "so why make such effort to cultivate it?" Yet when you actually consider the suffering of all beings, how could the discomfort of feeling compassion possibly outweigh that?

8-105.text: For if a single suffering Eliminates many miseries, Those with compassion will induce That suffering in themselves and others.
8-105.en_text: Because if a single, smaller suffering can prevent many greater miseries, then someone with real compassion will willingly bring that smaller suffering upon themselves, for the sake of both themselves and others.

8-106.text: Thus even though Supushpachandra Knew that the king would cause him harm, He did not shy away from pain To end the sufferings of many.
8-106.en_text: This is why, even knowing the king would harm him for it, Supushpachandra did not hold back from accepting pain, in order to put an end to the suffering of many.

8-107.text: Those who have trained their own mind streams Will enter even the Incessant With joy for quelling others’ woes, Like swans alighting on lotus ponds.
8-107.en_text: Those who have trained their own minds this way will willingly enter even the deepest hell with genuine joy, simply to ease the suffering of others - like swans gliding down onto a lotus pond.

8-108.text: When beings have been liberated, Is not the ocean of joy that brings Sufficient in and of itself? What good is wanting liberation?
8-108.en_text: When beings are finally set free from suffering, isn't the sheer ocean of joy that brings enough on its own? What further need is there to seek liberation just for oneself?

8-109.text: So though I have done good for others, I’m not conceited or amazed. Solely enjoying helping others, I’ve no hope for a ripened result.
8-109.en_text: So even though I've done good for others, I feel no pride or self-satisfaction about it. Simply enjoying the act of helping, I hold no expectation of any reward in return.

8-110.text: Thus just as I protect myself From any blame, no matter how slight, For others, I will likewise be Protective and compassionate.
8-110.en_text: Just as I protect myself from even the smallest criticism, I will, in that same way, be protective and compassionate toward others as well.

8-111.text: Just as, due to habituation, I know the drops of blood and semen That came from others as myself, Though that has no reality,
8-111.en_text: Just as, through sheer habit, I have come to think of the drops that formed this body as "myself," even though that idea has no real, ultimate basis,

8-112.text: Why don’t I similarly grasp The bodies of other beings as me? It also is not difficult To see my body as someone else.
8-112.en_text: why couldn't I, in the very same way, come to regard the bodies of other beings as "myself" too? It isn't actually any harder to see my own body as belonging to someone else.

8-113.text: Knowing that I have faults while others Are oceans of good qualities, I’ll meditate on giving up Self-clinging while adopting others.
8-113.en_text: Recognizing that I have my own faults, while others hold vast, ocean-like good qualities, I will meditate on letting go of my attachment to self and taking up the well-being of others instead.

8-114.text: In the same way as we accept That hands and such are body parts, Why do we not likewise accept The living are a part of the world?
8-114.en_text: Just as we naturally accept that our hands and other limbs are simply parts of one body, why shouldn't we accept, in the same way, that all living beings are simply parts of one interconnected world?

8-115.text: The thought this selfless body is me Arose due to habituation, So why will the idea others Are me not come with habituation?
8-115.en_text: The very idea that this selfless collection of parts is somehow "me" arose only through habit and repetition. So why couldn't the idea that others are also "me" arise through that same kind of habit and repetition?

8-116.text: So though I have done good for others, I’m not conceited or amazed, Just as there’s no hope for return When I eat my own food myself.
8-116.en_text: So even though I do good for others, I hold no pride or self-satisfaction about it - just as there's no expectation of thanks when I simply eat my own food to nourish myself.

8-117.text: Thus just as I protect myself From any blame, no matter how slight, I’ll cultivate compassionate, Protective thoughts for beings.
8-117.en_text: In just the same way that I protect myself from even the smallest fault, I will cultivate this same protective, compassionate care for all beings.

8-118.text: That is why Avalokiteshvara From his compassion, blessed his name To soothe the fears that wanderers Have even of being among people.
8-118.en_text: This is exactly why Avalokiteshvara, out of great compassion, blessed his own name with the power to calm the fears that beings feel, even in the middle of a crowd.

8-119.text: Do not turn back from difficulty— From the power of habituation, Though someone’s name did once strike fear, Without them, you will feel no joy.
8-119.en_text: So don't shy away from this difficult practice. Through the power of habit and repetition, even something that once caused fear - like hearing a certain name - eventually becomes something you can't feel at peace without.

8-120.text: All those who wish to swiftly give Protection to themselves and others Should practice the most excellent secret, The exchange of self and other.
8-120.en_text: All those who wish to quickly protect both themselves and others should take up this most excellent secret practice: exchanging concern for oneself with concern for others.

8-121.text: Due to attachment to our bodies, We’re scared by even the smallest fright. Who wouldn’t abhor this fearsome body As if it were an enemy?
8-121.en_text: Because of our attachment to this body, we become frightened even by the smallest threat. Who wouldn't want to be free of this fear-prone body, treating it almost like an enemy?

8-122.text: From the desire to cure the illness Of hunger, thirst, and such, the body Will make you kill birds, fish, and deer And wait in ambush by the road.
8-122.en_text: Driven by the wish to relieve hunger, thirst, and similar discomforts, the body will lead you to kill birds, fish, and deer, or lie in wait along the road to ambush travelers.

8-123.text: And if it makes you kill your parents Or steal what’s offered the three jewels For sake of gain or else respect So you’ll be burned in the Incessant,
8-123.en_text: And if it leads you to harm your own parents, or to steal what has been offered to the Three Jewels for the sake of gain or reputation, it can even lead you to be burned in the deepest hell.

8-124.text: No one who’s wise would want that body, Nor would they shield or venerate it. Who would not look at it and see An enemy? Who would not scorn it?
8-124.en_text: No wise person would want a body like this, nor would they protect it or hold it in high regard. Who wouldn't look at it and see something like an enemy? Who wouldn't feel some healthy detachment from it?

8-125.text: “If I give this, what will I enjoy?” Such selfish thoughts are the way of fiends. “If I enjoy this, what can I give?” Such altruism is divine dharma.
8-125.en_text: "If I give this away, what will I have left to enjoy?" - this kind of selfish thinking is the way of small-minded, self-centered beings. "If I enjoy this myself, what will I have left to give?" - this kind of generous thinking is the way of true, sacred practice.

8-126.text: If you harm others for your own sake, You’ll be tormented in hell and elsewhere. If you are harmed for others’ sake, You will gain everything excellent.
8-126.en_text: If you harm others for your own benefit, you will suffer for it in hell and elsewhere. If you accept harm for the benefit of others, you will gain everything truly excellent.

8-127.text: Those who want high rank for themselves Become lowly dolts in lower realms, But those who pass it on to others Will gain respect in the high realms.
8-127.en_text: Those who seek high status for themselves alone end up lowly and foolish in the lower realms, while those who offer that same status to others gain real respect in the higher realms.

8-128.text: If you use others for selfish ends, You will experience servitude. Using yourself for others’ sake, You will experience lordliness.
8-128.en_text: If you use others merely for your own selfish ends, you will end up experiencing servitude yourself. If you use your own efforts for the sake of others, you will experience true, natural leadership.

8-129.text: All happiness in the world is born Of wishing others happiness. All suffering in the world is born Of wanting happiness for yourself.
8-129.en_text: All the happiness that exists in the world comes from wishing happiness for others. All the suffering that exists in the world comes from wanting happiness only for oneself.

8-130.text: What need is there to explain at length? The childish act for their own ends; The sages act for others’ sake. Look at the difference between them.
8-130.en_text: What need is there to say more? Untrained, ordinary people act only for their own sake, while the truly wise act for the sake of others. Just look at the difference between the two.

8-131.text: If you do not exchange your pleasures For other beings’ miseries, You will not achieve buddhahood Or have any happiness in samsara.
8-131.en_text: If you don't learn to trade your own comfort for the discomfort of others, you will never achieve full enlightenment, nor will you find any real happiness even in this ordinary life.

8-132.text: No need to mention the next life. In this life, servants who don’t work And masters who do not pay wages Will also not achieve their aims.
8-132.en_text: Never mind the next life - even in this one, a servant who refuses to work, and a master who refuses to pay, will both fail to accomplish what they're actually after.

8-133.text: Fools throw away the perfect pleasure Of gaining seen and unseen joys, And, causing others misery, They take on terrible suffering.
8-133.en_text: Foolish people throw away the complete happiness that comes both now and later, and instead, by causing misery to others, they bring terrible suffering upon themselves.

8-134.text: All of the violence in the world And all the fear and suffering Arise from clinging to a self. What does that ogre do for me?
8-134.en_text: All the violence, fear, and suffering that exists in the world comes from clinging to a fixed sense of self. So really, what good does this so-called "self" actually do for me?

8-135.text: Without relinquishing your self, You can’t abandon suffering. Just as without relinquishing fire, You cannot avoid getting burned.
8-135.en_text: Without letting go of this clinging to self, you cannot let go of suffering - just as, without letting go of fire, you cannot avoid being burned by it.

8-136.text: Therefore to calm harms to myself And pacify others’ suffering, I’ll give myself away to others And cling to others as myself.
8-136.en_text: So, in order to calm the harm done to myself and ease the suffering of others, I will give myself over entirely to others, and hold onto others as though they were my own self.

8-137.text: Mind, understand with certainty That I am owned by other beings. Now do not think of anything else Than benefiting sentient beings.
8-137.en_text: Mind, understand this with real certainty: I now belong to other beings. From this point on, think of nothing except benefiting all beings.

8-138.text: It is not right to gain selfish ends With eyes and such that others own. It is not right to treat them badly With eyes that are for their benefit.
8-138.en_text: It isn't right to use eyes and other things that, in truth, belong to all beings, purely for selfish ends. And it isn't right to treat others poorly using capacities that exist to benefit them.

8-139.text: Therefore I will put beings first. Anything I see on my body, I’ll take away and put to use For sake of benefiting others.
8-139.en_text: So I will put the well-being of others first. Whatever I notice about my own body, I will set it aside and put it to use for the sake of benefiting others instead.

8-140.text: Make the inferior and so forth Yourself and make yourself the other. Then meditate without any thought On envy, rivalry, and pride.
8-140.en_text: Take those who seem lesser, and in your meditation, place yourself in their position, and place them in the position you once held as "yourself." Then meditate with a mind entirely free of envy, rivalry, and pride.

8-141.text: “They are respected; I am not. I do not get as much as them. They’re praised, while I am ridiculed, And they are happy, while I suffer.
8-141.en_text: "They are respected; I am not. I don't receive as much as they do. They are praised, while I am mocked, and they are happy, while I suffer.

8-142.text: “I am the one who does the work, But they live comfortably indeed. They’re known in society as great, While it’s said I’ve no qualities.
8-142.en_text: "I'm the one doing all the hard work, yet they live comfortably. They're seen as important by everyone, while I'm said to have no real qualities at all."

8-143.text: “No qualities? What can I do? But I have all the qualities. There are some they’re inferior to And some I am superior to.
8-143.en_text: "No good qualities? What am I supposed to do about that? Actually, I do have good qualities of my own. There are some people worse off than them, and some I'm even better than."

8-144.text: “My discipline, views, and so forth are Corrupted due to the afflictions. I’ve no control, so they should cure me As best they can; I’ll take the pain.
8-144.en_text: "My discipline, my understanding, and so on have all been affected by my negative emotions - I can't help it, so they should try to help me as best they can, and I'll accept whatever difficulty that involves."

8-145.text: “But I’m not someone they would heal. Why do they treat me with contempt? If they’re a person with qualities, What use are their qualities to me?
8-145.en_text: "But they don't even bother to help someone like me - why do they treat me with such contempt instead? And if they really do have good qualities, what use are those qualities to me anyway?"

8-146.text: “They’ve no compassion for those inside The maws of the dread lower realms. Conceited with external virtues, They want to vie against the wise.”
8-146.en_text: "They show no real compassion for those trapped in the terrifying grip of the lower realms. Puffed up with mere outward appearances of virtue, they only want to compete with those who are genuinely wise."

8-147.text: When I see those who are my peers, “To make myself superior, I’ll get their things and gain respect Even if I must fight for it.
8-147.en_text: When I see those who are truly my equals, this is how I might think: "To make myself look better than them, I'll take what they have and win the respect instead, even if I have to fight for it.

8-148.text: “No matter what, I’ll make it so My qualities are world renowned. I’ll make sure no one ever hears Of any of their qualities.
8-148.en_text: "No matter what, I'll make sure my own good qualities become known throughout the world. I'll make certain that no one ever hears about any of theirs.

8-149.text: “Furthermore, I will hide my faults So I am honored and they aren’t. Now I will easily get goods And be respected—they will not.
8-149.en_text: "And I'll hide my own faults carefully, so that I'm the one who's honored, and they are not. I'll make sure I gain possessions easily and receive respect - while they receive none."

8-150.text: “When they act inappropriately, I’ll watch for a long time with glee. I will make them a laughingstock That all revile among themselves.”
8-150.en_text: "When they act inappropriately, I'll watch with quiet satisfaction for a long time. I'll make sure they become a laughingstock, mocked by everyone around them."

8-151.text: “This wretch is trying to rival me, It’s said, but can they be my equal In learning or intelligence, In body, stature, or in wealth?
8-151.en_text: "This poor fool thinks they can rival me," people say - but can they really compare to me in learning, intelligence, appearance, stature, or wealth?

8-152.text: “When they hear of my qualities That are well known to everyone, Let them experience the rapture Of feeling shivers of delight.
8-152.en_text: "When they hear about my accomplishments, ones that everyone already knows about, let them feel a thrill of excitement just from hearing of them."

8-153.text: “Although they might possess some wealth, We’ll take it all away by force, And if they do some work for us, We’ll give them just enough to live.
8-153.en_text: "Even if they have some wealth, we'll take it all away by force. And if they do work for us, we'll only give them just enough to get by."

8-154.text: “We will deprive them of happiness And always yoke them to our torments. This one wrought miseries for us Hundreds of times in all samsara.”
8-154.en_text: "We'll deprive them of happiness and keep them constantly burdened with our own troubles instead. This person has caused us countless miseries, over and over, throughout this endless cycle of rebirth."

8-155.text: O mind, you have spent countless aeons Wanting to benefit yourself, But even with such great ordeals, You’ve only created suffering.
8-155.en_text: Mind, you have spent countless ages seeking only your own benefit, yet even with all that tremendous effort, all you've actually produced is more suffering.

8-156.text: Therefore you must apply yourself Completely to benefiting others. Later you’ll see the merits in this— The Sage’s words are undeceiving.
8-156.en_text: So you must now apply yourself completely to benefiting others instead. Later, you will see the real value in this - the wise teacher's words never mislead.

8-157.text: If you had done these acts before, A situation such as this That’s not a buddha’s perfect bliss Would never have been possible.
8-157.en_text: If you had taken up this practice earlier, a situation like this one - falling so far short of a buddha's perfect happiness - would never have come about.

8-158.text: And therefore, just as you have clung To drops of others’ sperm and blood As being yourself, likewise you must Meditate thus for others too.
8-158.en_text: And so, just as you have come to cling to the very drops that formed this body as being "yourself," you must, in that same way, learn to think of others as yourself too.

8-159.text: You should act as a spy for others. When you see anything on your body, Then take away that very thing And use it to benefit other beings.
8-159.en_text: You should act, in a sense, as a spy on behalf of others. Whatever you notice about your own body, take that very thing and use it to benefit other beings instead.

8-160.text: “I’m comfortable; others are not. I’m high in stature; others are low, And I am helped, while others aren’t.” Why aren’t you envious of yourself?
8-160.en_text: "I'm comfortable; others aren't. I have high standing; others are lowly. I'm well supported; others aren't." Why aren't you envious of yourself, hearing that?

8-161.text: Deprive yourself of happiness. Take others’ suffering on yourself. When you think, “What is this one doing?” Examine your own deficiencies.
8-161.en_text: Deprive yourself of comfort. Take on others' suffering as your own. Whenever you catch yourself thinking, "What is this person up to?" turn that same scrutiny onto your own shortcomings instead.

8-162.text: Even the wrongs that others do Must be transformed into your own faults. Even the minor wrongs you do Must be confessed to many people.
8-162.en_text: Even wrongs that others commit should be regarded, in your own reflection, as if they were your own faults. And even the small wrongs you yourself commit should be openly admitted to many others.

8-163.text: Proclaim especially others’ fame, So that it will outshine your own. Employ yourself to all their ends As if you were the lowest slave.
8-163.en_text: Make a point of spreading others' good reputation, so that it outshines your own. Put yourself entirely at their service, as if you were the lowliest of servants.

8-164.text: This one is rife with faults by nature, So do not praise their fleeting virtues. Do all you can so no one knows Anything of their qualities.
8-164.en_text: This mind of mine is, by nature, full of flaws - so don't praise its passing, occasional virtues. Do everything you can to make sure no one hears about whatever good qualities it might seem to have.

8-165.text: In brief, for your own selfish sake, You have caused injuries to others. Now make it so, for beings’ sake, That all the harm will fall on you.
8-165.en_text: In short, for the sake of your own selfish interests, you have caused injury to others in the past. Now make sure that, for the sake of all beings instead, every bit of that harm falls on you.

8-166.text: Don’t let this one be impetuous In arrogant and headstrong ways. Instead, leave it like a new bride Who’s shy and fearful and restrained.
8-166.en_text: Don't let this mind of yours act with careless arrogance or stubbornness. Instead, keep it restrained, as modest and cautious as a shy new bride.

8-167.text: “Do that! You must remain like this! And you must never act like that!” Exert your power over it; Punish it if it disobeys.
8-167.en_text: "Behave like this! You must stay exactly this way! And you must never act like that!" Exercise real authority over your own mind, and correct it firmly whenever it disobeys.

8-168.text: If, mind, you will not act like that Even though I have told you to, You will indeed be subjugated, Since all wrongs are because of you.
8-168.en_text: Mind, if you still won't listen even after being told this clearly, know that you will indeed be brought under control, since every wrongdoing ultimately comes from you.

8-169.text: The bygone days when you were able To ruin me were different. I see wherever you go now. I’ll destroy all your vanity.
8-169.en_text: The days when you were able to lead me astray are now behind us. I see clearly now, wherever you try to go. I will put an end to all your vanity and self-importance.

8-170.text: Give up the idea that you still Have purposes of your very own. Since I have sold you off to others, Offer your strength without despair.
8-170.en_text: Let go of the idea that you still have purposes that are purely your own. Since I have now dedicated you entirely to the service of others, offer up your strength willingly, without resentment.

8-171.text: If I get careless and do not Deliver you to sentient beings, It’s certain you’ll deliver me Down to the keepers of the hells.
8-171.en_text: If I grow careless and fail to dedicate you fully to the service of all beings, it's certain that you, in turn, will hand me over to the guardians of the lower realms.

8-172.text: I’ve suffered long the many times That you have given me away. Now I remember my resentment. I shall destroy your selfish thoughts.
8-172.en_text: I have suffered for a long time because of how often you have led me astray in this way. Now, remembering that, I will put an end to your selfish habits for good.

8-173.text: Therefore if you want to be pleased, Do not make pleasure for yourself. If you want to protect yourself, Continuously protect others.
8-173.en_text: So if you truly want happiness, stop seeking pleasure only for yourself. And if you truly want to protect yourself, keep protecting others instead, continuously.

8-174.text: The more that I protect this body, The more it gets too tender and falls.
8-174.en_text: The more I coddle and protect this body, the more fragile and prone to breaking down it becomes.

8-175.text: If the desires of one who’s fallen In such a way can’t be fulfilled By even this entire earth, Who is there that can meet their wants?
8-175.en_text: If the desires of someone who has fallen into this kind of self-indulgence couldn't be satisfied even by the entire earth, then who could possibly satisfy them at all?

8-176.text: Insatiable desires produce Afflictions and degenerate thoughts. Those not dependent on anything Have never-ending excellence.
8-176.en_text: Desires that can never be satisfied only give rise to more negative emotion and a weakening of good qualities. Those who depend on nothing outside themselves enjoy a kind of excellence that never runs out.

8-177.text: So don’t give physical desires An opportunity to grow. Not clinging to anything as being Desirable is the finest thing.
8-177.en_text: So don't give physical desires any chance to grow stronger. Not clinging to anything at all as something you must have is truly the finest way to live.

8-178.text: In the end, it will end up as ash, Unmoving, moved by someone else. Why do I grasp at this unclean And frightening form as being me?
8-178.en_text: In the end, this body will become nothing but ash - unmoving on its own, moved only by outside forces. So why do I cling to this unclean and, frankly, unsettling form as though it were truly "me"?

8-179.text: No matter whether it’s live or dead, What use have I of this machine? If it’s no different from a clod, Alas, why not be rid of pride?
8-179.en_text: Whether it's alive or dead, of what real use is this body-machine to me? If it's really no different from a lump of clay or wood, why on earth do I still cling to pride about it?

8-180.text: Because of doting on this body, I’ve brought myself pointless miseries. What use is getting attached or angry For this, which is the same as wood?
8-180.en_text: Because of my fondness for this body, I have brought needless suffering upon myself. What use is there in feeling attachment or anger over something that is, in truth, no different from a piece of wood?

8-181.text: Thus whether I take care of it, Or vultures and the like consume it, It feels no attachment or aversion, So why am I attached to it?
8-181.en_text: Whether I take great care of this body, or vultures and other creatures eventually consume it, the body itself feels neither attachment nor aversion either way - so why am I so attached to it?

8-182.text: If it is not itself aware Of anger when it is disparaged And pleasure when it is admired, Who am I tiring myself for?
8-182.en_text: If the body itself feels no anger when insulted and no pleasure when praised, then who exactly am I wearing myself out for?

8-183.text: If you should say that someone who Is fond of this body is my friend, Everyone’s fond of their own body, So why am I not fond of them?
8-183.en_text: If you say that whoever is fond of this body must be my true friend, well, everyone is fond of their own body in just the same way - so why am I not equally fond of them?

8-184.text: So I’ll give up, without attachment, This body for wanderers’ benefit. Therefore, though it has many faults, I’ll keep it, using it to act.
8-184.en_text: So I will give up my attachment to this body and instead use it entirely for the benefit of all beings. Even though it has many flaws, I will keep it around simply as a tool for doing good.

8-185.text: I’ve had enough of childish conduct. I’ll follow the footsteps of the wise. Recalling the words on carefulness, I’ll ward off sleep and sluggishness.
8-185.en_text: I have had enough of untrained, ordinary behavior. I will now follow in the footsteps of the wise. Recalling these teachings on carefulness, I will guard myself against sleepiness and sluggishness.

9-0.text: The eighth chapter, “Teachings on Meditation,” from Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva. ^8-a 9. Transcendent Prajna
9-0.en_text: The eighth chapter, "Teachings on Meditation," from Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva. 9. The Perfection of Wisdom

9-1.text: The Sage taught all these preparations For the sake of prajna, So those who wish to pacify Suffering should develop prajna.
9-1.en_text: The wise teacher taught all of these earlier practices for the sake of wisdom. So those who wish to bring suffering to an end should cultivate wisdom.

9-2.text: The relative and ultimate Are stated to be the two truths. The ultimate is not mind’s sphere; It’s said that mind is relative.
9-2.en_text: Two levels of truth are described: the everyday, conventional truth, and the ultimate truth. The ultimate truth is beyond the reach of an ordinary, confused mind - and it's this ordinary mind that operates at the conventional level.

9-3.text: With those, two types of people are seen, The yogic and the ordinary. Of these two, ordinary people Are confuted by the yogic.
9-3.en_text: Because of this, two kinds of people can be recognized: those with deep meditative insight, and ordinary people. Between the two, the views of ordinary people are shown to be mistaken by those with deeper insight.

9-4.text: Due to distinctions of intellect, Higher yogis confute the lower By analogies that both accept, Left unexamined for the result.
9-4.en_text: And because of differing depths of understanding, even among those with insight, the more advanced correct the views of those less advanced, using examples both sides already accept, without needing to settle every detail for this purpose.

9-5.text: As worldly people think that things Are real just as they are perceived And not illusory, the yogis Dispute the worldly over this.
9-5.en_text: Ordinary people think that the things they perceive are simply real, just as they appear, and not illusion-like at all. This is exactly where those with deeper insight disagree with the ordinary view.

9-6.text: It is consensus, not valid knowledge, That there’s perception of form and such. Like the consensus the unclean Is clean and so forth, it is false.
9-6.en_text: Even things like the perception of physical form are only a matter of common agreement, not real, valid knowledge - just as it's common agreement, yet false, that something impure could be considered clean.

9-7.text: In order to introduce the worldly, The Buddha taught that there are things. In fact, they are not momentary. “That contradicts the relative.”
9-7.en_text: In order to guide ordinary people gradually, the Buddha taught, at first, that things simply exist. In truth, though, they don't even last from one moment to the next. "But doesn't that contradict everyday truth?" you might ask.

9-8.text: The yogic relative has no fault. Compared to worldly, it’s seeing suchness, Or else the worldly could refute Their recognizing bodies as filth.
9-8.en_text: There's no problem here: this second, deeper way of seeing things is simply how someone with real insight sees reality as it truly is, compared to the ordinary view - similar to how someone might correct the ordinary view that this body is something other than impure matter.

9-9.text: The merit from illusory victors Is like that from existent ones. “If beings are illusory, After they die, how are they born?”
9-9.en_text: Buddhas who arise like illusions still produce real goodness, just as those who seem solid and real would. "But if beings are like illusions, how can they be reborn after death?"

9-10.text: Illusions will arise as long As the conditions are assembled. Does merely lasting a long time Mean sentient beings truly exist?
9-10.en_text: Illusions arise for as long as the right conditions come together. Does merely lasting a long time actually prove that beings truly, independently exist?

9-11.text: Killing illusory beings and such Are not misdeeds—they have no mind. But merit and misdeeds arise With those who have illusory minds.
9-11.en_text: Killing a being that is like an illusion carries no real wrongdoing, since an illusion has no mind of its own. But real goodness and wrongdoing do arise for beings whose minds, though illusion-like, still experience things.

9-12.text: Since spells and such don’t have that power, Illusory minds do not arise. Produced by various conditions, Illusions are various as well.
9-12.en_text: Because ordinary spells and such don't have the power to create a mind, illusions of that kind don't actually think or feel. But since illusions arise from many different kinds of conditions, illusions themselves come in many different kinds.

9-13.text: Nowhere is there a single condition That’s capable of everything. “If beings still cycle relatively, Though ultimately, they’re nirvana,
9-13.en_text: There is no single condition anywhere capable of producing every kind of result on its own. "If beings still go through this cycle of rebirth on the everyday level, even though, ultimately, they are already at peace,

9-14.text: “Then even buddhas would transmigrate— Why bother with the way of bodhi?” Unless the continuum of conditions Is severed, illusions will not cease.
9-14.en_text: then even the buddhas themselves would still be caught in this cycle - so why bother with the path to enlightenment at all?" Unless the ongoing chain of conditions is actually cut, the illusion will simply continue to arise.

9-15.text: They won’t arise, even relatively, When the conditions have been severed. “If confused mind does not exist, What is it that observes illusions?”
9-15.en_text: But once that chain of conditions has truly been cut, the illusion won't arise again, even on the everyday level. "But if there's no truly confused mind to begin with, then what exactly is it that perceives these illusions?"

9-16.text: But if for you, the illusion itself Does not exist, then what’s observed? “In suchness, there is something else; That image is the mind itself.”
9-16.en_text: But if, in your own view, the illusion itself doesn't ultimately exist, then what exactly is there left to be perceived? "In ultimate reality, there is still something else present - that appearance is simply the mind itself."

9-17.text: If mind itself is illusory, At that time, what is seen by what? And the Protector of the World Has said, “Mind is not seen by mind.”
