9-17.en_text: But if the mind itself is just as illusion-like as everything else, then at that point, what is it that perceives what? And the Buddha himself, the Protector of the World, has said, "Mind cannot see mind."

9-18.text: A sword blade cannot cut itself, And it is just the same with mind. If you say it is like a lamp Illuminating its own nature,
9-18.en_text: Just as a sword's blade cannot cut itself, the mind cannot perceive itself either. "But," you might say, "it's like a lamp, which illuminates its own nature as well as everything else."

9-19.text: A lamp is not illuminated, For it is not obscured by darkness. “Unlike a crystal, blue does not Depend on something else for blueness.
9-19.en_text: A lamp isn't actually something that needs to be illuminated in the first place, since it was never obscured by darkness to begin with. "But unlike a crystal, which needs something else to appear blue, blue itself doesn't depend on anything else to be blue."

9-20.text: “Likewise, it’s seen some things depend On something else, and some do not.” A thing that is not blue itself Does not itself make itself blue.
9-20.en_text: "In the same way, some things are seen to depend on something else to exist, while other things aren't." But something that isn't blue to begin with can't make itself blue on its own either.

9-21.text: There is a consciousness that knows And says a lamp is luminous, But what is it that knows and says That mind is luminous itself?
9-21.en_text: There is ordinary awareness that recognizes and describes a lamp as being luminous. But what exactly is it that recognizes and describes the mind itself as being inherently luminous?

9-22.text: Whether it’s luminous or not, If it’s not seen by anything, Like the charms of a barren woman’s daughter, Even discussing it is pointless.
9-22.en_text: Whether the mind is luminous or not, if it can't actually be perceived by anything else, then discussing it at all is as pointless as discussing the charms of the imaginary daughter of a childless woman.

9-23.text: “If self-awareness doesn’t exist, Then how is consciousness remembered?” When something else is experienced, It is recalled from the connection, Like the venom of a rat.
9-23.en_text: "But if there's no such thing as self-awareness, then how could we ever remember a past experience of consciousness at all?" When something else was experienced at the same time, the memory arises through that connection - like remembering the sting of a rat's venomous bite through the pain that followed it.

9-24.text: “It’s seen by those with other conditions, So it illuminates itself.” When magic eye salve is applied, You see a vase but not the salve.
9-24.en_text: "But this self-awareness is perceived because of other supporting conditions, so it genuinely illuminates itself." Yet when magic eye ointment is applied, you see the vase in front of you, but never the ointment itself, even though it's what allows you to see.

9-25.text: How things are seen or heard or known Is not what is rebutted here. Here it’s the cause of suffering— The thought they’re true—that is refuted.
9-25.en_text: What is actually being challenged here isn't the ordinary way that things are seen, heard, or known. What's being challenged is the deeper cause of suffering - the mistaken belief that these things are ultimately, independently real.

9-26.text: If you think that illusions are neither Other than mind nor the same as it, If real, then how are they not other? If they’re not other, it is not real.
9-26.en_text: If you think illusions are neither the same as the mind that perceives them nor entirely different from it - if they were truly real, how could they not be different from mind? And if they aren't different from mind, then they can't be truly, independently real either.

9-27.text: What’s seen—illusion—is not true, And neither is the seer, mind. “Samsara must have a real basis, Otherwise it would be like space.”
9-27.en_text: What is seen - the illusion - isn't ultimately real, and neither is the mind that perceives it, ultimately real either. "But this whole cycle of rebirth must have some truly real basis, otherwise it would be just like empty space, with nothing happening at all."

9-28.text: How does being based upon the real Mean the unreal performs an action? That mind of yours, with no companion, Would be entirely alone.
9-28.en_text: But how would something being based on something "real" actually explain how something unreal could perform any real action? And besides, if your mind existed with no connection to anything else at all, it would be completely alone and isolated.

9-29.text: When mind is free of the apprehended, Then all become tathagatas. In that case, what’s the benefit Of thinking there is only mind?
9-29.en_text: If the mind became free of any perceived object altogether, then everyone would already be a fully enlightened buddha. In that case, what real benefit is there in insisting that only mind exists, and nothing else?

9-30.text: “But how does merely knowing that All is illusion stop afflictions? Illusionists may still feel lust For dreamlike lovers they create.”
9-30.en_text: "But how does merely knowing that everything is like an illusion actually stop negative emotions from arising? After all, even an illusionist might still feel desire for the dreamlike lover they themselves conjured up."

9-31.text: Their makers have not yet abandoned The imprints of afflictions toward Known objects, so when they see them, Their imprint of emptiness is weak.
9-31.en_text: That illusionist simply hasn't yet let go of the deep habitual tendency toward negative emotions regarding the kinds of things they perceive, so when they see them, their habit of recognizing emptiness is still too weak to override it.

9-32.text: Ingraining the imprint of emptiness Eliminates the imprint of things. By meditating, “Nothing exists,” It also is abandoned later.
9-32.en_text: By deeply cultivating the habit of recognizing emptiness, we gradually remove the older habit of seeing things as solid and real. And once we've trained ourselves to see that "nothing ultimately exists," even that very idea is eventually let go of as well.

9-33.text: When one says “Nothing exists,” the thing That’s being examined isn’t observed. Deprived of basis, how can nothing Remain before the mind?
9-33.en_text: When we say "nothing ultimately exists," the very thing being examined isn't found to exist independently in the first place. And once it has no basis to stand on at all, how could the idea of "nothing" itself remain fixed before the mind?

9-34.text: And then when neither thing nor nothing Remains before the mind, Because there is no other way, There is no focus—utter peace.
9-34.en_text: And when neither "something" nor "nothing" remains fixed before the mind any longer, since there's no other alternative left to grasp onto, the mind rests with nothing left to focus on at all - complete, genuine peace.

9-35.text: Just as a wish-fulfilling jewel And heaven tree fill every wish, The kayas of the victors appear Due to disciples and aspirations.
9-35.en_text: Just as a wish-fulfilling jewel or a wish-granting tree fulfills every request made of it, the buddhas' magnificent forms appear in the world because of the aspirations and needs of those who follow their path.

9-36.text: The builder of the garuda pillar Passed away after it was blessed, But it still neutralizes poisons And such long after he is gone.
9-36.en_text: The craftsman who built a certain protective pillar passed away soon after blessing it, and yet the pillar still continues to neutralize poison long after his death.

9-37.text: A bodhisattva, following The way of awakening, will build A victor’s pillar and pass to Nirvana, yet perform all deeds.
9-37.en_text: In just the same way, a bodhisattva who follows the path to enlightenment builds this kind of "protective pillar" and then passes into final peace - yet continues to accomplish beneficial deeds long afterward.

9-38.text: “How is it making offerings To one who has no mind bears fruit?” This has been taught to be the same, Whether they’re present or in nirvana.
9-38.en_text: "But how can making offerings to someone who no longer has a mind actually produce any real result?" This has been taught to work the very same way, whether the buddha is presently alive or has already passed into final peace.

9-39.text: There are results, according to scripture, Whether they’re relative or suchness, Just as there would be a result From a true buddha, for example.
9-39.en_text: According to the scriptures, real results occur whether we're speaking on the everyday level or the level of ultimate truth - just as, for example, there would still be a real result from making an offering to a living buddha.

9-40.text: “One can be freed by seeing the truths; Why bother seeing emptiness?” Because there’s no awakening Without this path, the scriptures teach.
9-40.en_text: "One can already be freed just by directly seeing the four truths of suffering - so why bother seeing emptiness as well?" Because, as the scriptures teach, there is no true enlightenment possible without following this particular path.

9-41.text: If the Great Vehicle is not proven, How is it that your scriptures are? “Because they’re proven to us both.” At first, they were not proven to you.
9-41.en_text: "If the Great Vehicle teachings aren't proven to be authentic, then how are your own scriptures proven to be authentic either?" "Because they're accepted as authentic by both of us." But they weren't accepted as authentic by you from the very start either.

9-42.text: The reasons for believing in them Are the same for the Great Vehicle too. If they’re true since two parties accept them, The Vedas and such would also be true.
9-42.en_text: The very same reasons you use to justify believing your scriptures apply equally well to the Great Vehicle teachings. And if something is true simply because two parties happen to agree on it, then even the ancient scriptures of the Brahmins would have to be considered true as well.

9-43.text: If it’s because the Great Vehicle Is in dispute, reject your own scriptures Since they’re contested by non-Buddhists, As are some you and others challenge.
9-43.en_text: If your objection is that the Great Vehicle is disputed by others, then you should reject your own scriptures too, since they are also disputed by non-Buddhists - just as certain teachings are disputed between you and other Buddhist schools as well.

9-44.text: The teachings’ root is bhikshuhood, But bhikshuhood is difficult. For those whose minds still have a focus, Reaching nirvana is difficult.
9-44.en_text: The very foundation of the teachings is the life of a fully ordained monastic, and that life is genuinely difficult to sustain. For minds still fixed on some object of focus, reaching lasting peace is difficult as well.

9-45.text: If one is freed just by discarding Afflictions, it’s immediate. Yet it is seen that karma has power Over those who do not have afflictions.
9-45.en_text: If someone is freed from suffering simply by letting go of their negative emotions, that liberation should happen right away. And yet we still see the power of past actions affecting even those who no longer have negative emotions.

9-46.text: If at that time, it’s definite That they do not have the cause, craving, Why don’t they have, just like delusion, The unafflicted craving too?
9-46.en_text: "If it's certain, at that point, that they no longer have the underlying cause - craving - then why don't they also lack the more subtle habitual tendency of craving, in the same way that even confusion itself must eventually be uprooted?"

9-47.text: Craving is due to the condition Of feeling, and they do have feeling. A mind that has a focus dwells On one thing or another.
9-47.en_text: Ordinary craving depends on the condition of feeling, and such people still do have feeling. A mind still focused on some object continues to dwell on one thing or another.

9-48.text: As with conception-free absorption, A mind that lacks in emptiness Might cease but will arise again, So meditate on emptiness.
9-48.en_text: Just as with a certain meditative state free of ordinary thought, a mind lacking a true realization of emptiness might come to a temporary stop, but it will eventually arise again - so it's essential to meditate on emptiness itself.

9-49.text: If you accept as the Buddha’s teachings The words included in the sutras, Don’t you accept the Great Vehicle Is mostly the same as your sutras?
9-49.en_text: If you accept as the Buddha's genuine teaching whatever words are found within your own scriptures, then don't you have to accept that the Great Vehicle scriptures are, for the most part, essentially the same as yours?

9-50.text: If all of them are flawed because A single one is not included, Then since one sutra is the same, Why aren’t they all the Buddha’s words?
9-50.en_text: And if you say all of the Great Vehicle teachings are flawed simply because a single one of your scriptures isn't included among them, then since at least one of your scriptures is essentially identical to ours, why wouldn't all of it also count as the Buddha's genuine teaching?

9-51.text: Just because you don’t understand The teachings Mahakashyapa And so forth did not truly fathom, Who says they’re not to be accepted?
9-51.en_text: Just because even a great disciple like Mahakashyapa and others weren't able to fully fathom these teachings, who's to say they shouldn't still be accepted as genuine?

9-52.text: Freed from extremes of greed and fear, To stay in samsara for the sake Of those who suffer due to delusion Is the result of emptiness.
9-52.en_text: Free from the extremes of both craving and fear, remaining within this cycle of rebirth for the sake of those who suffer through their own confusion - this is precisely the fruit of realizing emptiness.

9-53.text: The refutations of the position Of emptiness are not reasonable, So do not harbor any doubts, And meditate on emptiness.
9-53.en_text: The various objections raised against the view of emptiness don't hold up under real scrutiny. So don't hold onto any doubts, and go ahead and meditate on emptiness.

9-54.text: The remedy for the darkness of The cognitive and afflictive veils Is emptiness. Wouldn’t they who want Omniscience quickly cultivate it?
9-54.en_text: Emptiness is the true remedy for the darkness caused both by mistaken views and by negative emotions. So wouldn't anyone who genuinely seeks complete, all-knowing wisdom want to cultivate it as quickly as possible?

9-55.text: If fearfulness is born out of The things that produce suffering, Then why is it that emptiness, The cure for suffering, provokes dread?
9-55.en_text: If fear arises from the very things that actually cause suffering, then why does emptiness - which is the true cure for suffering - provoke fear instead?

9-56.text: If there existed any me, There could be fear of anything. But since no me exists at all, Who is there that could be afraid?
9-56.en_text: If there really were some fixed, independent "me," then there could be genuine reason to fear all sorts of things. But since no such fixed self actually exists at all, who exactly is left to be afraid?

9-57.text: Teeth and hair and nails aren’t me. Bones and blood are not me either. Mucus is not, and phlegm is not, And neither lymph nor pus is me.
9-57.en_text: Teeth, hair, and nails are not "me." Bones and blood are not "me" either. Mucus is not "me," and neither is phlegm, nor lymph, nor pus.

9-58.text: Fat is not me; sweat is not me; Nor are the lungs or liver me. Neither are the other organs. Feces and urine are not me.
9-58.en_text: Fat is not "me"; sweat is not "me"; neither are the lungs or liver "me," nor are any of the other internal organs. Feces and urine are not "me" either.

9-59.text: Muscles and skin and body heat And breath aren’t me. The orifices Are not me, or in any way Are the six consciousnesses either.
9-59.en_text: Muscle, skin, and body heat are not "me," nor is the breath. The body's openings are not "me," and none of the six types of sensory awareness are "me" either.

9-60.text: If the cognition of sound were permanent, Sound would be apprehended at all times. When there is nothing to be known, what knows? And why is it described as a cognition?
9-60.en_text: If the awareness that hears sound were something permanent and unchanging, it would have to be perceiving sound at all times. But when there's nothing there to be known, what exactly is doing the knowing? And why would we even call it "awareness" at that point?

9-61.text: If it is a cognition without knowing, It follows blocks of wood are cognition too. Thus it is certain there is no cognition When there is nothing present to be known.
9-61.en_text: If you say it's an awareness that isn't actually aware of anything, then a block of wood would have to count as a kind of awareness too. So it must be certain that there is simply no awareness present when there's nothing there to be known.

9-62.text: And if that very one knows visual form, At that time, why does it not also hear? If that’s because there is no sound nearby, Then there is no cognition of it either.
9-62.en_text: And if that very same awareness that perceives visual form is what also hears sound, then why doesn't it hear sound at the very same moment it sees form? If you say that's because there's no sound present at that moment, then in that case, there's no awareness of sound present either.

9-63.text: How can a nature apprehending sound Become the apprehension of a form? One may be thought of as both parent and child, But that is not an actuality.
9-63.en_text: How could something whose nature is to perceive sound also become the very thing that perceives visual form? One might think of a single person as both a parent and a child at once, but that doesn't reflect how things truly, independently exist.

9-64.text: For in this way, the sattva, rajas, and tamas Are not a child and not a parent either. So it is not perceived to be a nature Possessing apprehension of a sound.
9-64.en_text: In just the same way, the three basic qualities of nature that some philosophers describe - goodness, activity, and inertia - can't truly be both parent and child at once either. So this same awareness can't really be understood as something with a single, unified nature that perceives sound.

9-65.text: If like an actor, that itself is seen In different ways, then it’s not permanent. And if the different manners are just that, Then such a oneness is unprecedented.
9-65.en_text: If, like a skilled actor playing different roles, this awareness simply appears in different forms, then it isn't actually permanent and unchanging at all. And if these different appearances were all genuinely one and the same thing, then that kind of oneness would be entirely unprecedented and doesn't match anything we actually observe.

9-66.text: But if the different manners are not true, Do tell me, please, what its own nature is. “Just consciousness,” you say, then in that case, It follows that all people would be one.
9-66.en_text: But if you say these different appearances aren't ultimately true at all, then please tell me: what exactly is this awareness's own true nature? If you say, "It's simply consciousness itself, plain and undifferentiated," then it would follow that all people are ultimately just one single thing.

9-67.text: The sentient and nonsentient would be one As well, since their existence is the same. When the particulars are also false, What basis is there for similarity?
9-67.en_text: It would even follow that living, sentient things and lifeless, non-sentient things are ultimately the same thing too, since their basic existence would be identical in this view. And once you say that their individual differences aren't ultimately real, what basis is left for claiming they're even similar to one another?

9-68.text: Nor can what is nonsentient be the self, Because it has no mind, like jugs and such. But if it knows from being conjoined with mind, It follows the nonsentient perishes.
9-68.en_text: Something that is non-sentient obviously cannot be a "self," since it has no mind of its own, just like a clay jug. But if you say it becomes aware simply by being joined together with mind, then it would follow that this non-sentient thing ceases to exist as such the moment it's joined with mind.

9-69.text: If there is no change in the self, What does cognition do for it? In this way, you have made unknowing And inert space into the self.
9-69.en_text: If there's truly no change at all in this fixed self, then what could awareness possibly do for it or add to it? In this way, you've effectively turned the supposed "self" into something as unaware and inert as empty space.

9-70.text: “With no self, the relationship Of act and result would make no sense. One perishes when the act is done, So whose act would it be?” you ask.
9-70.en_text: "But without a fixed self, the whole relationship between an action and its result would make no sense at all. Since the person who acts is gone the moment the act is finished, whose action would it even be?" you ask.

9-71.text: It’s proven to us both the bases Of act and result are separate And that the self does not act on them. Is this not pointless to debate?
9-71.en_text: We both already agree that the basis for the action and the basis for its later result are genuinely distinct from one another in time, and that no fixed, unchanging self is what actually performs or receives them. So isn't this whole debate ultimately beside the point?

9-72.text: It cannot possibly be seen That one with the cause would have the result. The actor and the reaper are taught Based on a single continuum.
9-72.en_text: It's simply not possible to observe a case where the very same person who creates the cause is also, at that same instant, the one who experiences the result. Instead, the relationship between someone who acts and someone who later experiences the result is explained simply in terms of belonging to a single, continuous stream of moments.

9-73.text: The past and future minds are not A me, since they do not exist. If the arisen mind is me, When it is gone, the me is no longer.
9-73.en_text: A past moment of mind and a future moment of mind are not truly "me," since neither one actually exists right now. And if the mind that has just arisen in this very moment were truly "me," then once that moment has passed, this "me" would no longer exist either.

9-74.text: Just as when one dissects the trunk Of a banana tree, there’s nothing, When scrutinized analytically, The me as well is nothing true.
9-74.en_text: Just as when you cut apart the trunk of a banana tree layer by layer, you find nothing solid at its core, in exactly the same way, when carefully examined and analyzed, this "me" turns out to have no real, independent existence either.

9-75.text: “If sentient beings do not exist, For whom should one arouse compassion?” For those projected by delusion, Whom we accept for the sake of results.
9-75.en_text: "But if sentient beings don't ultimately exist at all, then for whom should we even bother cultivating compassion?" For those beings who appear through the workings of confusion - beings we still recognize and accept for the sake of achieving real, beneficial results.

9-76.text: “Whose is the fruit if there are no beings?” That’s true; the wish is from delusion. For the sake of quelling suffering, Don’t block delusion about the result.
9-76.en_text: "But whose result would that compassion even bring about, if there are no truly existing beings to receive it?" That's true - the wish itself does arise out of this same underlying confusion. But for the sake of actually ending suffering, don't reject this kind of confusion when it comes to caring about the outcome.

9-77.text: Delusions of a self increase The cause of suffering—the ego. “But there’s no stopping that,” you say. To cultivate selflessness is supreme.
9-77.en_text: This same confused clinging to a fixed self only increases the very root cause of suffering - our attachment to "me." "But," you might say, "there's simply no way to stop that." Yet cultivating a clear understanding of selflessness is, in fact, the very best way to do exactly that.

9-78.text: The body’s not the feet or calves, Nor are the thighs or hips the body. It’s not the belly or the back; Neither is it the chest or arms.
9-78.en_text: The body isn't the feet or the calves, and it isn't the thighs or the hips either. It isn't the stomach or the back, and it isn't the chest or the arms.

9-79.text: It’s not the ribs, hands, armpits, shoulders, And it is not the organs either. The head and throat are not the body, So what, then, is the body here?
9-79.en_text: It isn't the ribs, the hands, the armpits, or the shoulders, and it isn't any of the internal organs either. The head and throat are not the body - so then, what exactly is "the body" here, if not simply a label for all these parts together?

9-80.text: Now if the body were to dwell Partially in all of them, Its parts would thus dwell in those parts, But where would it reside itself?
9-80.en_text: Now, if the body were said to exist only partially within each of these different parts, then each part would simply contain its own portion of itself - so where, in that case, would the body as a whole actually reside on its own?

9-81.text: But if the “body,” single and entire Is present in the hands and other members, However many parts there are, the hands and all the rest, You’ll find an equal quantity of “bodies.”
9-81.en_text: But if a single, complete "body" were fully present in the hands and every other part, then since there are many parts - hands and all the rest - you'd end up with just as many separate "bodies" as there are parts.

9-82.text: If “body” is not outside or within its parts, How is it, then, residing in its members? And since it is not other than its parts, How can you say that it exists at all?
9-82.en_text: If "body" doesn't exist outside its parts or within any single part, then how could it possibly reside among its parts at all? And since it isn't something separate from its parts, how can you say it exists as its own real thing?

9-83.text: Thus there is no “body.” It is through illusion, With regard to hands and other parts, that “body” as a notion is conceived— Just as on account of its specific shape A pile of stones is taken for a man.
9-83.en_text: So there really is no independent "body." It's simply through a kind of illusion that we look at hands and other parts arranged together and form the idea of "a body" - just as a pile of stones, arranged in a certain shape, might be mistaken for a person.

9-84.en_text: As long as the right conditions come together, that pile of stones will appear to be a person. In the very same way, as long as all the parts are present together, a "body" will appear to be there too.

9-85.text: Likewise, since it is a group of fingers, The hand itself does not exist as such. And so it is with fingers, made of joints— And joints themselves consist of many parts.
9-85.en_text: In the same way, since a hand is really just a collection of fingers, the hand itself has no independent existence either. And the fingers themselves are made of joints, and each joint is made up of still smaller parts.

9-86.text: These parts themselves will break down into particles, And particles divide according to direction. These fragments, too, lack partless parts; they are like space. Thus even particles have no existence.
9-86.en_text: Those smaller parts break down further into tiny particles, and even those particles can be divided according to direction and side. These fragments, too, have no truly partless core - they're just like empty space. So in the end, even particles have no independent existence.

9-87.text: All form, therefore, is like a dream, And who will be attached to it, who thus investigates? The body, in this way, has no existence; What, therefore, is male and what is female?
9-87.en_text: All physical form, then, is like something seen in a dream - so who, upon investigating this closely, would remain attached to it? The body, in this way, has no independent existence at all - so what, then, is truly "male" and what is truly "female"?

9-88.text: If suffering itself is truly real, Why is joy not altogether quenched thereby? If pleasure’s real, then why will pleasant tastes Not comfort and amuse a man in agony?
9-88.en_text: If suffering itself were truly, independently real, why wouldn't it be completely wiped out by joy? And if pleasure were truly real in the same way, why wouldn't a pleasant taste bring comfort and delight to someone in the depths of agony?

9-90.text: Perhaps you say that only subtle pain remains, Its grosser form has now been overmastered— Or rather it is felt as “mere pleasure.” But what is subtle still remains itself.
9-90.en_text: Perhaps you'll say that only a subtler form of the pain remains, its more obvious form simply overpowered by something else - or that it's now experienced as mere pleasure instead. But even this "subtle" version is still just what it always was.

9-91.en_text: And if discomfort simply fails to appear because its opposite happens to be present at the time, then isn't the whole claim that "this is a feeling" really nothing more than a label we've mentally added on?

9-92.en_text: Since this is so, the true remedy for suffering is meditation and careful examination of exactly this kind. This kind of focused reflection is, in truth, the very food and sustenance of serious meditators.

9-93.text: If between the sense power and a thing There is a space, how will the two terms meet? And if there is no space, they form a unity, And therefore what is it that meets with what?
9-93.en_text: If there's a gap between a sense faculty and its object, how could the two of them ever actually meet? And if there's no gap at all between them, then they'd simply be one and the same thing - so what, in that case, is even meeting what?

9-94.text: No penetration can there be of particle by particle, For they are both the same in lacking volume. But if they do not penetrate, they do not merge; And if they do not merge, there’s no encounter.
9-94.en_text: One tiny particle cannot truly penetrate into another, since both are equally without any real volume of their own. But if they can't penetrate one another, they can't truly merge either - and if they can't merge, there's no real encounter between them at all.

9-95.en_text: How, then, could anyone accept that something with no parts at all could ever be said to "meet" anything else? Show me, if you've ever actually observed it, a genuine case of two truly partless things making contact.
